The Holy Roman Empire was a political entity in Western, Central, and Southern Europe that developed during the Early Middle Ages and continued until its dissolution in 1806 during the Napoleonic Wars. From the accession of Otto I in 962 until the twelfth century, the Empire was the most powerful monarchy in Europe. It has been described as the most powerful European state of the Middle Ages. The functioning of government depended on the harmonic cooperation between monarch and vassals but this harmony was disturbed during the Salian period. The empire reached the apex of territorial expansion and power under the House of Hohenstaufen in the mid-thirteenth century, but overextending led to partial collapse.

The area now called England was first inhabited by modern humans during the Upper Paleolithic period, but takes its name from the Angles, a Germanic tribe deriving its name from the Anglia peninsula, who settled during the 5th and 6th centuries. England became a unified state in the 10th century and has had a significant cultural and legal impact on the wider world since the Age of Discovery, which began during the 15th century.

A more accurate name for the culture is Baltic Finns. This culture represents the following ethnoses of Aestians, Finns, Ingrians, Karelians, Livonians, Tavastians, Vepsians and Votians. In the High Middle Ages, the Aestians were the most active. They raided the Norsemens together with other Balts and Finns, defended themselves against the Novgorod Principality. The Livonians were under the influence of Polatsk. Votians in 1069 together with Polatsk raided Novgorod. According to one version, the Kylfingars consisted of the Votians. The Vepsians and Ingrians were under the influence of Novgorod. And over time they became the core of the Novgorod ethnos. The Karelians were the most technologically advanced on the territory of modern Finland thanks to trade and interaction with Novgorod. Some Karelians paid tribute to Novgorod, but in 1100 they were not part of Novgorod. In 1143 the Karelians raided Tavastians, in 1187 the Karelians pillaged Swedish Sigtuna. There are no written reports about the Finns, but most likely they were colonized and Christianized by Sweden. Over time, this ethnos gave the name to Finland.

The Georgians, or Kartvelians are a nation and indigenous Caucasian ethnic group native to Georgia and the South Caucasus. Georgians arose from Colchian and Iberian civilizations of classical antiquity. Colchis was interconnected with the Hellenic world, whereas Iberia was influenced by the Persian Achaemenid Empire until it was conquered by Alexander the Great. In the early 4th century, the Georgians became one of the first to embrace Christianity and now the majority of Georgians are Orthodox Christians, with most following their national autocephalous Georgian Orthodox Church, although there are small Georgian Catholic and Muslim communities, as well as a significant number who are irreligious.

The Kingdom of Hungary was a monarchy in Central Europe that existed for nearly a millennium, from the Middle Ages into the 20th century. The Principality of Hungary emerged as a Christian kingdom upon the coronation of the first king Stephen I at Esztergom around the year 1000; his family (the Árpád dynasty) led the monarchy for 300 years. By the 12th century, the kingdom became a European middle power within the Western world.

Italians are a Romance-speaking ethnic group native to the Italian geographical region and its neighboring insular territories. Italians share a common culture, history, ancestry and language. Their predecessors vary regionally, but include the ancient Greeks in Magna Graecia, the Etruscans in northern Italy and, most notably, the Romans in central Italy, who helped create and evolved into the modern Italian identity. Legally, Italian nationals are citizens of Italy, regardless of ancestry or nation of residence and may be distinguished from ethnic Italians in general or from people of Italian descent without Italian citizenship and ethnic Italians living in territories adjacent to the Italian peninsula without Italian citizenship. The Latin equivalent of the term Italian had been in use for natives of the geographical region since antiquity.

The Turkic peoples are a collection of diverse ethnic groups of West, Central, East, and North Asia as well as parts of Europe, who speak Turkic languages. According to most historians and linguists, the Proto-Turkic speakers originated in the Central-East Asia region, potentially in a region stretching from Eastern Mongolia to Tuva, or close to the homeland of early Mongolic and Tungusic speakers in Northeast Asia. The exact time and location for the origin of the proto-Turkic language is not known yet. Initially, Proto-Turkic speakers were potentially both hunter-gatherers and farmers, as the Proto-Turkic subsistence strategy included an agricultural component, a tradition that ultimately went back to the origin of millet agriculture in Northeast China, but later became nomadic pastoralists. Medieval Turkic groups exhibited a wide range of both West-Eurasian and East Asian physical appearances and genetic origins, in part through long-term contact with neighboring peoples such as Iranian, Mongolic, Tocharians, Yeniseian people, and others

Some researchers believe that the Kryvichs came from the lands of modern Poland or Germany. The Kryvichs left many archaeological monuments, such as the remnants of agricultural settlements with traces of ironworks, jeweler's art, blacksmith's work and other handicrafts; long burial mounds of the 6th to 9th centuries with cremated bodies; burial mounds of rich warriors with weapons; sets of distinctive jewelry. The Kryvichs are a largest Eastern European tribal union. It consisted mainly of Slavic and Baltic tribes. It also had Finns and Normans components. Over time, the culture divided into three branches: Połack (Polatsk), Smolensk and Pskov. In the second half of the 10th century the Kryvichs formed the Połack State, which existed for more than 500 years, from the second half of the 13th century as an autonomy within Lithuania. The Kryvichs greatly influenced on the forming of the Belarusian ethnos and the existence of the state. Nowadays Kryvichs are part of the Belarusian and Russian ethnoses. This ethnos also includes the Radimichs, as their history is closely intertwined with the Kryvichs. Over time, the synthesis of Kryvichs and Radimichs was named Belarussians. Over time, this name spread to modern Belarus.

In the 11th century, the mainland southern sicilian powers were hiring Norman mercenaries, who were Christian descendants of the Vikings; it was the Normans under Roger I (of the Hauteville dynasty) who conquered Sicily from the Muslims over a period of thirty years until finally controlling the entire island by 1091 as the County of Sicily. In 1130, Roger II founded the Norman Kingdom of Sicily as an independent state with its own Parliament, language, schooling, army and currency, while the Sicilian culture evolved distinct traditions, clothing, linguistic changes, cuisine and customs not found in mainland Italy.

The Novgorod principality began to form in the 9th century and existed until 1478. During this time the fourth Eastern Slavic ethnos was formed, which no longer exists. The Balto-Slavic ethnoses consisted of the Ilmen Slavs and Kryviches. But the basis of the population were Finnish tribes Izhorians, Karelians, Vepsians, Votians and other. Relations between ethnic groups evolved from simple tribute collection to full integration into the society. The Finns were assimilated and Slavicized. But the Finns had played an important role in the republic from the beginning and held quite a high position. For example, the name of the famous Novgorodian river pirates and mercenaries, Ushkuyniks, is a Finnish word that means boat, Ushkuyniks consisted of Slavs and Finns. Besides, the Ushkuyniks were a noble social class. In 1479, the Novgorod Republic was conquered and its ethnos partly exterminated, partly assimilated.

Following the Arab conquest of the Sasanian Empire in the medieval times, the Arab caliphates established their rule over the region for the next several centuries, during which the long process of the Islamization of Persia took place. A series of Muslim Persian kingdoms were later established on the fringes of the declining Abbasid Caliphate, including that of the ninth-century Samanids, under the reign of whom the Persian language was used officially for the first time in two centuries.

The history of human activity on Polish soil dates to circa 10,000 BC. Culturally diverse throughout late antiquity, the region became inhabited by tribal Polans who gave Poland its name in the early medieval period. The establishment of statehood in 966 coincided with a pagan ruler of the Polans converting to Christianity under the auspices of the Roman Church. The Kingdom of Poland emerged in 1025 and in 1569 cemented its longstanding association with Lithuania, thus forming the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth. It was one of the largest great powers of Europe at the time, with a uniquely liberal political system that adopted Europe's first modern constitution in 1791.

In 1100, the area that would become Portugal was a feudal County of Portugal under the rule of Henry, Count of Portugal, as a vassal of the Kingdom of León. The territory was part of the larger Reconquista, the Christian reconquest of the Iberian Peninsula from Muslim rule, and was not yet an independent kingdom.

Confusion with the term Rus. The term originally had 3 different definitions. First, Rus as a state. All ethnicities belonging to Rus can be called Rus. Second, Rus as ethnos which has created the state and from which the name of the state has gone. Russian scientist Boris Rybakov has analyzed all chronicles of the Rus period and has defined on what territory the population considered itself as Rus, and on what opposed itself to Rus. These data were correlated with archaeological cultures. Initially ethnoses of Severians and Polans considered themselves as Rus. In the 13th century Volhynians and White Croats began to consider themselves as Rus. But in the 13th century Rus as a state in most of the territory of the former empire stopped to exist. In the 13th-14th centuries, the third definition of Rus starts to use widely. Rus as an Orthodox person. In the religious meaning of an Orthodox person, the term extends to the territory of modern Belarus and Russia. Later, the term changed its meaning many times and had many meanings at the same time. In this mod only ethnoses of Severians and Polans are considered as Rus. They are the core of this civilization in the timeline.

In the centuries after the departure of the Romans from Britain, there were four groups within the borders of what is now Scotland. In the east were the Picts, with kingdoms between the river Forth and Shetland. In the late 6th century the dominant force was the Kingdom of Fortriu, whose lands were centred on Strathearn and Menteith and who raided along the eastern coast into modern England. In the west were the Gaelic (Goidelic)-speaking people of Dál Riata with their royal fortress at Dunadd in Argyll, with close links with the island of Ireland, from whom comes the name Scots. In the south was the British (Brythonic) Kingdom of Strathclyde, descendants of the peoples of the Roman influenced kingdoms of Hen Ogledd (Old north), often named Alt Clut, the Brythonic name for their capital at Dumbarton Rock. Finally, there were the English or Angles, Germanic invaders who had overrun much of southern Britain and held the Kingdom of Bernicia, in the south-east

The first Serb states, Raška and Duklja, were formed chiefly under the Vlastimirović and Vojislavljević dynasties respectively. The other Serb-inhabited lands, or principalities, that were mentioned included the countries of Paganija, Zahumlje, Travunija. With the decline of the Serbian state of Duklja in the late 11th century, Raška separated from it and replaced it as the most powerful Serbian state. Prince Stefan Nemanja conquered the neighbouring territories of Kosovo, Duklja and Zachlumia. The Nemanjić dynasty ruled over Serbia until the 14th century. Nemanja's older son, Stefan Nemanjić, became Serbia's first recognized king, while his younger son, Rastko, founded the Serbian Orthodox Church in the year 1219, and became known as Saint Sava after his death. Parts of modern-day Montenegro, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and central Serbia would come under the control of Nemanjić.

The Nordic countries are a geographical and cultural region in Northern Europe and the North Atlantic. It includes the sovereign states of Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway and Sweden; the autonomous territories of the Faroe Islands and Greenland; and the autonomous region of Åland. The Nordic countries have much in common in their way of life, history, religion and social structure. They have a long history of political unions and other close relations but do not form a singular entity today.

The Suzdalians were the people and the principality of Vladimir-Suzdal, a medieval state in northeast Rus' that emerged after the decline of Kievan Rus. Ruled by a branch of the Rurik dynasty, the principality centered around cities like Suzdal and Vladimir, shifting power northwards from Kiev during the 12th century.

The Franks were a group of Germanic peoples whose name was first mentioned in 3rd-century Roman sources, and associated with tribes between the Lower Rhine and the Ems River, on the edge of the Roman Empire. Later the term was associated with Romanized Germanic dynasties within the collapsing Western Roman Empire, who eventually commanded the whole region between the rivers Loire and Rhine. They imposed power over many other post-Roman kingdoms and Germanic peoples. Beginning with Charlemagne in 800, Frankish rulers were given recognition by the Catholic Church as successors to the old rulers of the Western Roman Empire.

On the territory of modern Volhynia and Galicia in the 7-8th centuries lived the tribes of Volhynians and White Croats. In the 10th century, the region was united by the Volhynian Duchy, which was part of the Rus state. In the 11th century, the Principality of Galicia began to form on the territory of the White Croats. In 1100 the locals didn't consider themselves Ruthenians yet, they pay tribute to Rus. But after the invasion of the Golden Horde into Rus in 1240 and the collapse of this proto-empire. The ruling dynasty of Rus was able to survive on the territory of Volhynia and Galicia, then to create Ruthenian Kingdom. From this point on, the local population begins to consider themselves Ruthenians, until now. In 1349 Ruthenian Kingdom will stop to exist with death of the last member of a dynasty. In the following centuries the Ruthenians were part of different states. Nowadays the Ruthenians are part of the Ukrainian nation.

A distinct Welsh culture emerged among the Celtic Britons after the Roman withdrawal from Britain in the 5th century, and Wales was briefly united under Gruffydd ap Llywelyn in 1055. After over 200 years of war, the conquest of Wales by King Edward I of England was completed by 1283, though Owain Glyndŵr led the Welsh Revolt against English rule in the early 15th century, and briefly re-established an independent Welsh state with its own national parliament. In the 16th century the whole of Wales was annexed by England and incorporated within the English legal system under the Laws in Wales Acts 1535 and 1542.

By the year 1100, Tageldit n Isiwan existed as a fiercely independent Berber Chiefdom centered around the ancient Aghurmi Oasis in the harsh Western Desert. Geographically isolated between the distant markets of Awilja to the west and al-Fayyum to the east, the oasis functioned as a vital, highly defensible stepping stone for trans-Saharan caravans. Its inhabitants, speaking a distinct Amazigh dialect, relied on the abundant local date palms, olive groves, and freshwater springs to sustain their economy and trade. Unlike the coastal empires, the leaders of Isiwan avoided large-scale pitched battles, instead utilizing their deep knowledge of the treacherous desert terrain to deter potential invaders. The military force of the oasis was relatively small but highly adapted, consisting of lightly armed tribal infantry and skirmishers who could strike quickly from the dunes. Though technically dwelling in the shadow of the powerful Fatimid Caliphate in Egypt, the sheer unforgiving nature of the surrounding desert granted the principality de facto autonomy. Thus, Tageldit n Isiwan remained a resilient, secluded sanctuary of traditional Berber culture, fiercely guarding its independence amidst the shifting sands of North Africa..

Estonia in the 1100-1200 AD was characterized by a decentralized political landscape. The Estonian people, primarily of Finno-Ugric descent, inhabited a land of dense forests, fertile plains, and a coastline dotted with small ports. The society was organized into various tribes or clans, each led by chieftains or elders. These tribes engaged in agriculture, fishing, and trading activities, forming the backbone of the economy. The Estonians were skilled craftsmen, known for their expertise in metalwork, woodworking, and textile production. Despite their decentralized structure, the Estonian tribes often united under a common cause to defend against external threats. They faced frequent raids from neighboring powers, such as the Swedes, Danes, Russians and Germans, who sought to expand their influence into the Baltic region. By the late 12th century, the influence of Christianity began to permeate Estonia through trade and missionary activities. However, the conversion process was gradual and met with resistance from some pagan factions. Overall, Estonia in the 1100-1200 AD was a land of diverse cultures, where tribal identities intersected with emerging political dynamics, shaping the course of its history.

In the year 1100, the Beylik of Ahlat is a rapidly rising Turkoman principality centered around the strategic city of Ahlat on the northwestern shores of Lake Van and the city of Van on the eastern shore. The faction is fiercely led by its founder, Sökmen el-Kutbî, a brilliant former Seljuk slave-commander who has successfully carved out his own domain in the rugged Armenian highlands. He is supported by his capable sons, Ibrahim and Ahmad, who stand ready to secure their father's hard-won legacy and expand the family's dynastic power. Ruling over a diverse, predominantly Christian population from their majestic lakeside stronghold, the Ahlatşahs act as a heavy military bulwark for the broader Seljuk world. Their armies rely heavily on traditional Seljuk military doctrines, fielding well-armored Turkoman cavalry and disciplined horse archers perfectly suited for campaigns in the mountainous terrain. Geopolitically, they are surrounded by ambitious neighbors, constantly vying for dominance against rival Turkoman warlords like the Dilmacids to the south and the Saltukids to the north. Marching beneath a striking marine-blue banner adorned with a golden geometric star, the Ahlatşahlar stand poised to transform their fledgling border state into a dominant regional empire..

By the year 1100, the Almoravid Empire had reached the absolute zenith of its military and political power under the legendary leadership of Yusuf ibn Tashfin. Originating as a fundamentalist Sanhaja Berber movement from the deep Sahara, they had successfully forged a massive transcontinental domain stretching from the fringes of Senegal to the heart of the Iberian Peninsula. In Al-Andalus, they had recently dismantled the fragmented and decadent Muslim Taifa kingdoms, uniting the region under their strict, puritanical interpretation of Maliki Sunni Islam. Their formidable armies, famously characterized by veil-wearing desert warriors and disciplined infantry phalanxes, posed an existential threat to the advancing Christian kingdoms of northern Iberia. Back in North Africa, their newly founded capital of Marrakech served as the bustling, austere nerve center of an empire fueled by the lucrative trans-Saharan gold trade. Despite their overwhelming military supremacy, they remained culturally isolated from the cosmopolitan traditions of the cities they conquered, enforcing a rigid societal order that often alienated the local urban elites. Thus, at the dawn of the 12th century, the Almoravids stood as an unstoppable, desert-born juggernaut that had radically reshaped the geopolitical and religious landscape of both the Maghreb and the Mediterranean.

By the year 1100, the kingdoms of Aragon and Pamplona were temporarily united under the rule of King Peter I, operating as a formidable Christian power in the Pyrenees. Originally starting as small, isolated mountainous enclaves, both realms had spent the preceding centuries fighting for survival against the dominant Islamic states of Al-Andalus to their south. Pamplona had previously reached a golden age under Sancho the Great in the early eleventh century, but severe dynastic infighting led to its political fracturing and its eventual absorption by the rising Kingdom of Aragon in 1076. Up until the turn of the century, this combined Aragonese-Navarrese state faced the continuous challenge of expanding its borders southward into the prosperous Ebro Valley while fending off the hegemonic ambitions of the neighboring Kingdom of Castile. Looking ahead, the immediate future promised significant military triumphs, culminating in the crucial conquest of the major Islamic stronghold of Zaragoza in 1118. However, this united Pyrenean powerhouse was destined to fracture permanently following the death of the heirless King Alfonso the Battler in 1134. Upon his death, Pamplona broke away to regain its independence as the Kingdom of Navarre, eventually finding itself geographically landlocked and politically overshadowed by its larger neighbors. Meanwhile, the Kingdom of Aragon would secure a monumental dynastic marriage with the County of Barcelona in 1137, officially birthing the Crown of Aragon and permanently transforming the inland realm into a sprawling Mediterranean empire..

In the year 1100, the Principality of Vahka was an emerging, fiercely independent Armenian mountain realm ruled by Constantine I of the Rubenid dynasty. Having recently captured the strategic fortress of Vahka from Byzantine control, the Rubenids transformed it into the impregnable heart of their expanding territory. They held the proud title Lords of the Mountains, relying on a rugged network of minor nobles and exiled knights rather than the wealthy plains cities. From their high vantage points in the Taurus Mountains, they controlled crucial passes connecting the Anatolian plateau to the Mediterranean coast. Geopolitically, the principality was surrounded by formidable rivals, forcing Constantine to carefully navigate tensions between Seljuk Turks, hostile Byzantines, and newly arrived Crusaders. Despite these imminent threats, the Rubenids skillfully utilized their harsh terrain and tactical alliances to maintain strict autonomy. This pivotal era laid the resilient, militaristic foundation that would eventually allow the dynasty to descend from the peaks and establish the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia..

By the year 1100, the Banu Athbaj occupied a uniquely powerful and complex geopolitical position as the wealthy kingmakers of the North African steppes. Instead of remaining aligned with their Bedouin cousins, they forged a cynical but highly lucrative alliance with the sedentary Hammadid dynasty. Heavily bribed with gold, weapons, and prime grazing lands in the defensible Aurès mountains around Khanshala, they effectively served as the dynasty's southern shield. This alliance came at a steep cost, as Banu Athbaj turned their weapons against the Banu Zughba, driving them westward and igniting a bitter blood feud. Meanwhile, they maintained a tense, cold-war rivalry with the arrogant Banu Riyah in the east, refusing to submit to any claims of tribal supremacy. Sitting securely in their mountain strongholds, the tribe enjoyed immense wealth from their sedentary paymasters while remaining militarily formidable. Ultimately, this delicate balancing act left them with a monumental strategic choice: remain loyal mercenaries to the Hammadids, or eventually betray the city-dwellers to conquer the region for themselves..

By the year 1100, the Banu Hilal bedouin tribes faced significant geopolitical and environmental challenges after their massive migration into North Africa. Having shattered the Zirid dynasty's centralized power decades earlier, they now struggled to consolidate their own fragmented tribal territories across the Maghreb. Their traditional nomadic lifestyle created constant friction with the indigenous sedentary Berber populations, leading to ongoing skirmishes over agricultural lands and water resources. Furthermore, internal rivalries between the main Hilalian sub-tribes, such as the Riyyah and Zughba, prevented the formation of a unified political front. They also had to navigate shifting economic realities, as their mass pastoralism disrupted established trans-Saharan trade routes and local agricultural economies. To the west, the formidable and expanding Almoravid Empire presented a severe military threat that strictly limited any further Hilalian expansion. Ultimately, navigating this complex web of inter-tribal warfare, Berber resistance, and imperial pressure defined the precarious existence of the Banu Hilal at the dawn of the twelfth century..

By the year 1100, the ancient and prestigious Banu Kalb tribe found themselves navigating an increasingly fractured and volatile political landscape across the Syrian Desert. Once the supreme tribal powerbrokers of the early Islamic era, their absolute political dominance had waned, yet they remained a formidable military presence across the vast steppe. The recent arrival of the Crusaders in the Levant and the devastating fall of Jerusalem in 1099 had plunged the entire region into unprecedented geopolitical chaos. Caught between the encroaching European knights to the west and the fierce rivalries of the Turkish Seljuk warlords in Damascus and Aleppo, the tribe was forced to adapt rapidly. They anchored their enduring power across a wide geographical network, projecting influence from their deep-desert sanctuary of Dumat al-Jandal, through the central oasis of Tadmur, and up to the strategic northern outpost of Shaizar. Operating from these vital strongholds, they leveraged their unrivaled mastery of the harsh environment to act as indispensable, fiercely independent light cavalry mercenaries for both the Seljuks and the Fatimids. Ultimately, the Banu Kalb in 1100 represented a proud nomadic society fiercely struggling to maintain its autonomy and ancestral territory amidst the apocalyptic clash of foreign empires.

In the year 1100, the Imarat of Banu Khazrun stood as a tremendously wealthy and heavily fortified Sunni city-state centered around the coastal metropolis of Tripoli. The ruling dynasty originally descended from the Berber Zenata tribes, but by this time, they had become fully urbanized and embraced a Mediterranean culture. Their survival relied entirely on massive city walls and professional guards to withstand the constant raids from the nomadic Banu Sulaym bedouins to the east. To the south, they also faced bitter ideological and military resistance from the puritanical Ibadi confederations hidden within the Sahara and the Nafusa Mountains. Despite these constant threats, the emirate flourished economically through its strict control over lucrative maritime trade routes and vital desert caravans. To project their power and religious orthodoxy, the rulers displayed magnificent black and gold banners, signaling their allegiance to the Sunni Caliph in Baghdad. Behind their towering walls, the emirs and their aristocratic wives lived an isolated palace life of luxury, completely shielded from the harsh desert reality outside..

By the year 1100, Dawlat Banu Khurasan stood as a prosperous and fiercely independent urban city-state centered around the heavily fortified metropolis of Tunis. Ruled by the shrewd Wali Abd al-Aziz, this civilized realm represented a beacon of administrative order in stark contrast to the surrounding tribal chaos. However, the city-state found itself geopolitically isolated, constantly threatened by the massive Banu Hilal nomad confederations that dominated the southern plains. To guarantee its survival and protect its vital water supply, Tunis relied heavily on the garrisoned southern mountain fortress of Zaghwan. This strategic chokepoint acted as the ultimate defensive buffer, preventing the sweeping Bedouin cavalry from reaching the vulnerable coastal heartlands. Despite these existential threats from the inland steppes, the lucrative maritime trade flowing through northern coastal domains like Banzart kept the state's treasury overflowing. Ultimately, Dawlat Banu Khurasan navigated a delicate daily balance between leveraging its immense economic wealth and maintaining impenetrable defenses against the encroaching nomadic tides..

In the year 1100, the Imarat Bani Mazyad stands as a remarkably wealthy and powerful Shiite Bedouin state in central Iraq. Ruled by the shrewd Amir Sadaqa ibn Mansur, the faction represents a unique hybrid of nomadic heritage and urban sophistication. The Mazyadids have firmly established their military and political dominance over rival Arab tribes, such as the recently subjugated Banu Khafaja. Although deeply connected to the ancient religious center of Kufa, the Amir has focused his true military might on a massive encamped settlement nearby. This strategic stronghold, which will soon be fortified with stone walls and officially named Al-Hillah, serves as the impregnable heart of their realm. Surrounded by the vast agricultural wealth of the Euphrates canals, Sadaqa's forces boast thousands of elite, lightly armored cavalrymen who fight under green banners bearing the Zulfiqar sword. Consequently, Imarat Bani Mazyad acts as a formidable Arab counterweight to both the Abbasid Caliph in Baghdad and the encroaching Turkish Seljuk empires..

By the year 1100, the Banu Tayy were a powerful and fiercely independent Bedouin confederation operating across a vast geographical area from Najd to southern Syria. Unlike other tribes that settled and integrated into local power structures, they maintained their nomadic mobility and refused to permanently submit to any single empire. Their influence stemmed from a pragmatic and often ruthless diplomacy, constantly playing the Fatimids, Seljuks, Byzantines, and newly arrived Crusaders against one another. This strategic independence allowed them to dominate the harsh desert regions and control vital infrastructure, including the lucrative Hajj pilgrimage routes and Red Sea caravan paths.Because neither the Fatimid Caliphate nor the Crusader states could project permanent military power into the deep desert, they were forced to constantly negotiate with and bribe the tribe's leaders. Ultimately, their ability to dictate terms to regional superpowers ensured that the Banu Tayy remained an unpredictable and formidable force throughout the shifting geopolitical landscape of the twelfth-century.

By the year 1100, the County of Barcelona was the dominant power among the Catalan counties, led by the ambitious Count Ramon Berenguer III. Originally established in the eighth century as a Carolingian buffer state against Moorish expansion, it had spent the previous centuries slowly asserting its complete autonomy from a weakened Frankish crown. Up until this point, the county's primary existential challenge had been surviving relentless military pressure from the Islamic states of Al-Andalus to the south. This struggle was epitomized by the devastating sack of Barcelona by the Moorish commander Al-Mansur in 985, an event that pushed the county to formally sever its reliance on the French kings. Internally, the counts of Barcelona also had to continuously subdue rebellious local nobles and systematically consolidate their authority over the surrounding, fragmented Catalan territories. Looking ahead, the twelfth century promised an era of unprecedented political and territorial expansion for the county. Ramon Berenguer III would soon expand his domains significantly through strategic marriages and military campaigns, extending Catalan influence as far north as Provence. The most transformative event, however, lay just decades away when his successor, Ramon Berenguer IV, married the heiress of the Kingdom of Aragon in 1137. This pivotal dynastic union birthed the Crown of Aragon, forever elevating the autonomous county into the administrative and economic core of a formidable Mediterranean empire..

In the year 1100, the Beylik of Danishmend was a powerful and rapidly expanding Turkish state centered in the central and eastern regions of Anatolia. Ruled by the formidable Danishmend Gazi, the beylik firmly controlled key strategic cities such as Sebasteia, Amasia, and Neocaesarea. The state found itself navigating a complex geopolitical landscape, surrounded by the Byzantine Empire, the newly established Crusader states, and their primary regional rivals, the Seljuks of Rum. The most defining event of this year for the Danishmends was their monumental victory at the Battle of Melitene. During this engagement, Danishmend forces successfully ambushed and captured the renowned Crusader leader, Prince Bohemond I of Antioch, who was marching to relieve the city. This high-profile capture brought the beylik immense political leverage, ransom wealth, and unprecedented prestige across the broader Islamic world. Consequently, the Danishmends firmly solidified their status as the premier military force in Anatolia, temporarily eclipsing the Seljuk Sultanate as the dominant regional power..

In the year 1100, the Beylik of Mengücek was a localized but strategically significant Turkmen principality situated in the rugged highlands of eastern Anatolia. Founded by the veteran commander Mengücek Ahmed Ghazi following the Battle of Manzikert, the realm was primarily centered around the fortified cities of Erzincan, Kemah, and Divriği. Unlike the aggressively expanding Danishmends, the Mengücekids focused on consolidating their mountainous domain and controlling the vital trade passes connecting the Anatolian plateau with the Caucasus and Iran. Geopolitically, they found themselves sandwiched between several formidable neighbors, including the Danishmends to the west, the Saltukids to the east, and the Seljuks of Rum to the southwest. Because of their relatively smaller military footprint, the Mengücekid rulers frequently relied on careful diplomacy rather than outright conquest to guarantee their survival. During this turbulent period, they generally maintained a pragmatic alliance with the more powerful Danishmends to deter Byzantine incursions and navigate the chaotic aftermath of the First Crusade. Despite these heavy external pressures, the beylik successfully preserved its autonomy in 1100, laying the early foundations for what would later become a highly prosperous cultural hub..

Around the year 1100, the Eastern Roman Empire was facing both internal and external challenges that influenced its history. The empire, with its capital in Constantinople, was ruled by Emperor Alexios I Komnenos. His reign marked a period of resurgence and stability following the turbulent times of the 11th century. Alexios I implemented administrative and military reforms to strengthen the empire and repel external threats. The Roman Empire faced numerous conflicts, including the ongoing struggle against the Seljuk Turks in Anatolia, as well as tensions with the Norman Kingdom of Sicily and the Crusader states in the East. Despite these challenges, the Roman Empire maintained its cultural and artistic achievements, with the flourishing of roman art and the continuation of the roman tradition.

In the High Middle Ages, Venice became wealthy through its control of trade between Europe and the Levant, and began to expand into the Adriatic Sea and beyond. Venice was involved in the Crusades almost from the very beginning; 200 Venetian ships assisted in capturing the coastal cities of Syria after the First Crusade, and in 1123 they were granted virtual autonomy in the Kingdom of Jerusalem through the Pactum Warmundi. In 1110, Ordelafo Faliero personally commanded a Venetian fleet of 100 ships to assist Baldwin I of Jerusalem in capturing the city of Sidon.

The Kingdom of Castile and León was a large and powerful state on the Iberian Peninsula during the Middle Ages. Its name comes from the host of castles constructed in the region. It began in the 9th century as the County of Castile (Condado de Castilla), an eastern frontier lordship of the Kingdom of León. During the 10th century, its counts increased their autonomy, but it was not until 1065 that it was separated from León and became a kingdom in its own right. Between 1072 and 1157, it was again united with León, and after 1230, this union became permanent.

The idea that Rus was a monolithic state with a single ethnos, formed by the later Empires, which wanted to create an illusion of unity of its population. In reality, Rus has never controlled the territory drawn on the maps. The territory was home to many ethnic groups and principalities that fought, traded, and befriended each other. The main unifying factor was Christianity, but it was practiced by a minority who were the elite. The main population was pagan. Over time, the elite spread the culture to the general population, but this happened many centuries after the collapse of Rus. In 1094 Oleg captured Chernigov. His main allies were the Cumans. After that he fought with the Monomakh dynasty for Chernigov and other lands. In 1097 to stop the endless wars was organized Liubech Congress, at which the separate branches of the once united dynasty divided the power. Sviatoslav Iaroslavych descendants have secured for themselves Chernigov, Novhorod-Siverskyi and Murom-Ryazan principalities. Despite the temporary reconciliation, Oleg Sviatoslavych soon founded the Olgovych dynasty, which struggled with other dynasties for power in the region.

The Crusader States, also known as Outremer, were four Catholic realms in the Middle East that lasted from 1098 to 1291. These feudal polities were created by the Latin Catholic leaders of the First Crusade through conquest and political intrigue. The four states were the County of Edessa the Principality of Antioch, the County of Tripoli, and the Kingdom of Jerusalem. The Kingdom of Jerusalem covered what is now Israel and Palestine, the West Bank, the Gaza Strip, and adjacent areas. The other northern states covered what are now Syria, south-eastern Turkey, and Lebanon. The description Crusader states can be misleading, as from 1130 very few of the Frankish population were crusaders. The term Outremer, used by medieval and modern writers as a synonym, is derived from the French for overseas.

The Cumans were a Turkic nomadic people from Central Asia, comprising the western branch of the Cuman–Kipchak confederation who spoke the Cuman language. After the Mongol invasion, many sought asylum in the Kingdom of Hungary, as many Cumans had settled in Hungary, the Second Bulgarian Empire playing an important role in the development of the state. Cumans played also an important role in the Roman Empire, the Latin Empire, and the Nicaea Empire's Anatolia. Related to the Pecheneg, they inhabited a shifting area north of the Black Sea and along the Volga River known as Cumania, from which the Cuman–Kipchaks meddled in the politics of the Caucasus and the Khwarazmian Empire. The Cumans were fierce and formidable nomadic warriors of the Eurasian Steppe who exerted an enduring influence on the medieval Balkans. They were numerous, culturally sophisticated, and militarily powerful.

From 650 there existed a large Scandinavian settlement, Grobin, which the Curonians conquered around 800. In 853, the Danes invaded Curonia, but were defeated. Two Curonian rulers are known that fought against the Vikings in the second half of the 9th century - Loker and Dorno. From Rimbert we know that already in the IX century the Curonians had a state formation consisting of five principalities. The fragmentary historical records that have survived to us show that in the IX-XII centuries, the Curonians continued both to trade and to war with the Scandinavians. In 1170, the Curonians plunder Eland. It was common for the Curonians to carry out joint raids and campaigns together with Estonians (Oeselians). According to some opinions, they took part in attacking Sweden's main city Sigtuna in 1187.

Around the year 1100, Denmark was a kingdom undergoing significant political and territorial developments. The reign of King Eric I of Denmark, also known as Eric Ejegod, marked a period of expansion and consolidation of royal power. Eric Ejegod sought to extend Danish influence through various military campaigns, including successful expeditions in present-day Norway and the Baltic region. During this time, Denmark was also impacted by the rise of the Catholic Church, which led to the establishment of several bishoprics and increased ecclesiastical authority. However, the kingdom faced internal challenges, including power struggles among noble families and conflicts over succession. The events of the 12th century set the stage for further transformations in Danish history, shaping the country's political landscape for centuries to come.

William I, usually known as William the Conqueror and sometimes William the Bastard, was the first Norman king of England, reigning from 1066 until his death in 1087. A descendant of Rollo, he was Duke of Normandy from 1035 onward. By 1060, following a long struggle to establish his throne, his hold on Normandy was secure. In 1066, following the death of Edward the Confessor, William invaded England, leading an army of Normans to victory over the Anglo-Saxon forces of Harold Godwinson at the Battle of Hastings, and suppressed subsequent English revolts in what has become known as the Norman Conquest. The rest of his life was marked by struggles to consolidate his hold over England and his continental lands, and by difficulties with his eldest son, Robert Curthose.

The Fatimid Caliphate was an Ismaili Shi'a caliphate extant from the tenth to the twelfth centuries AD. Spanning a large area of North Africa, it ranged from the Atlantic Ocean in the west to the Red Sea in the east. The Fatimids, a dynasty of Arab origin, trace their ancestry to Muhammad's daughter Fatima and her husband Ali b. Abi Talib, the first Shi‘a imam. The Fatimids were acknowledged as the rightful imams by different Isma‘ili communities, but also in many other Muslim lands, including Persia and the adjacent regions. Originating during the Abbasid Caliphate, the Fatimids conquered Tunisia and established the city of al-Mahdiyya. The Ismaili dynasty ruled territories across the Mediterranean coast of Africa and ultimately made Egypt the center of the caliphate. At its height, the caliphate included – in addition to Egypt – varying areas of the Maghreb, Sudan, Sicily, the Levant, and the Hijaz.

The Finns are an ethnos in the west of Finland. Over time, it has given its name to the country of Finland and its people. Written records about the Finns have not survived. The main source of information is archaeology. By 1100, the Swedes founded many colonies on the shores of present-day Finland. Christianization of the local population was underway. In 1155 the Swedish King Saint Erik IX started a crusade against the Finns to Christianize them. As a result of which Finland was subordinated to Sweden until 1809.

France originated as West Francia (Francia Occidentalis), the western half of the Carolingian Empire, with the Treaty of Verdun (843). A branch of the Carolingian dynasty continued to rule until 987, when Hugh Capet was elected king and founded the Capetian dynasty. The territory remained known as Francia and its ruler as rex Francorum (king of the Franks) well into the High Middle Ages. The first king calling himself rex Francie (King of France) was Philip II, in 1190, and officially from 1204. From then, France was continuously ruled by the Capetians and their cadet lines—the Valois and Bourbon—until the monarchy was abolished in 1792 during the French Revolution.

The Kingdom of Georgia, also known as the Georgian Empire, was a medieval Eurasian monarchy that was founded in c.1008 AD. It reached its Golden Age of political and economic strength during the reign of King David IV and Queen Tamar the Great from the 11th to 13th centuries. Georgia became one of the pre-eminent nations of the Christian East and its pan-Caucasian empire and maintained network of tributaries stretching from Eastern Europe to Anatolia and the northern frontiers of Iran. It was the principal historical precursor of present-day Georgia.

The Holy Roman Empire, also known as the Holy Roman Empire of the German Nation after 1512, was a political entity in Western, Central, and Southern Europe that developed in the Early Middle Ages and continued until its dissolution in 1806 during the Napoleonic Wars. From the accession of Otto I in 962 until the twelfth century, the Empire was the most powerful monarchy in Europe. The functioning of government depended on the harmonious cooperation between monarch and vassals, but this harmony was disturbed during the Salian period. The empire reached the apex of territorial expansion and power under the House of Hohenstaufen in the mid-thirteenth century, but overextending led to partial collapse.

The idea that Rus was a monolithic state with a single ethnos, formed by the later Empires, which wanted to create an illusion of unity of its population. In reality, Rus has never controlled the territory drawn on the maps. The territory was home to many ethnic groups and principalities that fought, traded, and befriended each other. The main unifying factor was Christianity, but it was practiced by a minority who were the elite. The main population was pagan. Over time, the elite spread the culture to the general population, but this happened many centuries after the collapse of Rus. The elite of the White Croatian ethnos retained the memory of their independent principalities. In 1084 with the help of Rurik Rostyslavich and his brothers successfully founded independent Croatian princedoms which acted in union and could defend the independence from Rus. In 1097 at the Liubech Congress independence was legally confirmed. By 1144 the principalities were united into the Principality of Halych.

In the year 1100, the Hammadid Emirate is managing a critical transition of their political center from their old capital, Qal'at Beni Hammad, to the flourishing Mediterranean coastal port of Al-Nasiriyya. This strategic relocation was largely forced by the mounting pressure and encroachment of nomadic Banu Hilal Arab tribes across the interior plains. While the inland agrarian base faces constant disruption and heavy tribute demands from these Bedouin groups, the new coastal capital is rapidly transforming into a booming hub for international trade with Italian merchants. Politically, the dynasty must constantly balance uneasy truces with the relentless Bedouin confederations while keeping a wary eye on their western rivals, the expanding Almoravids. Despite these heavy pressures, the Hammadids are actively working to consolidate their military strength, soon even managing to briefly project power westward by seizing Tlemcen. Internally, the court faces the delicate task of maintaining state cohesion and financing a burgeoning urban population amidst a deeply fractured regional landscape. Ultimately, the year 1100 finds the dynasty pivoting from a landlocked mountain emirate into a maritime-focused commercial power, striving to survive the shifting tides of the central Maghreb..

Around the year 1100, the Kingdom of Hungary was undergoing a transformative period in its history. At that time, Hungary was ruled by King Coloman, also known as Coloman the Learned or Coloman the Bookish. Coloman's reign marked a period of expansion and consolidation of royal power. He pursued an ambitious territorial agenda, incorporating territories such as Croatia, Dalmatia, and parts of present-day Slovakia into the kingdom. Coloman's rule was characterized by efforts to centralize authority and promote cultural and legal reforms. He aimed to strengthen the position of the crown and establish a more unified and organized kingdom. Coloman's policies were influenced by his commitment to Christianity, and he actively supported the Catholic Church's influence in the region. This period set the stage for Hungary's further development as a significant power in Central Europe.

Populated primarily by Ibadi Muslims, these desert dwellers were considered dangerous heretics by the orthodox Sunni Almoravid and Hammadid empires to the north. To escape religious persecution and imperial conquest, they had retreated into the harshest environments imaginable, building heavily fortified oasis settlements like Ouargla and Zuwila. Far from being impoverished exiles, these independent tribes grew immensely prosperous by dominating the lucrative trans-Saharan trade routes in gold, salt, and slaves. Rather than relying on massive standing armies, they masterfully used the lethal, waterless expanse of the deep desert itself as an impenetrable shield against foreign invasions. Their society remained highly decentralized, governed by strict councils of religious elders who prioritized the survival of their unique culture over territorial expansion.

In the year 1100, the independent Turcoman principality of Imarat Amid stands as an isolated but formidable fortress-state in the Diyar Bakr region, ruled by the steadfast Emir Ibrahim. The faction's survival relies heavily on the legendary, impenetrable black basalt walls of its capital city, Amid, which fiercely guards the vital trade routes of upper Mesopotamia. Surrounded by dangerous geopolitical predators, Ibrahim must constantly defend his territory against aggressive neighbors like the Artuqid warlords to the east and the newly established Crusader County of Edessa to the west. Internally, a fascinating political dynamic is unfolding as the wealthy and bureaucratic Banu Nisan clan steadily amasses significant influence at court, quietly acting as the true administrative power behind the Turcoman military elite. The Emir's dynasty and future legacy rest on the shoulders of his young son, Ilaldi, who is rapidly approaching the age where he will have to command the realm's armies in a hostile world. Militarily, the faction lacks the massive manpower of the Syrian Seljuks but compensates with highly skilled cavalry and immense wealth generated by the city's robust craftsmanship. Consequently, Imarat Amid remains a defensive powerhouse that fiercely protects its independence, perfectly content to outlast its rivals behind great walls while the rest of the Levant burns in endless conflict..

By the year 1100, the Emirate of Damascus is governed by the young Seljuk Emir Duqaq. While Duqaq is the formal ruler of the ruling Banu Saljuq clan, the true military power of the realm lies in the hands of his formidable Atabeg, Toghtekin. Toghtekin commands the loyal and powerful Banu Buri vassal clan, essentially acting as the shadow ruler from strategic southern fortresses like Bosra. Much like Aleppo, Damascus faces an existential threat from the encroaching Crusaders, who have recently conquered Jerusalem and established a new kingdom to the southwest. The faction also contends with the powerful Fatimid Caliphate pushing from the coastal cities, turning the southern Levant into a highly volatile war zone. Despite these massive external threats, the overriding political focus often remains the bitter dynastic war against Aleppo for total supremacy over Seljuk Syria. Consequently, Imarat Dimashq is a wealthy but internally divided kingdom, shaped by the political tension between a royal figurehead and his ambitious, waiting general..

In the year 1100, the Emirate of Aleppo is a fractured and embattled realm ruled by the calculating and pragmatic Seljuk Emir Ridwan. The faction is geographically cornered in northern Syria, constantly threatened by the aggressive expansion of the newly formed Crusader Principality of Antioch to the west. Ridwan's power base is further weakened by his bitter, ongoing blood feud with his younger brother, Duqaq of Damascus, which prevents any unified Muslim resistance in the region. Internally, the Emir relies on ruthless but capable commanders, such as the eunuch Lu'lu' al-Yaya and the vengeful veteran Shams al-Dawla, to secure his volatile borders. Despite losing his former top general to a rebellion in Homs, Ridwan maintains critical strongholds like Azaz and Atarib to defend his remaining territory. Driven purely by self-interest and survival, Ridwan is even willing to forge controversial alliances with the Fatimids or harbor the enigmatic Assassins to undermine his rivals. Thus, Imarat Halab stands as a paranoid and militarized state, desperately clinging to its strategic northern territories amidst enemies on all sides..

In the year 1100, the Imarat of Shabankara stands at the absolute height of its defiant power in the southern province of Fars. Claiming proud descent from the ancient Sassanid kings, these fierce Kurdish and Persian highlanders actively rebel against the crumbling Seljuk Empire. Under the shrewd leadership of Emir Mubaraz ad-Din Hazarasp of the Ramani clan, they have recently annihilated a major Seljuk army sent to crush them. Capitalizing on the chaotic civil war between the Seljuk princes, the Shabankara now ride freely across the rural landscapes and lucrative trade routes. Their ultimate ambition is to carve out a fully independent sovereign state, replacing Turkish overlords with their own native Persian aristocracy. Thus, the dawn of 1100 presents a volatile power vacuum where the Shabankara are poised to either restore the glory of the old empire or face brutal imperial retaliation..

In the year 1100, the Tribes of Banū Uqayl is an independent Arab Bedouin emirate strategically concentrated along the Euphrates river valley. Having lost their former capital of Mosul to the Seljuks, the Uqaylid dynasty now operates from their heavily fortified river stronghold of Al-Rahba and the city of Raqqah. The realm is cunningly governed by the veteran Amir Salim ibn Malik, who acts as a powerful toll master controlling the lucrative regional river trade. While the aging emir secures the impregnable fortress, his aggressive adult son and heir, Ali, leads the faction's swift military forces across the open plains. The emirate's military strength relies heavily on nomadic desert tribesmen, utilizing highly mobile light cavalry and camel skirmishers to outmaneuver heavily armored foes. This distinct tribal warfare doctrine provides a sharp, asymmetrical contrast to the heavy horse archers of the neighboring Turkoman and Seljuk principalities. Ultimately, the Uqaylid Emirate stands as a resilient and culturally distinct desert faction dominating the crucial southern waterways of the campaign map.

In the year 1100, the Imārat Tiflīs stands as an incredibly wealthy but highly vulnerable Islamic city-state isolated within the Caucasus. Following the collapse of its traditional dynastic rule, the emirate is uniquely governed by a powerful oligarchy of merchant patricians rather than a single emir. This ruling council of elders manages to maintain the city's fragile independence primarily by paying heavy financial tributes to the Great Seljuk Empire. Lacking a formidable native military, the city relies entirely on its immense mercantile wealth to hire mercenary armies and maintain its impregnable walls. To the west, the young and brilliant Christian King David IV of Georgia poses a constant, existential threat, actively viewing the Muslim-held city as his rightful future capital. Simultaneously, ambitious Seljuk warlords to the south constantly covet the emirate's overflowing treasury, forcing the patricians to navigate a perilous diplomatic tightrope. Ultimately, the Emirate of Tbilisi acts as a tense, defensive merchant republic, desperately trying to buy its survival amidst the ruthless expansionist wars of its neighbors..

In the 9th century, Vikings began raiding and founding settlements along Ireland's coasts and waterways, which became its first large towns. Over time, these settlers were assimilated and became the Norse-Gaels. After the Norman invasion of 1169–71, large swathes of Ireland came under the control of Norman lords, leading to centuries of conflict with the native Irish. The King of England claimed sovereignty over this territory – the Lordship of Ireland – and the island as a whole. However, the Gaelic system continued in areas outside Anglo-Norman control. The territory under English control gradually shrank to an area known as the Pale and, outside this, many Hiberno-Norman lords adopted Gaelic culture.

In 1100, the Ishkhanutyun of Melitene stood as a wealthy and independent Christian enclave ruled by the Armenian warlord Gabriel. Guarding the vital routes between Anatolia and Mesopotamia, the heavily fortified city acted as a crucial geopolitical buffer state. Its immense strategic value and isolation inevitably drew the attention of the expanding Turkish Danishmend dynasty to the north. During the summer, Danishmend Gazi led his forces southward to launch a massive siege against Melitene's walls. Facing overwhelming odds, Gabriel sent desperate envoys to the newly formed Crusader states to beg for immediate military relief. The renowned Norman leader, Bohemond I of Antioch, answered this call and marched his army north to rescue the beleaguered city. However, the campaign ended in disaster when Danishmend Gazi brilliantly ambushed the Crusader force, annihilating the army and taking Bohemond away in chains..

In 983 Prince Volodymyr I Sviatoslavych burned down the regional Jatvingian center on the place of modern Franapol and subjugated these lands. Brest became the frontier fortress of Rus and the main economic center of the region. Further attempts Rus to subdue the Jatvingian lands were unsuccessful. Usually on the territory of western Belarus draw Grodno Principality, which was part of Volhynia or Polatsk. On the lands of Rus existed hundreds of settlements with the name Goroden or similar. But there is no convincing evidence why it is exactly modern Grodno. The possessions of Volhynia knyaz Davyd Igorovich were in the region of Pogorynje. Rather there was located the Princedom, and Horoden is the modern Davyd-Haradok. In the 13th century there are many written reports about the region. They are related to the attempt of the Volhynia Principality to capture these lands. But they were already part of the Lithuanian Kingdom. After a successful invasion in 1258, Ruthenian king of Danylo Romanovych succeeded in capturing the Vaŭkavysk princedom, for a short time. The further destiny of the Jatvingian principalities is connected with joining to the Lithuania for resistance to common enemies: Golden Horde, Ruthenian Kingdom and Teutonic Order.

At the end of the 7th century, the semi-legendary Denmark king Ivar Vidfamne lost a battle to an army of Karelians and died. At the beginning of the 11th century, in the Olafs saga helga, the Karelian principality is mentioned. In the 11th century the Karelians expanded to the Olonets Isthmus. As a result of mixing with the local population, the Livviks and Ludiks ethnic groups were formed. In 1143 the Karelians raided Tavastians. In 1187 the Karelians pillaged Swedish Sigtuna. This mention of Karelian raids on Sweden in the chronicle is given as the main reason to found Stockholm, the current capital of Sweden. In 1253, Karelians aided Novgorod in its wars with Estonians. In 1269, the knyaz of Novgorod prepared a raid against Karelians, but he abandoned his plans as he was advised against it by his councilors. In 1278, Novgorod made war against Karelians and, according to the chronicle, put Karelian lands 'to sword and fire', which significantly reduced Karelian military power. As a result of these actions, most of the Karelians became part of the Novgorod Republic and were divided into 10 pogosts (administrative unit).

Absence of this state on the majority of maps is connected with desire to see Rus as the united state. Such a vision has been promoted for a very long time. First by the Church, then by large empires, such as the Russian Empire. Since the unity of the population is often considered as a factor of state stability and wealthy. Nevertheless, modern Russian science recognizes the existence of the Vyatiches state. It is known that the capital of the principality was in the city Kordno, and its ruler was Khodota, who had a son. Volodymyr Monomakh, one of the most powerful princes of Rus, twice organized campaigns against Vyatiches between 1078 and 1084, which had limited success. Vyatiches state have not been subordinated by Rus until 1240, after 1240 Rus has been ruined by Mongols. But in addition to this state, the Vyatiches created the Ryazan principality, which is usually considered as Rus, because it was subordinated to the Rurikids (Igoroviches) dynasty. Also Vyatiches lived in Chernigov and Vladimir princedoms where also ruled Rurikids (Igoroviches).

The idea that Rus was a monolithic state with a single ethnos, formed by the later Empires, which wanted to create an illusion of unity of its population. In reality, Rus has never controlled the territory drawn on the maps. The territory was home to many ethnic groups and principalities that fought, traded, and befriended each other. The main unifying factor was Christianity, but it was practiced by a minority who were the elite. The main population was pagan. Over time, the elite spread the culture to the general population, but this happened many centuries after the collapse of Rus. In 1097 to stop the endless wars was organized Liubech Congress, at which the separate branches of the once united dynasty divided the power. Sviatopolk II Iziaslavych fixed for himself the following possessions: Kyiv, Turau-Pinsk, Novgorod lands and Pogoryno. Legally these lands became part of the Kyivan Principality. But Novgorodians did not recognize the power of Sviatopolk and in fact Novgorod withdrew to Volodymyr Monomakh. This created tension between the princes and almost didn't lead to war. Tensions continued until Sviatopolk's death. Probably Sviatopolk II Iziaslavych was the instigator of the conflict that resulted in Vasylko Rostyslavych being blinded. In 1100, the Principality of Kyiv had the formal status of the main Rus Principality. In fact, it was the capital of Rus, but it could not govern most of the territories because they belonged to other principalities.

In the X-XIII centuries, Latgalians lived in the eastern part of present-day Vidzeme. The following principalities were fully or partially Latgalian: Atzele, Jersika, Idums, Lotigola, Koknese and Talava. In 1100 Latgalians, located along the river Daugava (Western Dvina), was in strong vassal dependence on Polatsk. The Princedom of Jersika was a part of the Polatsk state. In 1111 Novgorod prince Mstyslav Volodymyrovich The Great invaded in the Atzele principality. The campaign was unsuccessful, because in 1180 Novgorod organized a new attack on Atzele. Other principalities were independent but did not have a unified state.

Approximately from the 10th century vassal-union relations between Polatsk and Lithuania began to form. Lithuania's vassality/alliance is difficult to determine due to lack of information. The driver of relations was the joint struggle with Rus. Polatsk often went on campaigns together with Lithuania. In 1100 the principalities close to Polatsk were probably vassals (Nalša and Alša). Other principalities were independent but not united, they traded, fought with each other and against common enemies (Deltuva, Lietuva and Neris). To the first half of the 12th century Lithuania took the leading role, and the Polatsk through dynastic alliances became part of Lithuania.

By the year 1100, the Duchy of Naples stood as one of the last remaining independent coastal states in Southern Italy, ruled by Duke John VI. Originally a Byzantine province, it had slowly evolved into a fiercely autonomous maritime republic over the preceding centuries. To secure its survival, Naples had carefully managed its detachment from Constantinople while establishing its own local hereditary dynasty. The duchy had also survived relentless territorial pressure from the inland Lombard principalities of Benevento, Capua, and Salerno. To protect its borders and lucrative trade, Naples frequently resorted to controversial pragmatism, occasionally allying with Saracen raiders at the cost of papal excommunication. However, the most existential challenge of the eleventh century was the arrival of the Norman mercenaries, who quickly turned into conquerors and completely encircled the Neapolitan enclave. Looking ahead, Naples' centuries-old strategy of diplomatic balancing was doomed to fail against the rising ambition of Roger II. As the Normans consolidated Southern Italy into a unified state, the isolated city could no longer withstand their overwhelming military might. In 1137, the last reigning duke, Sergius VII, was forced to surrender the city, permanently bringing an end to the independent Duchy of Naples..

The term Norwegian Realm and Old Kingdom of Norway refer to the Kingdom of Norway's peak of power at the 13th century after a long period of civil war before 1240. The kingdom was a loosely unified nation including the territory of modern-day Norway, modern-day Swedish territory of Jämtland, Herjedalen, Ranrike (Bohuslän) and Idre and Särna, as well as Norway's overseas possessions which had been settled by Norwegian seafarers for centuries before being annexed or incorporated into the kingdom as tax territories.

Around the year 1100, the Obotrites stood as a powerful West Slavic tribal confederation inhabiting the region of modern-day Mecklenburg and eastern Holstein between the Elbe River and the Baltic Sea. Ruled by prominent chieftains like the veteran pagan leader Prince Kruto and later the formidable Prince Henry (Heinrich), the Obotrites successfully maintained their political independence, traditional Slavic religion, and maritime raiding culture while fiercely resisting the aggressive eastward expansion of the Saxon duchy and the Holy Roman Empire. Organized around formidable ring-fortresses (grad) such as Schwerin, Dobin, and Ratzeburg, they served as a vital, highly resilient pagan buffer zone between Christian Central Europe and the Scandinavian North on the eve of their eventual feudal subjugation and assimilation later in the 12th century..

The Pechenegs or Patzinaks were a semi-nomadic Turkic people from Central Asia who spoke the Pecheneg language. In the 9th and 10th centuries, the Pechenegs controlled much of the steppes of southeast Europe and the Crimean Peninsula. In the 9th century the Pechenegs began a period of wars against Kievan Rus, and for more than two centuries launched raids into the lands of Rus, which sometimes escalated into full-scale wars.

In 1100 Volodymyr Vsevolodovych Monomakh, the most powerful ruler in the history of Rus, ruled in Pereiaslav. In 1100, he was not yet on the throne of Rus (Kyiv), but he was very powerful, especially his dynasty. Through his sons, Monomakh ruled duchies of Smolensk, Novgorod, and part of Suzdal. The 'capital' city of the state, Pereiaslav, was very vulnerable to attacks of nomads, so Volodymyr Monomakh made great efforts to fight the Cumans. Monomakh avoided direct clashes with his relatives from the Rurikid dynasty. He often paid off and yielded to other Rurikids. He was treacherous towards the Cumans. But by the end of his life, he had become the most powerful ruler in Rus. Byzantine sources called him the Archon of all Rus. But after his death, Rus finally fragmented into separate principalities. Shortly after Monomakh's death, his dynasty was almost completely wiped out in battles with other members of the Rurikid dynasty, especially the Olgovichs.

At the dawn of the twelfth century, the Polish state plunged into a bitter civil war fueled by dynastic fracture and intense factionalism. The ailing High Duke Władysław I Herman had effectively surrendered real authority to his ruthless palatine, Sieciech of the Starża-Toporczyk clan, who ruled through heavy-handed centralisation and personal enrichment. This tyrannical grip alienated the traditional nobility and drove the duke's estranged sons, Prince Zbigniew and Prince Bolesław III Wrymouth, into an opportunistic alliance of convenience. Supported by powerful magnate families such as the Awdaniec, Łabędź, and Powała clans, the rebellious half-brothers mobilized regional forces to strip Sieciech of his power base. Their coordinated military pressure forced a major realignment, shattering the central government's dominance in Greater Poland, Silesia, and Lesser Poland. By 1100, this explosive confrontation reached its climax, ultimately sealing Sieciech's downfall and exile..

The first mention of Polatsk (Palteskja) is recorded in the semi-legendary Þiðreks saga af Bern (Thidrekssaga, Wilkinasaga). Around 447 Atilla captured and pillaged it. In the saga, the city is presented as a wealthy well-protected regional center. Quite often Połack is represented as part of the Rus state, despite the fact that in the chronicles Połack is constantly at war with Rus until its collapse. By 1100 Połack had captured from Rus the major regional centers of Minsk and Vitebsk. For more than 500 years history of existence of PolatPołacksk Principality Rus princes ruled in Połack only 26 years. During the reign of the Usiasłaŭ II the Seer, the Połack Principality reached its greatest prosperity. In the second half of the 13th century, the principality became part of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania as an autonomous part. A few centuries later, when the term Ruthenian became equal to Orthodox, Połack became Ruthenian.

In the late 1090s up through 1100, the Pomeranian tribes waged a fierce border war along the Noteć and Warta rivers to defend their independence and pagan faith against Christian Polish expansion. Strategic strongholds like Santok and Nakło repeatedly changed hands amidst relentless ambushes and sieges. Taking advantage of the Polish civil war between Duke Władysław Herman, his palatine Sieciech, and the rebellious princes Zbigniew and Bolesław III Krzywousty, Pomeranian warbands launched swift, devastating raids deep into Greater Poland and Kuyavia. Rather than operating as a centralized army, autonomous clans like the Borko and coastal Volinians fought under the sacred banners of Triglav, relying on fluid forest and river warfare. Although the young Bolesław launched punitive campaigns northward to stabilize the frontier, Pomerania's fortified forest fastnesses remained unyielding, leaving the tribes fully independent at the turn of the century..

The state had its origins in the rise of Christianity throughout Italy, and with it the rising influence of the Christian Church. By the mid-8th century, with the decline of the Roman Empire in Italy, the Papacy became effectively sovereign. Several Christian rulers, including the Frankish kings Charlemagne and Pepin the Short, further donated lands to be governed by the Church. During the Renaissance, the papal territory expanded greatly and the pope became one of Italy's most important secular rulers as well as the head of the Church. At their zenith, the Papal States covered most of the modern Italian regions of Lazio (which includes Rome), Marche, Umbria and Romagna, and portions of Emilia.

In 1100 the Prussians were not united by a common state. Prussia was divided into 11 principalities: Pameddi, Wārmi, Paguddi, Notangi, Semba, Nadrāuwa, Barta, Skallawa, Sūdawa, Galinda and Kulmus. These principalities traded and fought with each other and united against common enemies. In 996 Mieszko I attempted to conquer the principalities. Beginning in 1147, the Polish duke Bolesław IV the Curly tried to subdue Prussia. Several attacks by Konrad of Masovia in the early 13th century were successfully repelled by the Prussians. In 1226, Konrad I, Duke of Masovia, appealed to the Knights to defend his borders and subdue the pagan Prussians, allowing the Teutonic Knights use of Chełmno Land as a base for their campaign. By the second half of the 13th century, the Teutonic Order had conquered Prussia.

In 1100 AD, the Rani ruled the Baltic island of Râna (Rügen) as a formidable sea power and the religious heart of the West Slavs. Governed from the temple fortress of Arkona under the high priest of Svantevit and a hereditary prince, their feared navy and red stanitsa banner dominated regional trade and resisted Christian Scandinavian expansion..

The Sultanate of Rum was a culturally Turco-Persian Sunni Muslim state, established over conquered Roman territories and peoples of Anatolia by the Seljuk Turks following their entry into Anatolia after the Battle of Manzikert (1071). The name Rûm was a synonym for the medieval Eastern Roman Empire and its peoples, as it remains in modern Turkish. The Sultanate of Rum seceded from the Great Seljuk Empire under Suleiman ibn Qutalmish in 1077, just six years after the roman provinces of central Anatolia were conquered at the Battle of Manzikert (1071). It had its capital first at Nicaea and then at Iconium.

By the year 1100, the Seljuk Sultanate of Kerman operated as a prosperous and highly independent state in southeastern Iran, largely insulated from the devastating civil wars consuming the Great Seljuk Empire. The region was ruled by Amir Iran-Shah, who had ascended to power in 1096 and maintained a firm grip on the lucrative trade routes connecting the Persian Gulf and Oman. Thanks to this geographic isolation and economic stability, Kerman flourished as a vital commercial hub while the rest of the broader Seljuk domains fractured. However, Iran-Shah's reign was becoming increasingly controversial due to his growing association with the radical Nizari Ismaili sect. This perceived religious deviation deeply alarmed the orthodox Sunni ulema and the powerful local military commanders within his court. Consequently, a fierce internal political crisis was brewing beneath the surface of the state's outward economic prosperity. This mounting religious and political tension would soon culminate in a violent rebellion the following year, ultimately leading to Iran-Shah's deposition and execution in 1101..

In the year 1100, the Saltuklu Beyliği stands as a fiercely independent and geographically isolated Turcoman principality ruling over the harsh highlands of eastern Anatolia. Governed by the seasoned veteran Emir Ebu'l-Kasım Saltuk Bey, the faction operates from its heavily fortified capital of Erzurum. Although nominally loyal to the fragmented Great Seljuk Empire in the east, the Beylik functions as a completely autonomous state due to the ongoing Seljuk civil wars. The faction's military strength relies heavily on resilient Oghuz Turcoman tribesmen adept at navigating and defending the treacherous mountainous terrain. To protect its borders and vital trade routes, the realm is anchored by formidable regional strongholds such as Bayburt in the west and Micingerd in the east. Geopolitically, the Saltukids are largely shielded from the distant Crusaders and the Sultanate of Rum, instead focusing their defensive efforts against the rising power of the Christian Georgian kingdoms to the north. Consequently, the Beylik of Saltuk represents a rugged, defensive powerhouse perfectly adapted to outlast external threats from behind the safety of its mountain passes.

By the year 1100, the Taifa of Saraqusta stood as the very last independent Muslim kingdom in the Iberian Peninsula. Ruled by the cunning Emir Ahmad II al-Musta'in of the Banu Hud dynasty, this wealthy state was entirely surrounded by existential threats. To the south, the relentless Almoravid Empire had already swallowed every other Andalusian Taifa and now turned its expansionist gaze toward the Ebro valley. Meanwhile, to the north, the aggressive Christian realms of Aragon and Castile constantly raided their borders, eager to conquer their rich agricultural lands. To survive this precarious political vise, al-Musta'in relied on a desperate diplomatic balancing act, paying heavy gold tributes and hiring opportunistic Christian mercenaries. He also gathered the last remaining minor lords, such as the aging ruler of the Banu Razin clan, to form a fragile network of buffer states. Consequently, Saraqusta remained a gleaming, isolated bastion of Andalusian culture, fighting a brilliant but ultimately doomed struggle to delay its inevitable fall..

Scotland was a sovereign state in northwest Europe traditionally said to have been founded in 843. Its territories expanded and shrank, but it came to occupy the northern third of the island of Great Britain, sharing a land border to the south with the Kingdom of England. It suffered many invasions by the English, but under Robert the Bruce it fought a successful War of Independence and remained an independent state throughout the late Middle Ages.

By the year 1100, the Great Seljuk Empire under Sultan Barkiyaruq was deeply crippled by internal fragmentation and endless dynastic civil wars. Although Barkiyaruq was the nominal supreme ruler, his authority was fiercely challenged by his half-brother Muhammad I Tapar, who had launched a massive rebellion from his stronghold in Azerbaijan. This devastating fratricidal conflict forced Barkiyaruq to expend the empire's military and economic resources on fighting his own family rather than governing. Meanwhile, another brother, Ahmad Sanjar, ruled almost independently in the eastern province of Khorasan, further decentralizing the empire's once-unified power base. Because the Seljuk elite were entirely consumed by these internal succession struggles, they failed to recognize or adequately respond to the existential threat posed by the First Crusade. Consequently, Barkiyaruq was completely unable to send imperial armies to assist the western amirs in the Levant, allowing the Crusaders to consolidate their recent conquests of Antioch and Jerusalem. Ultimately, his reign during this critical period was a desperate struggle for political survival that permanently weakened the central authority of the Great Seljuk state.

By the year 1100, the Seljuks were embroiled in a massive civil war that was tearing the Great Seljuk Empire apart. The region served as the primary power base for Muhammad I Tapar, who had launched a fierce rebellion against his half-brother, Sultan Barkiyaruq, for the supreme throne. Supported by influential local amirs and the calculating vizier Mu'ayyid al-Mulk, Muhammad transformed Azerbaijan into the military and economic engine of his uprising.
