He utilized the wealthy provinces of Arran and Azerbaijan to rapidly mobilize armies and secure vital resources for his extensive campaigns. This rebellion turned the region into a highly militarized staging ground, deeply entrenched in brutal dynastic clashes with Barkiyaruq’s loyalist forces. Because of this intense internal conflict, the political and military focus of the regional Seljuk elite was entirely consumed by the struggle for supremacy. Consequently, this devastating civil war effectively paralyzed the empire's ability to mount a unified defense against external threats like the First Crusade and the resurgent Byzantines..

By the year 1100, the Seljuks of Khurasan were consolidating their regional power under the young and capable leadership of Ahmad Sanjar. Appointed as the ruler of the eastern provinces by his half-brother Sultan Barkiyaruq in 1097, Sanjar operated with a highly significant degree of autonomy. While the Great Seljuk Empire's western domains were consumed by the devastating civil war between Barkiyaruq and Muhammad I Tapar, Khurasan remained relatively insulated from the worst of this dynastic turmoil. Instead of marching west to engage in the fratricidal conflict, Sanjar focused on securing his own frontiers against formidable external rivals, particularly the Ghaznavids and the Qara-Khanids. He actively campaigned to suppress local rebellions and assert firm Seljuk dominance over the prosperous trade cities of the region, such as Nishapur, Merv, and Balkh. This strategic stabilization transformed Khurasan into a wealthy, militarized powerhouse that functioned almost entirely independently from the fracturing imperial center. Ultimately, Sanjar's successful early administration in 1100 laid the critical foundation for his long reign and his future destiny as the supreme Great Seljuk Sultan..

The County of Sicily, also known as County of Sicily and Calabria, was a Norman state comprising the islands of Sicily and Malta and part of Calabria from 1071 until 1130. The county began to form during the Christian reconquest of Sicily (1061–91) from the Muslim Emirate, established by conquest in 965. The county is thus a transitional period in the history of Sicily. After the Muslims had been defeated and either forced out or incorporated into the Norman military, a further period of transition took place for the county and the Sicilians.

In the year 1100, the Stodorani tribe, a prominent Polabian Slavic group, held a precarious but independent position centered around their fortress of Brenna on the Havel river. Having violently overthrown Saxon rule over a century earlier, they remained a fiercely pagan stronghold amidst a rapidly Christianizing European landscape. Their strategic location allowed them to dominate local river trade, generating the wealth necessary to fortify their settlements and fund their continuous defensive campaigns. Despite their military resilience, they faced mounting pressure from the expanding Holy Roman Empire, whose margraves and bishops viewed the subjugation of the Stodorani as both a political and religious imperative. Internally, the tribe was governed by a traditional aristocracy that balanced the demands of warfare with the preservation of their polytheistic Slavic identity. However, this era marked the twilight of their absolute autonomy as neighboring Christian princes began to exploit internal tribal divisions to gain influence over the region. Ultimately, the political and military landscape of 1100 set the stage for their eventual absorption into the Margraviate of Brandenburg in the decades that followed..

By 1100 AD, the Banu Sulaym had firmly established themselves as the undisputed masters of the eastern North African steppes, spanning from Cyrenaica to the borders of Ifriqiya. Operating as a massive, decentralized nomadic confederation rather than a traditional urban kingdom, they thrived in the arid inland regions that static empires could not control. The confederation was structured around several powerful sub-clans, most notably the Banu Debbab who dominated Tripolitania and the Banu Heib who controlled the eastern flanks. From their primary stronghold in the coastal city of Surt and fortified Saharan oases like Waddan and Zallah, they commanded lucrative inland trade routes. They maintained complete political independence from the Zirid Emirate to the west, relying on highly mobile light cavalry to project power across the desert. At the apex of this tribal hierarchy stood the Amir al-Arab, a supreme patriarch who united the fierce bedouin factions under a single red banner during times of war. Through this formidable blend of martial prowess and nomadic resilience, the Banu Sulaym remained an existential threat to the settled coastal states and a dominant geopolitical force in the region..

Around the year 1100, Sweden was undergoing significant changes that shaped its history. The country was ruled by various regional powers, and the era witnessed a struggle for dominance between different factions. The reign of King Philip of Sweden, a descendant of the House of Stenkil, marked a period of centralization and attempts to strengthen royal authority. Concurrently, Sweden was influenced by the rising power of the Catholic Church, which played a crucial role in the spread of Christianity throughout the region. This period also saw interactions with neighboring states, including Denmark and Norway, as well as conflicts with indigenous Sami tribes in the northern territories. The events of the 12th century set the stage for further political developments and consolidation of power in Sweden.

In the year 1100, the Kingdom of Syunik survives as a precarious and isolated bastion of Christian Armenian independence, desperately clinging to the rugged Zangezur mountains. The realm faces constant, overwhelming military pressure from the powerful Seljuk Turks to the east and south, who seek to eradicate this final pocket of local resistance. Compounding this existential threat is a severe crisis of leadership, as the crown is held by the vulnerable child-king Grigor II Senekerim, leaving the royal bloodline perilously fragile. Consequently, the heavy burden of governance and diplomatic survival falls upon the shoulders of the formidable Queen Mother Shahandukht II. Down in the valleys around Kapan, the kingdom's tactical defense is almost entirely dependent on the brilliant but overstretched General Bgheno Khosrovik. He leads a desperate campaign using heavy mountain infantry to repel endless waves of nomadic cavalry and heavily armored Seljuk incursions originating from Ganja. Ultimately, Syunik is a realm on the brink of annihilation, relying on its impregnable mountain fortress of Baghaberd and sheer martial stubbornness to buy a few more years of freedom.

Few records about the 12th century Tavastians are known. Therefore, the main source is modern archaeology. In 1143 the Karelians raided Tavastians. The core area of ancient Tavastia was formed around Lake Vanajavesi. Example of organized cooperation of iron age Tavastians are the hillforts that form a clear line in south-north direction around Hämeenlinna. Most remarkable from these hillforts is the Rapola Castle which is the biggest hillfort found in Finland, but also Tenhola hillfort in Hattula and Hakoinen Castle were important fortresses. Villages were often developed around the fortresses and for example Hattula and Vanaja-Janakkala had their beginning in this way. The Novgorod First Chronicle describes Tavastians in frequent conflicts with Novgorod and Karelians as well as other Baltic Finns from the 11th to 14th centuries.

The Taifa of Balansiya originally emerged as a wealthy, independent Muslim state following the collapse of the Caliphate of Córdoba in the early eleventh century. Its strategic coastal location and immense agricultural prosperity made it a constant battleground for rival Moorish warlords and ambitious Christian monarchs alike. The political landscape shifted radically when the exiled Castilian commander El Cid conquered the city in 1094, forging his own independent principality. By the year 1100, following his death, his widow Jimena Díaz rules this isolated enclave, struggling to maintain her husband's hard-won domain. Her most terrifying challenge moving forward is the relentless advance of the North African Almoravid Empire, which seeks to reclaim the entire region. Without guaranteed reinforcements from the fractured Christian kingdoms to the north, the city's local defenses are severely overextended and highly vulnerable to prolonged sieges. Ultimately, the survival of this precarious independent state relies on desperate diplomacy and unyielding martial resilience against seemingly impossible odds..

The idea that Rus was a monolithic state with a single ethnos, formed by the later Empires, which wanted to create an illusion of unity of its population. In reality, Rus has never controlled the territory drawn on the maps. The territory was home to many ethnic groups and principalities that fought, traded, and befriended each other. The main unifying factor was Christianity, but it was practiced by a minority who were the elite. The main population was pagan. Over time, the elite spread the culture to the general population, but this happened many centuries after the collapse of Rus. In 1097 to stop the endless wars was organized Liubech Congress, at which the separate branches of the once united dynasty divided the power. Possession of the Volhynian Principality was legally given to Davyd Igorovich. In the same year 1097, with the support of the Kyivan Grand Knyaz, Davyd Igorovich started a war with the Terebovlian prince, whom he blinded. Toward the end of his life, as a result of diplomatic and military games, Davyd Igorovich lost the title of Volhynian Prince, but had extensive holdings.

The Kingdom of Gwynedd was a sovereign state in northwest Europe traditionally said to have been founded in 843. Its territories expanded and shrank, but it came to occupy the northern third of the island of Great Britain, sharing a land border to the south with the Kingdom of England. It suffered many invasions by the English, but under Robert the Bruce it fought a successful War of Independence and remained an independent state throughout the late Middle Ages.

The archaeological Žemaitian culture of burial grounds existed from the 5th to the 14th century. In 1100 there was no unified state on the territory of Žemaitia (Samogitia). The region was divided among several tribal Žemaitian principalities, which united against common enemies, traded among themselves and fought each other (Karšuva, Knituva, Kulenė, Šaule, Upytė). Due to the lack of written sources, information about the region has been reconstructed from archaeology and later written sources.

During the Viking Age, the Zemgalians (Semigallians) fought against Swedish Vikings for control of the lower part of the Daugava waterway. In 1100 there was no unified state on the territory of Zemgalia (Semigallia). The region was divided among several tribal Zemgalian principalities, which united against common enemies, traded among themselves and fought each other. In 1106 Polatsk made an attempt to conquer the Zemgalian lands, but was defeated and lost 9.000 warriors (the number is obviously exaggerated, but the losses for Polatsk were very significant). At the start of German conquests Zemgalians lands were divided in Upmale, Dobele, Spārnene, Dobe, Rakte, Silene and Tērvete tribal principalities.

By the year 1100, The Imarat of Zirid had been reduced to a precarious coastal enclave, severely weakened by the ongoing Banu Hilal and Banu Sulaym bedouin invasions. Ruling from the heavily fortified peninsular capital of Mahdia, Emir Tamim ibn al-Mu'izz desperately sought to maintain his dynasty's sovereignty and maritime influence. The vast inland territories, including the former political center of Kairouan, had largely been lost to the advancing nomadic confederations, forcing the Zirid administration to rely almost entirely on naval trade. To ensure their survival, the Zirids concentrated their military efforts on defending their remaining wealthy port cities, such as Sousse and Sfax, transforming them into vital economic lifelines. Although they shared a common Sanhaja Berber lineage with the neighboring Hammadid State to the west, relations between the two realms remained strained by historical betrayals and competing territorial claims. This geopolitical isolation catalyzed a profound societal shift, as the Zirid Emirate transitioned from an expansive continental power into an embattled, seafaring city-state network. Despite these insurmountable pressures, the Zirid court in Mahdia managed to preserve a sophisticated Islamic civilization, sustaining a fragile balance of power in the central Mediterranean..

You call it honor. Others might call it foolish pride.
I swore I would earn fame enough to drown out every silken emir’s name. Glory, like gold, should be shared among those who win it.
I will speak plainly. But if you repeat this tale, your tongue will be mine.
I made my living as a killer of killers. If a man wished to challenge an enemy and live, he paid me to provoke him. I never struck first. To do so would shame me before God.

But without family patrons, a healer’s door remains empty. The learned men feast with the emirs, while the poor die in the alleys. So I joined a caravan, tending the sick across the sands between Aleppo and Basra.
A hard life indeed, though rich in experience.
Well said. Glory must be earned, not inherited.
Listen well, for this is a story of pride — and of injustice.
I was trained in Aleppo, where men duel for sport in the courtyards of princes. My blade has tasted more honor than wine. Yet I despise armies — too many cowards hiding behind banners.
So, no rich patrons, no soft bed. A tragedy indeed.

Hmm. Many men begin their tales by naming their forefathers back to Adnan. I will not. A man should be judged by his own deeds, not by the bones of his ancestors. And besides, my kin cast me out long ago.
When raiders burned our tents, I led the survivors across three days of sand. None died of thirst, though I thought I might.
I fought at Harran, at Aleppo, and at the frontier against the Franks. I saw cowards praised as heroes and brave men forgotten because their fathers were poor.
The Fatimid caliphs ruled from gilded halls, but in the alleys, the guilds ruled with knives. I kept order for the spice quarter, made sure debts were remembered.
Still, I have some silver, and the road ahead. Perhaps your warband has need of a steady hand and sharper mind than most soldiers?
Now I invest not in caravans, but in swords. Armies are the truest merchants: they buy with blood and sell with fire.
Hah! The emirs of today are merchants’ sons and slaves’ grandsons. I serve no such men. But for gold, I will show any prince what true noble blood can do.
A duelist from Aleppo who swore never to strike from behind. Cast out by a cowardly lord, he now sells his sword to those with honor enough to meet his price.
A skilled engineer exiled from Mosul after a failed siege. He now hires out his expertise in fortification and destruction alike.
Since then, I’ve kept my blade and my word for those who pay honestly — and threaten those who don’t.
The desert raises harder children than any city. I am proof.
Of course. But what of your own deeds, not your grandsires’?
Perhaps. Still, if your banner is clean and your word good, I will draw for you.
But one emir, too cowardly to face me, sent his guards instead. I can kill one man, not ten. So I fled, taking only my sword and my oath never again to bow to a liar.

I was born to a slave girl in the house of a qadi of Damascus. He raised me with his sons, teaching me the letters of Galen and Ibn Sina, so I might one day become a physician. I thought knowledge would win me respect.
Do you wield the sword as well as the tongue, or only the latter?
My clan descends from a lesser branch of the Banu Kilab. When the Sultan calls, we ride beside the great banners, yet when poets sing, they name only the chiefs of the powerful.
Now I return to the world, not to preach but to test my faith in fire and sword. Perhaps in war I shall find what peace denied me.
A former scholar turned ascetic who lived in the desert for years. He now walks the world again, seeking divine purpose through hardship.
You seem distracted. Have you not heard of the Banu Sulaym’s valor at Sirte and Kairouan?
Now I write my lessons in steel. Each battle is a line, each victory a verse.
I learned much on those journeys — wounds from ghazi raids, fevers from the marshes, and all the torments of men and beasts. Yet the endless dust and the arrogance of captains wear the spirit thin.
You seek my story? Very well. It is written in dust and prayer.
I studied at the Dar al-‘Ilm in Cairo, memorizing the laws of men who never saw a battlefield. I grew tired of arguing parchment while the world burned.
I studied engines in Mosul and built siege towers for the Seljuk lords. My designs were praised, until they failed — through no fault of mine.
I’ve walked every road between Damascus and Sana’a, and buried friends on most of them.
My father led a small clan near Palmyra. I learned to ride and shoot before I could braid my hair. My brothers laughed — until the day I brought home a gazelle.
For twenty years I rode with caravans, guarding silk, incense, and fools with more gold than sense. Sandstorms and thieves are easy; treachery is harder.
Now I sell my craft to whoever pays — engines, bridges, fortresses. War is the only employer who never runs out of work.
Once I was a scholar in Basra, arguing the words of men long dead. Then plague came, and the mosques filled with the dying. I fled to the desert to find what truth remained in silence.
The wall collapsed before dawn, killing the vizier’s nephew. I escaped the noose only by bribing a guard with my last dinars.
I shall tell you… Ahem, attend closely, for mine is a noble line.
Then one night, the emir’s men raided us for unpaid tribute. I left three of them bleeding in the street and fled across the Nile before dawn.
For seven years I lived among the Bedouin, drinking from wells no map knows. The wind teaches patience better than any teacher of law.
Some whisper that our ancestor Zais was born out of wedlock — lies spread by the jealous Banu Ghutan. Yet I hold his sword, the proof of his honor, blessed by a faqih at Mecca.
I prefer silver to songs. But I respect your fire.
Perhaps your banner will be the one beneath which my name is finally remembered.
Heh. I used to collect taxes for an emir in Cairo — the kind who never paid what they owed.
A ruined merchant from Aden who once traded from India to Syria. Now he trades in war, where profit is quickest and risk certain.
You’d fit well in a company that honors courage.
Now I sell my aim to those who respect a good bow, no matter the hand that draws it.
You need walls taken or built? I am your man, though the sultan might disagree.
Ah, you have the eyes of a trader. I can tell. Let us speak of profit, not glory.
A lesser-born warrior of the Banu Kilab who seeks his own fame. The poets may not yet know his name, but the battlefield soon will.
Still, I cannot rest. Roads are in my blood. And danger keeps me honest.
When the vizier’s guards came for my mentor, I struck one down. Books can teach courage — but courage makes enemies.
A scholar turned soldier who abandoned Cairo’s libraries for the sword. His wit is sharp, but his blade sharper.
I began with one mule and a few jars of pepper bought in Aden. In three years, I had ships docking at Aqaba and Tyre.
My last caravan vanished near Petra. Only I survived — and I do not know if I fled from men or jinn.
You see the ink on my fingers? Once, it was the mark of learning. Now, it only stains my sword hilt.
A street enforcer from Cairo who once worked the spice markets. He knows every trick of intimidation and debt collection the city can teach.
My lineage runs deep into the sands of Najd, but few care for ancestry now. So I fight — and let my sword write the next line of my family’s history.
A Bedouin huntress and survivor whose skill with bow and horse rivals any man’s. She fights for silver, and for the freedom of the open dunes.
Born the son of a slave, raised in the house of a qadi, I studied the healing arts of Ibn Sina. When learned men refused me, I took my craft to the caravans and battlefields instead.
My father was Aytham, son of Thamuq, son of Munbilas the elder, who rode with the Banu Sulaym when they took Ifriqiya. Our blood traces to the tribes of Najd, pure and untainted.
A hardened caravan guard from the routes of Arabia. Superstitious, loyal, and deadly to those who threaten his charges.
Then pirates took my fleet, and a false partner took the rest. All that remained was my seal ring — and the memory of trade routes across half the world.
No doubt a sad state of affairs. So what do you do?
Oh, I suppose I can tell you. Nothing that no one doesn't already know, no how.
You're a nosy one, I see.
You want to know about me? Well, that's a story, that's a story.
Well, there's always work for the brave and the resourceful.
Ah, yes. Wise words. Do go on.
It is not without some reluctance that I tell this story, for it hardly does honor to my name.
So... What are you good at?
You're a cheerful one. Good day to you.
Refill my glass and I'll tell you.
You too are a victim of the hideous power of the state.
Yes... I can tell you my tale...

My father was an imperial cataphract. Alas, he died in battle against the Arabs, and I was placed under the local archon's guardianship. He had eyes for my father's estate, modest as it was, so he arranged for me to be married to his cousin.
I'll tell you my story. If it bothers you, I'd prefer you keep it to yourself - unless you've lived months on crusts of bread and chaff of grain, that is.
That's it? The dishonorable part? That you work for merchants? I'd thought it would be a lot worse.

I was an orphan, you see. Worked for a gang, as our kind must so often do. Did their foul work for them. But they perished in a siege, and I decided to strike out on my own, see what this fine land of Calradia could offer me.
A hard life, but I must admire your fortitude, at least.
Takes more to being a warrior than a horse and a sword, young one.
Heresy, rebellion, and looting are three intertwined serpents. You should bear that brand yourself, knave.

So, here I am, looking for a captain under whom to serve. I know the ways of an archon's court, and I know how to ride, but I am looking to master the ways of the sword. And if I learn my trade well, perhaps I shall one day reclaim my birthright!
Ah, the old days. And no doubt back then they complained about the older days. I've heard enough.
Aye, so you want my story then?
Anyway, I wandered about a bit, but now I think it's time I found steady work. You wouldn't need someone to stick a knife in those that need sticking, do you?
Then came the day that {IMPERIALCAPITAL} burned, and everyone was out looting and robbing, and that was my chance. Lifted a bag of silver from the Centaurs' stash and lit out on the road.

I'm an engineer. Most of us learned our trade and got our contacts through the army. It was a good system: it was the emperor's money, so the emperor's servants kept a close eye on us. But as everyone knows, the emperor ran out of money. The lords are in charge of fortifications now, and all they have to go on is the say-so of other engineers.
See, there's a lot of tales about me, and only some of them are true. The Turks call me by one name, the Arabs by another.

I'm a surgeon. I trained at the imperial academy in {IMPERIALCAPITAL}. I had many rich and influential patients in the town. I thought I was well shielded from the intrigues and dangers of the armenians.
My father was a cataphract in the east. We had a small estate to pay for his horse and armor. I was raised to take his place on the imperial troop rosters when he came of age.

I'm a soldier by trade. I've served in the Armenians' legions for 20 years. Once upon a time they were worthy of being called 'legions.' We served together for years, and we'd die rather than see our standards falter or fall.

Me and some lads from my village, we thought we'd run away, join some other lads up there who make their living on the highways, if you know what I mean. Didn't much want to go scratching a plow across the dry fields all year every year like my father did.
What do you want to know about? My family? Piss on them. I left home as a child and never had cause to regret it. My brothers can take my inheritance, and I hope they choke on it.

You may have heard of Ladimos the Red. He preached that the Heavens were getting ready to unload their wrath on landowners and merchant, that we had to drive them out and live pure lives and we'd be rewarded with a Pure Emperor, come down from the skies. This was some 10 years ago. Well, a lot of us ran off to follow him, some of us believed him and some of us had debts and some just wanted to take a lick at those that oppressed us.

My family had debts, so I signed up to be a soldier under one of Old Neretzes's kinsmen. I guess I always liked men's work more than women's work. The legions took hill women as scouts but I was never the hidey-sneaky type. So I did what I did to be in the spear line.

My father was a merchant in {IMPERIALCAPITAL}. We lived in a rich house, with many servants. I wanted for nothing. Our neighbor was a moneylender, who specialized in loans to the imperial guard. That turned out to be a bad neighborhood in which to live, when the riots came.

Far back as I remember, I was living on the streets of {IMPERIALCAPITAL} with a bunch of other dirty, barefoot scrogs. A group of men in our alley, they called themselves the Centaurs, I guess they took a liking to me. Gave me special errands to run from them - started with picking pockets, ended with sticking knives into their enemies. Back then I'd do anything for a handful of figs and cheese and a pat on the head.

You can imagine - it's a bit of a racket. People build arches that fall down, and his colleagues go on recommending him because he's someone's brother or old apprentice. The greatest sin in our brotherhood is criticizing the work of other engineers.
I've been in a lot of fights and I've killed a lot of people. Ask you around - you shouldn't just take my word for it. But never one who didn't deserve it, and never once outside a fair fight.

But one day I was contacted by an agent of the Bureau of Barbarian Affairs. I do not know how well you know them. Their original mission was to keep the foreign tribes divided and weak, but they expanded their remit into all the affairs of the Armenians, anything that might be deemed a threat. At first they wanted small harmless details about my patients. To do so was a violation of my oath, but I was anxious to have the favor of the Bureau. But soon they began to call on me for more and more.

But the Turks overran us, and he was slain, and our land was taken. Its revenues now belong to some tarkhan. Alas, the Armenians have little land to grant today, even to trained cavalrymen like myself who wish to serve. And horses are expensive.

But the Emperor led the pick of the legions into an ambush in the German woods. You may have heard that story. I was laid up sick at the time. But a lot of my comrades didn't come back, and things were never the same afterward.

But I was young and foolish. Bandits - well, who'd have thought? They're real animals. Always drunk and stabbing each other, or too drunk to feel cold so they catch the plague and end up coughing up blood, or drunk and asleep when the patrol comes around so they end up on the gallows - I suspect you get the idea.
I've fought in a few wars, for one side or the other. You want to know about my-comrades-in-arms? Piss on them too. They all turn on you in the end.

We built a great temple in the back country, out in the bush, called it the Kingdom of Truth. We whipped two imperial detachments sent to track us down. But Ladimos died, 'Called up to Heaven' he said on his deathbed, and then we lost our way a bit. We needed food and we needed money, so our chiefs started collecting 'taxes' from the villages below. Some started taking money from lords and merchants for protection of caravans. And those who grumbled - well, they started turning up dead in the dry streambeds.
Dressed as a man, of course. Weren't difficult to do. Not hard to fool men. Bound my breasts and watched where I pissed. It was easy.

The guardsmen came to burn our neighbor's house, so their debts would be forgotten. The flames spread to our house, and it was destroyed. My father tried to save his strongbox, and that was his undoing. A riot is a holiday for thieves and robbers, and some saw him dragging it through the streets, so they knifed him and took it. We tried to find shelter with my uncle, but there was no food in the city, and he turned us out. So we joined the refugees in the country, living on what we could steal from the fields.

Got a bit older though, and their interest in me changed. Filthy drunken louts pressing themselves against me, grabbing at me - I wasn't having that. Made up my mind to leave, but wasn't sure where to go.
Well, I don't play that game. If something's going to fall down and kill someone, I'll point that out. So, naturally, all my 'brothers' cut me out of contracts.

Let me tell you something else - war is not a game. It's not a game. Play by the rules and you die. The streets aren't the arena. If you think someone's your enemy, you take them down - don't wait for a polite challenge.

You may call it pride, but I do not wish to enlist as a foot soldier. So I work here in town, for merchants, for pay, a hired sword. All I can say is that I hope one day to purchase the land I need to serve our emperor, whoever sits in the throne, as my father did.

After Arenicos's so-called reforms, they try to maintain an army on the cheap, letting the rich run the show out of their own pocket. No wonder the whole thing's collapsed into a bunch of squabbling factions and we're mocked by the barbarians we used to rule.
So that was no kind of life, neither. I left the woods, paid a little money to friends who got my name off the outlaw list, and now I'm a regular law-abiding citizen. Officially, that is.
About my past, that's all I have to say.

So I left. And a short while later the emperor sent a third detachment, bigger than the others, and that was the end of the Kingdom of Truth. My old comrades - I see them sometimes from time to time, some in a lord's retinue, others in a cage with R for 'robber' branded on their forehead.

Then one day our commander led us into an ambush. The apple doesn't far fall from the tree, you could say. I didn't see the battle but was part of the rout. That was the end of army life for me. Don't care for glory-hounding lords leading me to my death. But I still like to fight.

I found a guardsman, alone and drunk. I have no idea whether he was one of the ones that set fire to our neighborhood. Maybe I should not have done to him what I did to him. But now I have his sword. It's been very useful.

So, anyway, I am forced to spend my time in taverns, taking whatever work can be found. I can oversee the building of most structures, or, if the need is there, I am also adept at knocking them down with catapults, rams, and mines.

I don't like to brag about my own deeds, so I'll leave it at that. I do a lot of work for the merchants around here, but they don't own me. I'm my own man. I just take their money. It's not like I'm a mercenary or something like that.
I try at least to pick and choose my master, and hope at least that some of our equestrian honor rubs off on the men of commerce.

Well, I can't just sit around and drink myself to death, so I sell my sword to anyone worth following. I'm a good trainer - I don't bother with horsemen or archers, but if you've got good steady footmen I can do a lot with them. I know a bit about siege machinery too.
Life's better here in the city. More 'civilized,' you could say. Oh, the work can be a bit rough and tumble, but I feel I can relax after a long day with more refined company, like your good self.
I can fight. And I don't mind doing work that others would shirk.

I learned a few skills up in the hills, how to follow a trail and spot an ambush, most useful to caravaneers. So I reckon I can probably stay ahead of the hangman. A regular job wouldn't hurt, though.

Yeah.. The merchants give me jobs. But I'm not sure I care much for guarding caravans. A lot of sitting around listening to boring talk about prices. Look, I can wield a sword or spear and I can also repair them. Wouldn't mind trying my hand them at making them too. If you've know a captain with a good company, a fighting company, maybe he'd be interested.
I think my story shows that I am adaptable, at least. If there was room for me in a warlord's retinue, say, I imagine I could quickly learn whatever skills were needed.
A rather sad tale of deceit and disgrace.
The starving do what they must.
Yeah, I'll tell you my story. Pass the wine and listen close.
I'm an engineer, with imperial army training. I'm sure by now you've met a few of us around, and know a bit about what we can do.
I'm a warrior. A soldier of fortune, you might say. A damn good one, too, as my enemies would tell you if they could speak from the other world.
I'm a former imperial cataphract. Our skills, and our honor, needs no further introduction. But I was unable to afford my horse and armor, so I took work with merchants, as a hired sword.

I'm a soldier of the imperial legions. How we came to this sorry state is a sad tale that you've no doubt heard already from my comrades. But I'm sure you're familiar with our mettle in battle, and our skill at turning youths into soldiers.

When I was a lad, I dabbled in crime and banditry a bit, but am now seeking more honest work. I still like the fighting and killing part, though. Anyway, I'm sure you've met a fair amount of men like me on your journeys.
I kill for a living. You don't look too wet behind the ears, so I'm sure I don't need to tell you any more about myself than that.
Aye, well, once I was a rebel up in the back country, but rebels never last too long. Now I just want to serve and get paid. You've been around. You've met men like me before, I'm sure.
I dressed as a man to serve in the legions. There are many of us who've done that, believe it or not. You've probably met one of us before, even if you didn't know it.

I was a merchant's daughter. There was a bout of unrest in our home city, and our home and warehouses were burned and our family made penniless. I shall spare you the details. I am sure you've heard plenty of similar tales in these times.
You truly are the dregs of the street, my lady.
You broke your oath. It is not surprising that you fell further.
And to think you had all the advantages of an educated childhood.

So, here I am. Perhaps I am not the most experienced of warriors, but I can learn. I cannot go back - I learned that the archon filed suit that I stole a horse - my own horse, by right! - which shows you what a cad he is.
I don't mind talking about it.
A man of integrity, or simply one who backbites his peers? I have no idea, and wouldn't want to take the risk of hiring you.

But this cousin... I would not marry that man! He was a boor, a drunk - never there was a night that he did not reek of wine, never a morning that he did not reek of vomit! But a cataphract's daughter is not some chit you can marry against her will. I took a horse from my father's estate - my horse, legally - his old sword, and rode off.
You've said nothing about yourself, and your one word contradicts the other. I have better things to do.

I was a surgeon, trained at the imperial academy. But my home and infirmary were burned in a bout of unrest, and now I must wander the world a bit. There are many of us out there, you know, forced to make what living we can.
I can tell you my story, though it is painful to recall.
A cavalier of the Armenians doing errands for traders! The shame of it!

One time they came at midnight - they had a man who plotted against the Emperor, they said, and they needed a confession, and wished me to use my art to elicit that confession. If I refused, they said, they would disclose our relationship to my patients - I would be ruined. I went with them, to my shame, and what I was asked to do to that man's body -- I shall not repeat it.
You've got spirit, I'll give you that.

I fled a bad marriage. There are many like me; I meet them in every tavern in Calradia. I am lucky in that my father was a cataphract, and taught me to ride and fight before he died, and I suppose that's how I must make a living.

I should have refused - my practice was ruined anyway. To blot out the memory of that night, I took opium, until my pallid face so alarmed my patients that they no longer called on me. So I fled the city, and have wandered from town to town ever since. I would welcome steady work, if I could find it.
A knave who could not abide other men's knavery! May such wonders never cease.
It's not many who ask that question.
I'll tell you my story. Why not?
I am sorry for your fate, my lady.
Yes.. My story... Jealousy, envy of my talents. That's always been my undoing.
Certainly - I make no secret of my ambitions.

I lived in a village to the north of here, across the gulf. It is a cruel land; there is no strong king, and lords think nothing of ravaging their neighbor's lands. My mother was skilled in the use of herbs to treat disease and wounds. I had a happy peaceful childhood - until one day, a month before I was to be married.

When I was a boy, I was the best fighter in my village. 'You're stronger as a boy than a full-grown warrior,' people would say. I'm not boasting here - that's what they'd tell me. So when I came of age I went off to make my fortune.

My father was one of the leading warriors of our clan, but in his last battle his hamstring was cut. We've lived well off the wealth he brought home from his raids, buying land and thralls, but now I feel it's time that I bring home some silver of my own.

I'll tell you - what most people believe is a pack of lies. I was in the Royal Guard in the time of the old King. We took our discipline seriously; we were proud of it. Then the riots happened. What I saw in {IMPERIALCAPITAL}.. Even now it makes me feel ashamed.
I was a farmer. But I split a man's head open with a hoe. He was also a farmer. It was a dispute over a broken fence, between my pasture and his. I had no intention of killing him.

We Balts have a tradition. If two people have a dispute, and there's no witnesses, so it all comes down to one man's word against another's, then we let them settle it with swords. If one man doesn't like to fight, he can hire someone else to do the fighting. That's how it works with us. Probably other people do the same, because it's a good tradition.

My parents died when I was young. My sister married. Her husband wanted my parents' farm. So he hired a devious man, a fast-talker, who knew the law well. He said... I don't even remember what he said, in court, before the council. But the council awarded both of them the farm.

My father was a draftsman. He helped build towers and walls for the boyars. I used to help him in his work, drawing up his plans. I had a good hand for that. We went from town to town, employer to employer, just the two of us. It was a wonderful time, until he dropped dead, just before I entered my twelfth year.

I came from a good family, with much land. Since I was a girl, I wished to be a shield-maiden. I practiced fighting with the village boys and the old warriors. But it is a strange thing - while some families in our lands take pride in a daughter who takes up arms, others accord it a great shame, and my father was of the latter type.
How would I put it? I guess I'd say I'm a lady who's gotten a reputation for doing a man's work better then the men. I guess I'm a bit of a rarity. Although that's a bit of a surprise to me.

That was the day my life changed. A band from a nearby village came and attacked us. We had done them no harm; we had never even thought of them as our enemies. But they wanted our cattle. They killed my mother and the youth who I was to marry, and burned our village. Everything gone. Those who lived fled into the woods.

Started in the Vaegir guard. I found that I was the only real warrior among them. They were all about marching here and there in their pretty uniforms, not pulling sword from scabbard for months on end. I told them what I thought, and my captain told me to keep my mouth shut or leave. So I left.

I need to buy a ship, and hire men to row it. But I do not wish to sell our land to outfit a risky voyage, to risk depriving my father and mother of their comforts in old age, and my brothers of their hopes for a good marriage.

It wasn't easy for the men. They felt the city turn against them, blame them for killing the emperor. Whereas we were sure that we were innocent of his blood, that there was some sort of trick. But even so, there was no excuse.

His cousins came for me, to take me to judgment. I would have gone willingly; I would have paid blood-money. Gladly. But one of them laid hands on me, and a black rage came over me, and I killed two of them, too. I didn't want to kill them either.

I like to fight, so I made it known that I'd fight for anyone if the price is right. Shed a little blood, make a little coin, drink it away, make a little more, all in the cause of justice. Not a bad life, eh?
It did not matter much. I always preferred the woods. I made a better living shooting squirrels and rabbits and selling fur.

My mother had already died, so I was taken in by my uncle. But he didn't really want me. See, I had a birthmark on my shoulder, the kind that some people means the bearer can cast the Evil Eye. Whenever there was sickness in the streets of my uncles' village, the people would mutter and curse at me. Eventually they demanded my uncle drive me out of the village. It was no great loss for him to comply. Probably saved him worry over where he was going to find the money to marry me off.

I had no special desire to be married but my family found me a groom anyway. I consented, but my husband and I detested each other from the first. Once he insulted me in the marketplace, I cursed his manhood, he struck me, and I pulled a knife and he pulled his. I won.
You won't find me passed out in the straw in my own vomit when needed for a task. You won't have to bribe the guard to get me out of a cell because I got on a fight on my way to work.

I expect that my kin will soon return to their homes, but I will not. I cannot... I cannot be in a place where I am at the mercy of any beast on the rampage. I will ply my trade among warriors. I will learn to harm as well as to heal. And if the time comes for me to marry, I will live in a land where there is a king, even a tyrant, rather than raising a family amid the war of all against all.

Then I joined the Jomsvikings. The 'Shield Brothers.' It's a good name, you know? They spent most of their time hunkering behind their shields. Ha! Me, I'd wade into the midst of the enemy, dealing out death right and left - and, well, all they had to say afterward was 'Why didn't you keep ranks?'

So I have resolved to hire out my sword and make enough money for such a ship. Having done so, I shall take it to faraway shores and bring home silver and slaves so that we may buy land enough for all. In this way I will do my duty to my family.

We could have marched out in battle array. No one would have stood against us. If we couldn't restore order, at least we could have gone home with honor. But instead, we turned our anger against the city. My comrades looted, set fires, even murdered those who we were supposed to protect. It was a disgrace.
That was that. I could pay blood money for one man but not three. I fled. I cannot return.

Well, I guess I showed myself a bit too eager. The councils stopped accepting me as champion. Told me I sold my sword too cheaply, they said. What can I say? I have to look for other work now. It's a damn shame. I like duels - you don't worry about arrows, or someone coming up from behind. No need to stay sober for hours on end waiting for a fight that never comes. Just a few minutes of trouble, a bit of blood, and then usually a good meal afterwards.

But I've been thinking.. Maybe I want to marry. And I guess I need more silver for that, probably more than I can get from the squirrels. So... People tell me that warleaders will pay for a good scout. And I know the woods well.

I wandered from village to village, begging and stealing. You may imagine how I fared at the mercy of the robbers of the road, who had no more fear of sorcery then they did of man's laws. But eventually I learned to protect myself, and the body of one careless bandit afforded me with my first sword and leather jerkin.

The elders sat in judgment on our case. As it turned out, they had plenty of precedent. They accorded our fight a fair duel, and thus I was innocent of murder. On the other hand, I was excluded from his inheritance. I suppose that was fair, although I would have enjoyed wearing his jewels and riding his horse in front of his family.
Instead, for my fee, I'll make sure that those who need protecting are protected, and those who need to die are dead.
At any rate, if you know of a warband who is looking for someone who knows how to treat wounds, I would be grateful.
So I'm having no more of that. I'm on the look-out for an outfit that employs real fighters.
At any rate, if you know the leader of warband who's generous and honorable, he'll find no braver warrior to follow him than me.
I thought of going home. But I lost what denars I had saved during the riots. If there is a warband looking for good men, I would like to earn it back.

If the choice I had been mine, I would have never hurt anyone. I would live on my land, eat what I had grown, marry and have children. But the Heavens have decreed that I should eat by shedding other men's blood. In the city, rich men pay me well for that.
But look - I'd still be a fine addition to a fighting company. I know how to swing a sword and an axe, and know a thing or two about forging them and keeping them sharp as well.
I know the woods well. I can move quickly in them. I'll tell you all about a war party from the branches it broke marching through.

That is all there is to say, really. I still have the sword, and it is for hire, to those who pay well. I still remember a bit of my father's trade, too. I'll do most whatever is needed. The world had no mercy on me, so I feel no need to show any.

Suffice to say, I could not return to my father's house. I went on my way, happy to live the life of a warrior I had always dreamed of living. But soon I found out - the tales I loved as a girl, of shield-maidens who fought for honor, do not pertain to a woman with no family or land. One cannot fight for honor when one doesn't know where the next meal comes from. So I fight for pay.
Anyway, you come across a chief who needs a reliable sword in his warband, you let me know.
I was an herbalist in a village in the north. But our home was raided, and I've been forced to wander in search of work. There are many like me on the roads of Calradia.

Let me tell you friend, I'm hard. I've fought with the Jomsvikings, the Vaegirs, any mercenaries worth their salt, I've been with them. Others may tell you've they've done what I've done, but I'm the real thing.
My father sent me off into the world, to build our fortune with my sword. This is a common story among the sons of our people.

I was part of the old King's Royal Guard. But the people turned on us after his death, and attacked us. Maybe you've heard the story before. There's a whole lot of us, spat out into the world by the ungrateful Calradians.

I was a farmer once. I killed a man in a fight and could not pay the blood money, so I had to flee. It's a common enough tale in the northlands. I accept that my destiny will be blood and hardship, rather than the simple life on the land I once craved.

I was a sword for hire. Specialized in duels - you know, when there's a trial, and you can't work it out any other way. But you can run that racket too long - eventually the councils start banning you from fighting - so now here I am.

I'm a trapper, a hunter. Used to be I could make a good living through furs... But with all these bandits about.... I'd rather be part of an army, I think. Spent my whole life in the woods and I reckon I could do well as a scout.

I don't know where I came from. First thing I remember is wandering the roads with a bunch of other orphans, going from village to village begging and stealing. But now, you see, I've stolen a sword from a group of bandits we found sleeping off a drunken night, and I figure maybe I can be something different.
I am a warrior. A shield-maiden, as the Nords say. It is not uncommon in the northern lands. Perhaps you have met some of us before.
I guess I'd say that I'm just a lady who didn't care for her distaff, and took up a spear instead. If you want to know more, hire me, point me at your enemies, and I'll show you rather than tell you.
Aye - you've heard about the death of the last Emperor?
Look, friend, I'm here to drink, not talk. But if you really want to know, I'll give it to you in brief.
I'll tell you my tale. But I will warn you in advance: It is of no concern to me whether you approve or disapprove of what I did.
Pour yourself a drink stranger. I'll tell you all you need to know.
You are a most dutiful son and brother.
I have heard about the riots in {IMPERIALCAPITAL}. It was an ugly thing all round.
It sounds like you had no choice.
Councils these days. Always making changes...
That seems a reasonable ambition. A good scout can command a high price.
Indeed. No doubt such traditions encourages husbands to behave better than they might do otherwise.
Yes... So hard to find a dependable fighter these days.
It's a cruel world, and if you think a warrior's life is any easier, you have a painful lesson in store.
Has no one told you that leaving a gap in a shield wall is as good as treason?
Such pieties from a man who intends to pillage the labor of others.
The Guard didn't kill the Emperor? Funny, that's not what the witnesses said.
A man who cannot master his rage is a greater threat then the man who murders with intent.
You call that the cause of justice?
What woman wouldn't relish a husband smelling of half-cured skins, slept in for the whole winter?
Heavens protect us from evil! Away! Away!
You slew your husband in a duel? Get away!
I don't begrudge a warrior a few drinks and a fight from time to time.
I'll tell you, but I don't know why you'd be interested.
You know, we women suffer greatly when you warriors have your sport...

I was a cowherd. In most villages, this is a boy's job, because one must be alone in the hills. In our village there were few boys, and I was a good shot with a sling, good at keeping the wolves away.

My family was in a feud. Over stolen cattle, as is often the case in the upcountry. Well, the family we fought turned out to be rather stronger than us, and most of us were killed. The rest were scattered. I lived for a while as a thief, stealing to eat, but that is a bitter path, and now I am looking for something better.

The boys of the neighboring village would pester me. One of them, the chief's son, would not leave me alone. They wanted from me what all boys want. One day he came up behind me and tried to take me by force. But I had a knife...
One moment. I need a drink.
Hard to blame you for that, I suppose.

Every time I've fought with a band of my 'countrymen,' I've told them: 'Hold your lines. Stay firm. Fight as the Empires does: as a solid hammer, not a gaggle of goats.' And every time I have seen them disintegrate into a screaming rush as soon as the arrows start flying, to dash themselves on the enemy's shields or be cut down by cavalry coming in on the sides.
The trouble with prophecies... People remember the one that came true, never the ten that were false.

I could tell you of all my deeds, and you'd never believe me. But you know, if you'd met me a year back, I could have taken you to my hall some time and shown you them. Shown you my deeds! You heard that!

I was raised in a well-known clan, but my father died and my stepfather cast me out. It is a common enough story among our people. You may find many of us wandering the roads, our swords our only inheritance.
When a victim turns thief, that does not right the world.

The women in our family passed down the art of healing from generation to generation, and other... em... services, that can be accomplished with herbs. But for all our skill we remained poor, while richly robed, well-fed men with half our skill walked about the towns tending to the lords and ladies.
I am a connoisseur of horseflesh, my friend. No one knows horses better than I. But I find, alas, that often the best horses are wasted on unworthy owners, so I try to rectify that.
I'll tell you. You may wish to get yourself a drink.
Yes - many is the healer who has come to specialize in the diseases of the rich.

But I had killed three men with a spear that day, and found I had a taste for it. And I learned that thieves grow rich, while honest men die. So I lived in the hills, and took the cows of families more fortunate then my own. But I sold the cows I took, and kept the denars close to my chest.
I did not know what to do with his body. I buried it up in the hills, then told my parents. For fear of bloodshed, they told me to leave, to find my way in the world some other way.
A man should fight for his hearth and his kin, however much they disappoint him.
Perhaps one should not press a courtship too far, when one is a bandit.
Anyway, well, I've had it with narrow escapes from charging cataphracts, and I'm going to seek work in a more professional force.
Good thing you were exempt from the laws of man, eh?

Aye, once I made a fine living, in the Empire, stopping merchants on the roads and asking 'em for a bit of change. But there was a lass there, beautiful as the moon and just as cold, and she was my undoing. Courted by an imperial prefect but I thought, I can do better than that, with my takings, and I brought her the pick of the rings and finery and asked her to pass the evening with me.
Very responsible of you. Can't go killing off the whole village, now.
Give me a minute. It has been a long time since I spoke more than a few words at a time to others.
So anyway, I need money to build a new hall, and start a new collection. So if someone wants to pay me my worth as a warrior, my spear is theirs!
There are customs for that sort of thing, trials, blood money, you know.
I shall tell you. Is there a bard in the house? He may wish to take notes. I believe this is fine material for a song.
When my second suitor passed of a fever, I was unnerved. When my third suitor was thrown from his horse on a hunt, I knew I must do something..
May all of us have such honorable foes!
We came down on the thief's village one day at dawn. They were too many, and we were beaten. My brothers and most of my kin were all slain. I had nowhere to go.

I was a robber on the highways, in the Empire, making a fine living from the merchants on the roads. But I loved a girl in town, and snuck in to visit her from time to time. Then I got caught, and had to reveal the hiding place all my hard-earned loot to the guards to escape the noose. So here I am now.

They would sit around the fire at night and belittle each other. I was never quick with my tongue and the others learned to gang up on me. At one point I could take it no longer - I stabbed one in a fight. No one knew how to treat the wound, so he bled to death. And then I fled.

I was raised as a stableboy. But I had a gift for breaking horses, and for my hard work, and the risks I took to my neck taming young stallions, the old lord promised me that on my fifteenth birthday I should have a horse of my own.
Indeed. There's much to be learned from the foreigner, whoever the foreigner is to you.

So I acquired some denars - I will not say how - and with it bought a silk robe and some jewelry. This got me inside the doors of rich men's houses, and the cures I worked, and the reputation I earned, have done the rest.
So, you want to know about the games that Fate has played with me?

I am a horsethief. I come from a region where to be a horsethief is an honorable profession, and I am very good at it. But it is dangerous work, as owners can be vindictive people, and I am seeking safer work - as a mercenary, perhaps.
Sounds like you have a good head for business.
Envy, yes, the only possible explanation for why your clan drove you out. Such a terrible sin!

Soon after I came of age, we got wind that our neighbors would raid us for cattle. We did not know by which road they would come. I was sent with a few of our tenants to hold a ford that was far out of the way.

Well, he did not believe in such things, so he laughed, tossed her a few coins, and sent her on her way. I grew up. When my first suitor was skewered by a spear in battle, I grieved, but thought little of it.
It sounds as though you had no choice.
I'm a former Wolfskin. No doubt you have heard of us. I am not proud of what I did as a Wolfskin. But I am proud of the woodcraft I learned.

I am Battanian. But for 20 years, I fought for the Empire. Indeed, most Battanians my age learned their trade in the legions. We saw no dishonor in it. They fed us well, they paid us well, they respected our courage.

My family was not one of the greatest clans of the Battanians, but neither are we among the poorest. When I came of age, my family sent me to join the Wolfskins. You may have heard of this tradition - for three years we live in the woods and do not eat cooked meat, wear spun cloth, or sleep under a roof, and according to the law we are beasts, not bound by the laws of men.

My uncle - he had a great herd of cows, and in the Battanian upcountry that is only kind of wealth we value. But they were taken by his chief herdsman, a man we trusted. So we took up spears to get them back, but my uncle was now poor, but the thief had many kinsmen. Having nothing else to lose, my uncle ordered that even the women of our family take up spears and ride out to fight, and so we did.

I do things in the old way, and so whenever an enemy falls to my spear, I take their head! Let's see - I have Brechtan the Old, Lamaich the Lame -- don't let the names fool you, these were great warriors - Archan the Bull, so many others! A true Battanian never boasts, because his deeds are hung over the hearth for all to see. At least that's the way it used to be.

But there's no legions any more. And since Caladog became king, well, he's gotten the young to think that to fight for the Empire is treason. Treason to what? 'Battania'? There is no Battania. Never has been. Just a bunch of quarreling warlords, who'll steal your cows as soon as you turn your back on them.
Some speak well of their time in the Wolfskins. It is intended to teach you the ways of the woods. But the 'pack' I joined were all rich feral children, playing at being animals.

I am the prince of horsethieves! I have stolen Aserai mares from amid the tents and ridden them across the desert under the moon, I have taken Vlandian stallions from their paddocks, the sturdy ponies of the Khuzaits, and the steady geldings of the imperial lancers. But, I'll be the first to admit, it is risky work, so sometimes I do other jobs.
So, what you're saying is that you're a horsethief.

I come from the highlands. My people were suspicious folk. It is easy to them to get into their heads that a child, especially a girl, practices witchcraft. I had two neighbors die of fevers within the same season, and so I was chased from my home and driven to fend for myself. Which I can, and did. I forge my own weapons and can wield them as well, but now I'm looking for steady work.

When I returned to my stepfather's hall, my mother met me outside, in tears. She had given me up for dead - my stepfather knew the direction from which the enemy clan would come, and had intended for me to die. She did nothing to stop him, but since I had survived, she bid me flee - for if not, she feared, it was inevitable that our clan should sink into the abyss of kinslaying. So here I am, looking for a worthy lord for whom to fight.

By the time I became a woman I was sick of filthy huts and puking babies. I came to the towns and inquired after which households, among those who had wealth, might have a patient for me. Of course when I showed up at the door in my torn, stained dress they slammed it in my face.
A boy like you killed three champions, eh? Well, all things are possible, I suppose.
But I don't intend to live this way forever. There are a thousand paths to turning outlaw, you see, but they mostly come to a single end. So I'm here, in the town, looking for other work.
Barbarians. Just when you think you've heard it all... Good day to you.

I resolved to take up the profession of arms, so that all men know that I am not the marrying type. I forge my own weapons, to avoid going into town whenever possible. And I tell all others of the curse upon me, as soon as I meet them. And I am far from my family, so no man will go to my father to ask for my hand.

Well now, I am a warrior of the Battanians. There is no greater boast than that, I will tell you! But perhaps if you hire me, I can tell you more later about the great names I have slain and the heads I have taken.

I am Battanian by birth but I served with the Empire. Many of us did. A brave lord, a captain who cares for his men... What does it matter in which language your oath of fealty is given, as long as you honor it?

At first I was angered, because I believed that I was being kept away from battle and glory. But as it turned out, that's the way the enemy army came. When I saw them at the ford, I challenged their leaders to single combat, as that was our way. They accepted, and sent forth a champion. To make a long story short, I slew him, and then two more who came after him. The rest graciously admitted that my victories meant they were obliged to retreat.

But I've noticed something - more denars is spent on war than on anything else. So, if someone's raised an army, and doesn't want to lose their investment to infected wounds and fevers, well, it might be worthwhile to employ me.

I saw how much tradition was worth. I was not answerable to the law, but I heard soon enough that the family of the youth I'd stabbed hired men to kill me. I stayed in the woods, living alone. I am happy there, most of the time. But sometimes I yearn to be among other men, and come to the city to look for work.
My story? This is my tale in a nutshell - men's greed for cattle cost me my home and my kin.
Pull up a chair, friend - you'll be glad you asked!
Certainly. The more who know about my skills, the better.

A lot of heads... You can imagine, a lot of other warriors were envious of me. Some in my village even conspired against me, had me expelled. I lost my hall, and I had to bury the heads. I doubt you could recognize them any more. What a pity, eh? A collection like that will never be seen again.
I am no warrior, not yet - but I could be one. I am good with a sling, and a knife. I can run fast. I can bear hardship. I would stand my ground, because I have nowhere to run.

She agreed, eagerly enough! There was wine and talk, but too much wine, and I slept off. Then woke in the morning, I did, and hooves were clattering outside and up comes the prefect and a file of horsemen, and away they took me to the town to be hanged.

Blessed be the Gods, happened that my cousin Aed was in the guard. He sprung me that night from the prison, and together we went roaming round the country. But a passing magistrate decided he weren't parting with his purse, and pulled his blade rather than handing it over like a sensible lad. I took him down, but now before my poor Aed was butchered. See now the price of woman's ingratitude?

I was a shepherd. Normally the job is given to boys, but I always had a knack for bows and slings, which we use to keep the wolves away. The trouble with being a shepherd, though, is that there's always the chance of quarrels with the herders of the neighboring village over disputed pastures or missing sheep. Perhaps I was too good with a bow - I killed a neighbor. My parents were poor and could not afford the blood money, so I fled.

When I was just a baby, a woman said to have the Sight came to my father's hall. When she saw me, she told him that she saw the mark of the faeries upon me. She performed a divination, and said she had learned that I was to be a prank played on mankind: I should grow up to be a great beauty, but that any man who proposes to marry me shall die.
Once I was just another back-country healer, attending to squalling babies and superstitious villagers. But now I'm trying to make the money that my skill with medicine deserves.
Oh, I'll tell you. It's a fine tale, full of adventure and romance, but tragic too.

You may have heard of my father - Cynan fen Aedeg. Many called him Cynan the Brave. It's my life's goal to be his worthy son, though he died when I was a baby. My stepfather, though rich in land and cows, does not have the same reputation, although I resolved early in my life that duty to my mother necessitated that I serve him as loyally as I would my natural father.
I doubt you have such a collection, and if you did, it would be the last thing I'd like to see.

So here I am now, drinking to my poor cousin's memory, and looking for a bit of honest work. Well, it needn't be too honest, I suppose. I have a few skills that might be of use - among other things, if you ever happen to acquire any contraband you wish to sell, I reckon I can spot you a good price in the markets.
Aye, I can tell you my story.
Of course. Every felon is just an honest man wronged. I've heard a hundred such tales and I've no wish to hear another.

But the old lord died, alas, and when my birthday came, his heir laughed at me. He told me that a fine horse would be wasted on me; perhaps I would like a goat. So that night I took the best animal in the stable, and rode off.
I was the son of a household slave in a coastal kasbah, but my father bought my freedom when I was young and sent me to learn from a healer and a caravan-master.
I learned words of plants and of long routes across the High Plateaux; when trade wagons left for Sijilmasa or across to al-Andalus I would go with them and tend the men.
Medicine did not promise steady coin, so I took to travelling with caravans as a surgeon and guard. The desert makes a man patient — and sharp with a blade when he must be.
Now I wait for a caravan or an emir who pays fairly. I can stitch, bind, and guide; I can also show a caravan the secret springs of the desert.
Born low, trained to heal and guide caravans. I seek employers who value knowledge of the desert and hands that mend as well as strike.

Hmm. Many men would begin their story by reciting their ancestry. I will not do this. A man should be judged on his own deeds, and a long list of ancestors does him no credit. Also, my family does not acknowledge me, so why should I acknowledge them?
Service on caravans breeds more thieves than saints.
My father was a qadi; I'd been tutored to study law and scripture, to be learned and measured.
But when my teacher told me the world wants practical men — those who know siege engines and how to stop pestilence — I discovered my head fit numbers and geometry better than words.
So I became an engineer of sorts, making contrivances for sieges and for irrigation, though learned men scorned me for leaving the madrasa.
Siege-work pays when the city falls. When it does not, receipts are but paper. I take what coin I can find and keep moving.
Trained in geometry and siegecraft, I am an engineer who prefers earth and rope to ink. Seek me if you need walls taken or mended.
I'll tell you my story. A fine lesson in fate, if nothing else.
A scholar of action rather than words.
Ha — the quarries want hands more than verses.
My father's name is known across a dozen valleys, my grandfather's as well — we have a lineage that some men recite with pride. I can recite our genealogy as others recite prayers.
These things matter when chiefs parley and bonds are sworn. But lineage alone does not feed a sword-arm or buy a good mount.
So I sell my blade where men will pay for skill, not only for a name. The desert listens to deeds more than to pedigrees.
I fight for those who count coin and oath alike. If you need a sworn man who remembers from whence he came, I'm for hire.
A man of proud blood who nevertheless takes service. If you pay honorably, you'll have a man who remembers to keep his word.
A princely tone for a mercenary life.
If your lineage buys you nothing, I recommend a new one that pays.
I belong to a lesser clan who answer to larger confederations when called; when banners were raised for the emir the great names took most of the glory.
We are not unknown for lack of courage, only for lack of poets. After a victory the songs speak of the great house while our axes go unmentioned.
So I left to find my own renown under a banner that might recognize me as more than a shadow of another. Perhaps a captain will grant a man a name worth singing.
I'll find a master who sees the man as well as the clan. Or I'll find land and buy the poet myself.
A warrior of a lesser clan who seeks a banner that will let him rise from the ranks and earn his own song.
I will tell you. Perhaps you will think I am petty-minded, but a man's reputation is a valuable thing...
Glory and its unequal distribution is an old complaint.
Better to have coin and land than a song that fades.
I have a gift for blades. A man I cross will step out and draw steel before he knows why he has done so.
I do not like courts and mustered hosts. A battlefield is ugly and chaotic; I prefer an artful stroke when the terms are mine.
But a lord who refuses to pay me once laughed and turned me out. I can take one man fairly; I can't stand ten at once. So here I am, looking for work with captains who keep their word.
For now I’ll join a captain who keeps faith. I fight fair, but I fight hard.
A sword for hire with a strict code: all fights must be fair. One who values courtesy in the cutting of throats.
I will tell you my story. I haven't... I haven't spoken of this before, to anyone. Perhaps it's the wine here.
A dangerous man with a code.
Honor is a convenient excuse for murder.
I grew up where every bazaar lane had its protector — men who kept watch over trade and exacted a cut. My father was one of them, and I learned how to keep order in narrow alleys.
When a new governor's captain came and demanded bribes and 'cooperation', my father refused. He was beaten and our house was marked.
We left rather than bend the knee. I now make my living in far towns where no one knows my surname and I can sell my arm as needed.
I will guard caravans or a market for honest coin. My loyalty goes where it is earned.
An alley-warden who will not bend to corruption. If you need a watch on goods or a steady hand in a fight, I'm for hire.
Better to serve a lawful captain than a corrupt official.
I'm a blade's man. I take coin, no piety; nobles spin tales of being forced into violence. Piss on that.
If a man stands against me and will not yield, I end it quickly. I prefer good wine and the comfort of a warm tent.
Ask if I will work for you, and I will answer plainly: name your price and I will tell you whether I will accept it.
If you need a killing done, do not ask for sentiment. Ask for coin and discretion.
I kill for coin and pleasure. Pay well and have no regrets.
You want a story? Then toss a coin — stories are expensive.
The searing plains and the high gorges know me. I have guided flocks, led raids across the passes, and brought caravans safely through sand and bandit.
The viper and scorpion pass me by; no storm has broken my camp. The desert teaches its favourites to read wind and hoof like men read speech.
I am {MET_WANDERER.FIRSTNAME}, and I answer to names of beasts and stars alike. If you need a guide, I know the hidden wells and the tracks the caravans use in dark months.
I roam the desert and sell my knowledge. Horses cost coin even to the Bedouin; I must sometimes take service to keep my mounts.
A desert-scout and caravan-master; I know springs and ambushes and will bring your wagons through if you pay fairly.
Since you ask who I am, stranger, I will tell you.
{MET_WANDERER.FIRSTNAME} is enough. Will you guide a caravan?
Master of empty words, are you?
We were a clan in the green foothills until raiders and rival chiefs took our grazing; we fought and managed to keep our herds by single combat, but it left kinless and weary men behind.
When clansmen mocked that our women fought for us, old grudges flared. Bloodfeuds took our young men until the household could not recover.
I left to find my own fortune — fight for wage, not for the shame or pride of others, and one day buy land to restore our name.
I fight far from home so the taunts won't follow my family. If I can earn enough to buy pasture, I will return and be honoured as I desire.
A daughter of dispossessed stock who learned arms; she fights to restore family standing with coin and deed.
Hmf. Very well. I'll tell you - and you can decide whether my family should be ashamed of me.
A hard path but an honourable one.
Honor first, money second, as always.
My father was a merchant and left me a share of caravans and wares. When he died, my brothers went east; I stayed to mind the goods.
I bought a load of pepper at a discount, trusting the warehouse and its watchmen, only to have a brazier knocked over by a camel or servant in the night.
The store went up and so did my capital. Now merchants laugh at me as a rash woman who trusted poorly. I left that trade and took to wandering.
Fortune goes to the brave and the lucky. I wager again now, in men and in opportunity rather than warehouses.
A merchant's daughter ruined by fire who now sells her sword or services; trade taught me to judge men fast.
I can tell you my story, as merchants love to trade in tales of ruin and recovery.
A merchant's risk, misfortune was yours.
All of one's spice in one store — a harsh lesson.
As a child my mother sent me to the souk to beg and pick pockets; the big man of our quarter took a cut, as is the way of those who rule the back-alleys.
One day he beat my mother to death over a share. The truth is messy — that man was also my father; the sort of thing such streets breed.
I fled then, and made a living with the skills my parents taught me. Now I prefer blades to begging.
If you have ventures of dubious legality needing a discreet and sharp watcher, I may be of service.
An alley orphan who learned to steal and to fight; now I use those skills on the road for coin.
Oh, I'll tell you my story. I don't mind who knows.
You can rise above the mean beginning.
Those are dire tales from the alleys indeed.
My kin were farmers and herdsmen, but I trained in the sword from youth, for war often came to our doors.
I learned to haggle, to listen, and to fight when tempers ran high.
As a youth, I worked with masons rebuilding fallen walls.
I learned the ropes of ships young, and the cut of blades soon after.
My father tended sheep, but I learned the bow to fend off wolves and thieves.
I learned to row, to fish, and to fight upon the water.
From the stables to the hall, I learned the ways of the sword and horse.
My village burned when I was small, and I was taken in by soldiers.
I grew up among stone walls and the clang of weapons.
I learned my letters young, but war called me away from the monastery’s walls.
My kin taught me to farm, but raiders taught me to kill.
As a boy, I scavenged battlefields, learning the ways of weapons from corpses.
I fought in the levy under a local boyar when the Byzantines pressed their claim.
Later, I carried goods across mountain passes, blade at my side.
But stonework paid little, so I took service with soldiers.
As a youth, I sailed with corsairs who plundered merchant cogs.
Soon, my skill drew the attention of band leaders who sought my aim.
In time, I joined river bandits who plundered passing barges.
When my lord fell to intrigue, I lost all favor and standing.
I grew up in camps, learning spear and shield from veterans.
As I grew, I became a guard on the walls, watching traders and invaders alike.
I took up arms instead of ink, though I still recall the old prayers.
When the harvests failed, I turned to banditry, as many did.
A mercenary band took me in, raising me as one of their own.
Though we lost, I lived — hardened and with nothing left but my blade.
A caravan raid took all — but left me alive, with vengeance burning.
Soon I knew spear drill better than mortar and brick.
I left that life before it ended me, though I keep the sea in my heart.
I left them, for I wanted more than petty theft and blood feuds.
When the Byzantines sent soldiers against us, I fled with only my axe.
I took to the road, armor stripped, but pride intact.
When the army disbanded, I remained — a soldier without a banner.
But when wages failed, so did my loyalty. I left, blade in hand.
Now I carry both faith and steel, wandering where I am needed.
Yet I tired of preying on the weak and sought better fortune.
When they disbanded, I remained, a lone survivor of too many wars.
From the plains of Moesia, hardened by war.
From the merchant city of Ohrid, once rich with trade.
From Plovdiv, heir to ruins and wars alike.
From the Black Sea coast, ever torn between waves and war.

Once a novice among monks, now a man of the sword.
A peasant turned brigand, now seeking honest pay.
I grew up among the hills of Moesia, where the villages stood watch against raiders from the steppes.
My childhood was spent in the markets of Ohrid, where merchants from all lands crossed paths.
I was born in Plovdiv, where Romans once ruled and traders still pass.
I hail from the Black Sea coast, where sailors wrestle with storms and pirates alike.
I was born near the Rhodope Mountains, where shepherds and brigands often shared the same paths.

I was raised near Tarnovo, in the household of a boyar’s retinue.
