I grew up in the Balkan foothills, where life was harsh and neighbors harsher.
My family lived near Skopje, where armies marched often and villages burned.
Battle and hardship have shaped me. I seek coin and a lord who values loyalty.
Trade taught me patience, loss taught me strength.
I know walls — how to build them, and how to break them.
I know storms, steel, and the sway of decks beneath my feet.
My bow finds its mark. I do not waste words or arrows.
I have lived as both thief and fighter. Now I choose my own master.
I am trained in war, though fortune has cast me down.
War is all I know. Let me fight, and I will not disappoint.
A fortress taught me patience, discipline, and vigilance.
I am not a priest, but I remember wisdom in words.
I have lived rough, but I know loyalty when I see it.
Death and ruin taught me everything. I do not fear battle.
What I offer is my arm and my oath, for those who treat me fairly.
I seek work, not pity. Let us leave the past in dust.
If you need an arm steady in siege, mine is yours.
If you need a sailor who can fight, I am yours.
If you need a keen eye, I am your hunter.
If you feed me well and give me work, I’ll be loyal.
Give me command, and I will show my worth.

Steel and scripture both guide my hand.

I'm a surgeon. I trained at the imperial academy in {IMPERIALCAPITAL}. I had many rich and influential patients in the town. I thought I was well shielded from the intrigues and dangers of the byzantines.

I'm a soldier by trade. I've served in the Romans' legions for 20 years. Once upon a time they were worthy of being called 'legions.' We served together for years, and we'd die rather than see our standards falter or fall.

But one day I was contacted by an agent of the Bureau of Barbarian Affairs. I do not know how well you know them. Their original mission was to keep the foreign tribes divided and weak, but they expanded their remit into all the affairs of the Romans, anything that might be deemed a threat. At first they wanted small harmless details about my patients. To do so was a violation of my oath, but I was anxious to have the favor of the Bureau. But soon they began to call on me for more and more.

But the Turks overran us, and he was slain, and our land was taken. Its revenues now belong to some tarkhan. Alas, the Romans have little land to grant today, even to trained cavalrymen like myself who wish to serve. And horses are expensive.
A cavalier of the Romans doing errands for traders! The shame of it!
Aye, I can tell you of my craft, if you’ve a moment and a flagon to share.

I was born in Ulm, apprenticed to a guild mason who served both abbots and dukes. We built churches that kissed Heaven and bridges that defied the Rhine’s fury. I learned that stone listens only to patience, not pride.
When the bishop backed the Pope, the Emperor seized his estates. We were cast adrift—lords without title, soldiers without pay. I learned that chivalry tastes bitter when seasoned with hunger.
Now I sell my sword to any banner that flies high and pays honest coin. God forgive me, but loyalty alone feeds no man.
A knight by duty, not birth. That earns respect more than gold ever will.
I’ll not fault a man for surviving his lord’s ruin.
If you’ve need of a steady lance and sober counsel, I can serve. I’ve ridden with priests and princes alike, and I know the weight of both.
A dispossessed ministerialis knight of Mainz, loyal once to Church and now to whoever keeps faith with silver.
By Saint Ulrich, I’ve fought for every fool who could afford a banner.
I began as a footman under Count Welf’s levy, slogging through mud and fire in Italy. When the paymaster forgot our wages, I took command of those who’d still follow me—and found I’d a gift for it.
We sold our strength to city leagues and quarrelsome dukes alike. Once I kept order in Augsburg for three months, till the burghers realized they’d hired wolves to guard their sheep.
Now I ride alone. The men I led lie buried from Lombardy to the Elbe, and my sword still hungers. War is my trade, but death’s the only sure wage.

When the Emperor quarreled with Rome, our monastery patrons lost their coin. The masons scattered, some to Italy, some to ruin. I took my compass and chisel and walked where work still called for them.
A captain without a company is a fire without wood—eager to catch again.
You’ve seen too many campaigns to need sermons from me.
If you seek order among rabble, I’ll forge it. I ask no titles—only coin, discipline, and a cause worth dying for.
A battle-scarred mercenary captain of Bavarian stock, once commander of a Free Company. Cunning, loyal, and utterly without illusion.
You’d not guess by my robes, but I once stood beside princes at council.
I studied letters in Würzburg and law in Bologna, copying charters till my eyes burned. For a time I served as notary to an archbishop, drafting decrees that bound lords tighter than chains.
When the Investiture quarrel tore Empire from Church, my ink turned from scripture to accusation. One day I wrote the writ that condemned my own mentor. I left that night and never returned.
Now I lend my quill to merchants and warlords. A sharp mind buys freedom, if one’s conscience can afford the cost.
Knowledge is a blade few wield safely. You seem to manage it.
A learned man in rough company—let’s hope your wit cuts faster than a sword.
Now I sell my hands to whoever builds strongholds or tears them down. Stone is honest—men, less so.
If you need letters written, laws twisted, or treaties sealed, I’m your man. I swear my ink flows true, even when the truth bends.
A wandering clerk and scholar from Würzburg, once in service to bishops. Quick with quill and conscience alike.
Ja, I’ve been called brigand, thief, and worse. But hunger has no saints.
I was born to peasants near Erfurt. When famine came, I took to the woods with others like me. We robbed grain carts bound for the abbey and fed the starving. For that, they named us bandits.
I saw good men hang while fat monks prayed for their souls. I swore never again to kneel before a lord who’d sell salvation for coin.
Now I know the backroads, the tollkeepers, and which sheriffs take bribes. Call me outlaw if you must—but remember, outlaws still know honor.
A man who steals for bread may yet fight for justice.
Keep your hands where I can see them, friend.
If you need safe passage or quiet work done under moonlight, I can manage it. I’ve made peace with the law—by staying two steps ahead of it.
A Thuringian outlaw turned guide and scout, shrewd and loyal once trust is earned.
You sound a craftsman with both pride and sense. I’ll remember that.
You’ll find few who wish to hear a surgeon’s tale over supper.
I learned medicine in the infirmary at Regensburg, stitching pilgrims and monks alike. Blood teaches faster than books—if you live long enough to learn.
When plague struck, I bled men by the dozen and prayed thrice as often. Some lived, most did not. The abbey blamed my hands, not God’s will, and cast me out.
Since then I’ve tended soldiers in the field, nobles in secret, and thieves in alleyways. All men are equal when their breath rattles.
Mercy takes many forms. Yours simply stains the hands.
If you can keep my men standing, I’ll not ask which saints approve.
I’ll serve your company faithfully. I charge by the wound, not the soul.
A Regensburg-trained surgeon, cast from holy service yet still sworn to heal. Stoic, weary, and indispensable.
A man who serves both abbots and dukes must know how to survive between hammer and anvil.
Hire me, and I’ll raise your towers square and true—or pull your enemy’s down to dust.
A Swabian mason-engineer, versed in cathedral and castle alike. Once loyal to abbots, now loyal to silver.
God’s grace, you wish my story? Few men care for the tale of a servant knight.
My family were ministeriales, unfree knights sworn to a bishop in Mainz. We held land at his pleasure, rode at his command, and bled at his wars. I dreamed of honor, yet found only obedience.
Well, before we begin, here's a flagon of ale to your health - both physical and spiritual.
Mmm... I do appreciate virtue, but villainy makes for a much spicier tale.
Coin may be your goal, but skill is your worth.
My tale is not soft, but it is mine.
I am an Anglo-Saxon hunter, trained by hunger and hardship, skilled in bow and track alike.
I was born in Wessex, son of a reeve. My father wished me to till fields. I wished to sing of heroes.
I am an Anglo-Saxon thegn, dispossessed, wandering in England, offering my sword to those who value skill and courage.
I fought duels, won some, lost more. But I learned chivalry, and I learned the taste of dust.
I'm drunk, so I'll tell you.
I can tell you my story, but I don't know how interesting you will find it.
A woman forged by grief into steel.
I fought in sieges, in rebellions, in border wars in Wales. Always with contract, always with pay.
Soon I found it was not only game I could hunt — men too leave trails, and men too can be brought down by arrow or snare.
I once served a king, now I serve only chance and coin.
A displaced thegn, noble by birth, skilled by experience.
I sought glory — and still I do.
Freedom is worth more than comfort.
Skill counts for more than name sometimes.
Still, I wander. Each battlefield is a chance to prove worth, each victory a step toward glory.
I was the son of a thegn in Mercia, trained in arms and horse. Our lands fell to Norman lords, and I had to flee.
Forest laws are cruel things. You turned hunger into skill.
I now travel, lending counsel and subtlety where brute force alone would fail.
The world takes and gives back little, but skill counts always.
I learned that words can raise courage or rebellion as sure as steel.
I take commissions where arrows are valued, and the dead are counted by honor, not coin.
Coin buys loyalty, but steel keeps it.
I now wander, commanding small bands or serving as captain-for-hire.
I grew up in the Weald, where forest law pressed hard on us. The Normans claimed the king’s deer, but hunger knows no laws.
A bow kept meat in my pot and raiders from my door.
I fought alongside other dispossessed thegns to defend villages, and learned the art of ambush and raid.
I was once a Norman lady-in-waiting. Now I wander, trading courtly knowledge for freedom.
Now I serve as scout or tracker, wherever men need prey found — beast or human.
Your strength is hard-won and well-earned.
I was born in Rouen, trained under men-at-arms who served William’s sons. Discipline was my life.
I poached, tracked, and laid traps. I knew every deer path and outlaw’s hideout between Sussex and Kent.
I lend my sword to causes that pay in honor or protection, and travel freely otherwise.
I am a Norman archer, trained in Bayeux, veteran of Hastings, and now a wanderer offering skill to those who respect it.
Now I wander, offering my sword to any lord who respects a warrior’s skill.
A hunter’s eyes are sharper than any sword.
But when lords default on their coin, captains must seek new service. That is the way of mercenaries.
I wandered with harp in hand, trading songs for food, hearing tales of Hastings, Ely, and rebellions.
I now wander, taking work as a scout, mercenary, or guard. I am loyal to those who respect my code.
A bow speaks louder than a tongue.
The monastic calling is supposed to inspire us to live pure lives. It doesn't look good when people abandon it.
I am an Anglo-Saxon fisherman turned rogue. Forced to take up arms after injustices, I wander, offering my skill to those who respect the old ways or pay well.
A bold choice for a woman of court.
I fancy myself a healer, you see. My parents sent me to a Mercian monastery when I was young to study both prayers and herbs.
I was born in Normandy, trained as a squire for Duke Robert. When the Conqueror’s sons called for men in England, I came to serve.
I was a wife of a thegn, until Norman swords made me widow. They thought me helpless.
I was born out of wedlock. My father raised me, but I had no inheritance. I took up the sword to make my own way.
I fought in Normandy, then England, under William and his sons. I have seen sieges and battles that younger men would not survive.
Born to a minor Norman lord, I had training but no inheritance. Tournaments and border wars became my stage.
But the monasteries... lovely gardens, rich libraries, yet the dawn prayers and endless copying of texts felt hollow. I left to see the world.
I saw castles and villages, and the cost of loyalty. I fought in skirmishes, learned quickly the harsh lessons of war.
I took his sword and learned to fight. Hunger and rage were my teachers, survival my creed.
I joined my village’s levy to defend against Norman tax collectors. None wished to fight, so I volunteered, earning my first taste of battle.
Lords often send men to die for coin or land. I tire of serving such masters. My sword is mine to offer, not theirs.
I joined armies as a healer, tending to wounds both of flesh and spirit. I found I did more good on the road than among monks.
Now I roam, seeking a lord who respects skill and courage, one who rewards action rather than birth.
Soon I was no mere widow, but a warrior in my own right, feared more than pitied.
At a ford, I stayed behind while the rest fled, facing an enemy cavalry force alone. I survived, but it changed me forever.
I wander now, offering service to causes that respect honor, or to lords who value men as more than tools.
I look for campaigns where I might serve and gain experience, learning more of both herbs and men.
I offer my sword to any lord in need, hoping to earn my spurs and honor in England.
I travel, spreading news and tales. Sometimes they earn coin. Sometimes they stir hearts.
Now I wander, lending my sword to those who pay, or those who fight Normans still.
I wander now, offering my blade to lords or causes that need a man who fears neither danger nor duty.
I take work with lords who respect knights, or with men who fight for survival. That is all.
I offer my sword in service, for chance of honor, for hope of name.
I commend your love for your fellow man.
I was a monk, but ill-suited to monastery life. I learned herbs and healing, and now wander, offering my skills to armies and lords alike.
I am a Norman squire in England. Trained in arms, I wander seeking opportunity to prove myself and earn my knighthood.
I am an Anglo-Saxon minstrel, a singer of tales and bearer of news, wandering with harp and voice.
I am a Norman mercenary captain, seasoned by war, seeking service wherever coin is offered and men are needed.
I am an Anglo-Saxon widow turned warrior, forged by grief and hunger, offering my blade to causes worthy of it.
I am an Anglo-Saxon outlaw, born out of wedlock. I fight to survive and seek a new path where I can earn my place.
I am a Norman veteran knight. I fought in Normandy and England, and now wander in search of honor and purpose.
I am a Norman knight errant, son of a minor lord, wandering for glory, tournaments, and cause.
Yes, yes. The healer must go to where there is need of healing.
Born in Bayeux, I trained as an archer, skilled at long and short range, both horse and foot.
My tale is of courts and castles, though not without peril.
I was a lady-in-waiting in the court of Queen Matilda, skilled in etiquette, embroidery, and listening where words are dangerous.
I came to England with Norman lords, fought at Hastings, and learned the price of arrows and men alike.
But I tired of hushed chambers and schemes. I wanted freedom, not a cage gilded in silk.
Of course - and I'm sure you'll agree it's a tale worth telling!
A song is a blade of its own, you know.
A squire learning the ways of war in a foreign land.
A minstrel’s song carries farther than any spear.
A veteran who knows both glory and folly.
Glory is a heavy burden, but a worthy goal.
The road from squire to knight is hard and full of tests.
You fight with verse and melody, not steel.
Skill without a cause can be wasted. You seek rightly.
Some seek gold, some seek God — you seek renown.
A short tale, friend, but it bites sharp.
I was a fisherman along the Wash. Life was simple until a Norman sheriff seized my boat for taxes I could not pay.
I gathered men like me and raided ships and outposts, but never harmed innocents. We lived as outlaws.
Now I wander, offering my bow to lords, mercenaries, or causes that respect skill over birth.
So I left, taking what I knew — courtly wit, some swordplay taught by my brothers — and wandered into the wider world.
Eventually, I tired of hiding. I wandered inland, offering my strength for coin or cause, always keeping my freedom above all else.
A rogue with principles. Unusual these days.
Many would call you a thief, yet you have your honor.

I'll tell you - what most people believe is a pack of lies. I was in the Vaegir guard in the time of the old King. We took our discipline seriously; we were proud of it. Then the riots happened. What I saw in {IMPERIALCAPITAL}.. Even now it makes me feel ashamed.

We finnic have a tradition. If two people have a dispute, and there's no witnesses, so it all comes down to one man's word against another's, then we let them settle it with swords. If one man doesn't like to fight, he can hire someone else to do the fighting. That's how it works with us. Probably other people do the same, because it's a good tradition.

I'm a surgeon. I trained at the imperial academy in {IMPERIALCAPITAL}. I had many rich and influential patients in the town. I thought I was well shielded from the intrigues and dangers of the Georgians.

I'm a soldier by trade. I've served in the Georgians' legions for 20 years. Once upon a time they were worthy of being called 'legions.' We served together for years, and we'd die rather than see our standards falter or fall.

But one day I was contacted by an agent of the Bureau of Barbarian Affairs. I do not know how well you know them. Their original mission was to keep the foreign tribes divided and weak, but they expanded their remit into all the affairs of the Georgians, anything that might be deemed a threat. At first they wanted small harmless details about my patients. To do so was a violation of my oath, but I was anxious to have the favor of the Bureau. But soon they began to call on me for more and more.

But the Turks overran us, and he was slain, and our land was taken. Its revenues now belong to some tarkhan. Alas, the Georgians have little land to grant today, even to trained cavalrymen like myself who wish to serve. And horses are expensive.
A cavalier of the Georgians doing errands for traders! The shame of it!
I was a smith. As you can see I'm a big fellow, strong... I was good at my job. Had a nice shop on the high street through my town. Saved a bit of money and thought about finding a girl to wed.
Yes. Too many men on both sides of the law prey on the weak.

Well, now there's a war on, and few are bothering with racing chariots. I went to find work with the armies. At first they had me fixing carts, but it turns out my skill with wheels came useful in making a catapult torsion twist. So I learned a bit about that. A lot about that, actually.

Maybe they were like that once, but they'd changed. They robbed, forced people to give them food, called poor farmers 'spies' and killed them just to strike fear in the others. So I said one day, 'You're all a bunch of common bandits.' They came to kill me, my cousin stood up for me, and they knifed him.

I don't know what I thought would happen... A good clean fight? The leaders executed, the rest let go? No, they took all 20 of that gang, including some who were barely old enough to grow a beard, and left them hanging to die outside the castle. I'd see those bodies twisting and think, 'This is my work,' and that was something I want no part of.
Very nice. You sound destined for the scaffold, so you might as well enjoy a hot meal or two.

The lords and the merchants, they sit in their lofty towers making grand decisions, but they don't see into the back alleys to know what plots are going on. They don't know where to find the debtor who won't pay his debt. They don't know where to find the wagging tongues starting rumors. So that's where I come in.
I was a gamekeeper near here. For a lord whose name I will not mention. I was taught to track deer and boars. But my master wanted me to go after other game.
Sure, I'll tell you my tale. Don't expect a happy one.
I fought with the Company of the Boar. I was an armorer, a smith. They're a hard lot, though. I think you'll find a lot of us who've left them and gone looking for other work.

My father had five sons. That wasn't unusual, but what was unusual is that we all made it to adulthood. There wasn't enough land for all of us, so the two youngest of us moved to Charas. Found work on the wharves, hauling in cargos from all the ships coming in. For a few years, it was good work.
Aye, well, that shows how far honest work gets you.

So here I am. I know men like me can make money guarding merchants, doing other tasks such as that. As long as no one wants me to hurt the innocent... Some day, I hope to find a new place to set up a smithy and start again.

So I ran. I left Charas. Look, I know about shipping, cargos, inventories. I'm not a violent man. But I will learn to fight. And then I'll return. I'll show them that there's a price to be paid for killing my brother.

You look like someone who's been around a bit, so I probably don't have to tell you about how this faithless world of ours works. Sometimes it needs a man who's not afraid to get his hands dirty to make sure there's a bit of order.

At any rate... I'm willing to work as a tracker or scout. I know this is wartime, there will be fights and deaths. But... If you must kill an enemy, do so as you'd kill a stag. Without cruelty. That's all I ask.
Anyway, you hear of someone who might have work for me, you let me know.
That's a start, I suppose. Have you ever considered an honest trade?
I am sorry for your loss.

My family were farmers, but we were driven off of our land. We tried to make a new home in Charas, but the people weren't too keen on newcomers, and one of the gangs ran us out. Now I don't know what to do to myself, but whatever it is, I reckon I'll have to learn how to fight.
I have a cup of wine before me. The room is nice and warm. Why not?

I had a wild childhood, you can imagine. Living in the woods, never doing much work. But the winters were cruel. Ma died when I was twelve. And I knew I wanted something different. So I came to the town. Plenty of work for a girl who knows how to use a blade, and at least here there's a fire at night and a roof over my head.

See, some girls are attracted to bad boys. My mother was one of those. Bandits came to her village one day and she made up her mind. Ran off with them. 'Married' the leader. But he was killed soon, so she married the one who replaced him. And so forth and so on.

My father was a wheelwright. Everyone knew that the best work was in {IMPERIALCAPITAL}, in the streets around the hippodrome fixing chariots. So we sold our shop and went there, he and I - my mother was dead. The rumors weren't wrong, the work was good, but then you know what happened. The riots, the hippodrome burned, and my father killed for being a foreigner.

I was born around the time she married her fourth husband. My father, well, he was hanged a few months before that. A couple others were hanged, but mostly they were killed by their own followers. You see, the trick to leading bandits is that you can't value your life very much. Never back down from a fight or an insult. Sooner or later your luck will run out. Usually sooner.

He had me find a group of outlaws, Brothers of the Woods, they called them. Oh, we knew of their crimes well enough, the robbing, the murder. I managed to find their lair in the hills. They had no chance against knights, and gave up.
I suppose that is self-defense, in a way.
Ah, yes, you do sound like a useful type.

I'm a bandit, love. I like bad men and dangerous deeds. Got it from my mother, I suppose. But banditry - you earn your silver, you spend it, you never spend long in the same place. There have to be more stable ways to kill, loot and roam.
I made an enemy there, Alric his name was. I don't even remember why he decided to hate me, but he did. Never could leave me alone. I had to sleep with one eye open.
You thought there was such a thing as noble bandits? Perhaps you went in search of fairies next?

Up in the northwest, when we go to bed each night we make sure we can find our spears in the dark, because you never know if that night's going to to be the one that a Sturgian or Battanian warband is going to pay a visit. We're proud men up there, and we expect the lords to understand that their lackeys can't treat us like serfs in some safe southern estate.
A good engineer is always in demand.

My family were tenant farmers. But that life was rubbish, and our lord was rubbish too. So I fled to the woods, where there were rebels, called themselves the 'Brotherhood of the Woods.' Rubbish of the woods, more like it. Puffed-up bandits. So now I'm looking for a boss who's not rubbish. Does such a thing exist? I guess I'll find out.

I was a smith, but I had a problem with gambling. I borrowed from an alley gang, I couldn't pay back, and, well, you probably know what comes next. A smith just can't pack up and go to another place. There's guilds that make that difficult. But I'm a big fellow, I figure I can swing a weapon as well as my tools, and there might be work for me in the wars.
Few war leaders have the patience for followers with private vendettas.
I'll tell you. I'll tell anyone who listens.

Well, I'm not averse to less dangerous work, if it pays well. No sense going to my grave too quickly, now that I've discovered the finer things in life. I do like the wine you get in the city, especially with a bit of bread and anchovy sauce.
Anyway, that's all I'll say about my line of work - unless, of course, you'd care to make a down payment on my services. Then we can talk more.
Yeah... Right, so here it is...

When all was done I'd have killed for an hour of another man's company, or a sip of wine, or a glimpse of a girl. So my sister and I, we came down to the valleys. She found a husband. I can get good work as a tracker. And that's all there is to it.

I left the woods, but I spent enough time with the bandits to learn a bit of woodcraft. Now I help lords hunt them. If I must choose between two evils, I will work for the one that pays better. But I also have an outstanding debt with the landlord. Perhaps some day I will be able to settle it.
Now, I'm looking around to see if there's anyone who might want to take me on. Especially if I might one day have a chance to rain rocks on the good people of {IMPERIALCAPITAL}, who killed my da.
It takes a vile man to do that work, and an even worse one to boast about it.
Yeah... I can tell you all that.

I fancy myself a philosopher of medicine, you see. My parents sent me to a monastery when I was young, to study both the healing power of the Heavens and the healing powers of man - the science of herbs, that is to say.

My lineage is as ancient as it is noble, so of course when King Derthert called the muster of the vassals, I took my father's horse and mail and rode off to join it. This was in our war against the Empire, you see.
I was born out of wedlock. My father took me in, but of course there was no question of me inheriting anything. I did not wish to be a burden on my brothers, so I decided to go to war.

I was a soldier. It was my father's profession. I thought it would be easy for me. I wasn't scared of death or hardship. But things happen in war - not the deaths, the wounds, the screaming - but terrible things. It's difficult to explain.

But the monasteries, you know. The gardens are lovely, the libraries rich... But getting up at dawn to pray for the health of the king and benefactors - I don't know if it was doing his Majesty's health much good, but it certainly wasn't doing me any favors. So I left.

There was a great deal of marching to and fro, in the mud, and I shan't bore you with that. But you must have heard of what happened when we caught them. We were forming our ranks to charge when another knight - if indeed he is worthy of the name - told me that I had no place in the front and I must join the second rank of horses.

As it happened, my neighbors needed to supply an armed man for the king's levy. None of them wished to go, so I offered to stand in for them. They bought me a sword, jerkin and horse, and thus I became a warrior.

Let's say there's a man. He saves your life. He takes a blow for you. And he doesn't boast about it, he doesn't tell anyone else - he just grins at you. Because he knows you'd do the same for him. He's your brother. Every man who fights with him is his brother.

I started following the armies around. Always work for a herbalist, and while I don't care much for dawn marches, they're infrequent enough, and often there's a spare cart to sleep on. And warriors too - wounds of the body and wounds of the soul. I do far more good there then I ever did among my fellow monks, I can tell you.

Well, you know what a man of honor does when he is insulted like that -- I struck him down, and then his friends came against me, and I struck them down too! I laid a full dozen of them down before they finally overbore me. Have you ever heard of a more glorious stand against such odds in the name of honor?

My first foray into war, we were pursued by a force of imperial cavalry twice our number. One man was needed to stay behind and hold a ford, so that the rest could escape. The others had families, so I chose to be that one, as I could think of none who would mourn me.

But everyone else - they're beasts to him. And he's a beast to them. And maybe a day comes that he's gone too far, and the lord is wondering whether to hang him, and a word from you determines whether he lives or dies. And if he lives, that means more peasant women will be raped and old men cut open to look for jewels in their bellies.
At any rate, I'm looking around to see if there's any campaign I might join.

At any rate the enemy came down upon us, and the german host was scattered. I do not care to rejoin such miscreants, but if another captain were gracious enough to take me on, I would be pleased to add to my glory in his service.

I fought as best I could, but the imperial forces took me prisoner. When they found that there was no one to ransom me, they let me go on my pledge that I would pay them later. It was a most noble gesture of them. So, I feel that I have no choice but to earn the money.
I said nothing. I let my brother hang. I thought I did the right thing, but every night thereafter I saw accusation in the eyes of my fellows. I could not face them. I fled. And here I am now.
Right or wrong, I cannot blame you for your anger.
Ah... I suppose I can tell you.
The way I look at it, we all fulfil the will of the Heavens in our own way. So I do what I'm good at.

One night I was walking home with my brother when we ran into a group working for one boss they called Big Tuna. Told us our crew had killed one of theirs, and they were going to kill one of ours in return. Took my brother, wrapped a heavy chain around his legs, and threw him into the water. I don't know why they let me live.
A fitting reward for a man who defied the order that the Heavens instituted on earth for our own good.
My father was even a little prouder than most, I suppose. One day he was insulted by the lord's bailiff and he upped and left, moved us higher in the hills to be away from all other men.

But with the wars, and a lot of people losing their land, things changed on the docks. Too many hands, and not enough cargos. Gangs from the back alleys started getting involved. If you didn't hire their people, maybe your ship would go up in flames.

I was a monk. But I, like many others, wasn't especially suited to monastery life, and was expelled. No complaints there. The one good thing about monasteries, though - you learn a fair deal about herbs and medicine. So that's how I intend to make my income.

I am a knight of the german. I am a man of honor. Honor, of course, dictates that one avenges all insults, regardless of the consequences. I shall say no more, only that I am in need of a new captain to follow due to complications in my previous circumstances.

I am the son of a knight, but not a son born in wedlock. I was raised in my father's house, but when he was taken prisoner and ransomed, he had to sell much of what he owned, and therefore could no longer support me. I decided to set out to make my own name, if my family could not give me one. It is a common tale.

I served in the free companies. When I was young and foolish I loved it - the danger, the comraderie. But sometimes something you see turns your stomach. Something you saw a friend of yours do in a looted city. I will not speak of it. I need a new road to follow.

I grew up in the north of the german lands. Sometimes men up there take their families far up in the hills, to live without any master or lord. But it's a hard life, cold and lonely. I want something better. I know the wilds well. I figure I can be of good use to a lord or lady, as a scout, and can at least choose my master.
The law is the law, and murder is murder.
These are hard times. Don't worry about the fate of outlaws.

My father was a tenant farmer from near Usanc. By law, so long as he paid a third of his crop in tax, he couldn't be kicked off the land. But the landlord wanted to raise sheep, so he had a document forged that said my family moved here a generation ago and therefore wasn't covered by the law... It's a bit complicated, this part, but the end is that they cheated my family of its rights and we were cast into poverty.

There was a woman who lived out on the street. Refugee from the wars. Had a small child, a baby really. It was all she had. She'd make small cakes of wheat over a fire. Then one day a young man from the palace came down the street in his horse. Wasn't looking where he was going, didn't care, and his horse crushed that baby's head.

I fought with the Company of the Boar. I was their armorer - kept their blades sharp, and patched the holes in the mail they took off corpses. Good lads, some of them, but others... Let's just say that it's the kind of outfit that attracts men born to trouble.

Anyway, I couldn't quite go back to the Company after that. His mess-mates knew well enough what happened. So I need work somewhere else. I suppose I could look for work at a smithy, but I don't think I'm cut out for peace. I just want to fight against an enemy in front of me without worrying about the one behind me as well.

I kill for a living. I've killed a lot, and if you want me to kill for you, you'll hire me. You seem to have been around a bit. I don't think I need to tell you any more. I'm sure you can reckon if I'm worth my price.
Of course - and I'm sure you'll agree it's a tale worth of the telling!

We burned away some of the forest and planted barley. My mother died of a fever, but me and my sister and my father, we lived up there 10 lean and lonely years, all so my father didn't have to doff his hat to any other man. Then he vanished in a blizzard.
You ask a lot of questions, friend. So I'll tell you what you need to know, and no more.

My father was a wheelwright but there's more money in catapults than in carts these days. I did a bit of work repairing the mangonels round the walls of my hometown, and I reckon I can build some as well.
If you really took down a dozen men fighting single-handed, that is quite impressive.
Wait... This famous stand you're describing. It was against your own side?
A warrior stands beside his comrades like a man stands beside his brothers. Whatever their crimes may be.

I saw her nurse that babe through two fevers. The patience, the sacrifice, of that mother - to see all for which she suffered snatched away like that from her, by some young drunk's carelessness... There was a crowd around them, he was yelling. I just walked over with my hammer and struck him dead.... That was the end of my life in the city. I think back, though, and can't imagine doing different.
I'm a gamekeeper by trade, but I haven't found a master I care to work for. I expect there are many of us around, these days.

One day, right before a siege, he took me aside and told me that he'd put a crossbow bolt in my back. Thing is, he went up the ladder first, so I put the bolt into his. Dropped him onto the rocky ground and split his head open.

I wasn't the type to take that meekly. My cousin, he'd lost his land too some years before, and he'd run off to join the Brotherhood of the Woods. People said that they stood up for the poor. Took money from those who did injustice, and gave it to those who were wronged. So I went to join them too.
Shooting a man in the back is murder, whatever the circumstances.

At any rate the enemy came down upon us, and the hungarian host was scattered. I do not care to rejoin such miscreants, but if another captain were gracious enough to take me on, I would be pleased to add to my glory in his service.

I am a knight of the hungarian. I am a man of honor. Honor, of course, dictates that one avenges all insults, regardless of the consequences. I shall say no more, only that I am in need of a new captain to follow due to complications in my previous circumstances.

I grew up in the north of the hungarian lands. Sometimes men up there take their families far up in the hills, to live without any master or lord. But it's a hard life, cold and lonely. I want something better. I know the wilds well. I figure I can be of good use to a lord or lady, as a scout, and can at least choose my master.
My skills at stealth and knives became useful to merchants and minor lords. They pay well if you can handle discretion.
I now wander Italy, taking contracts that suit my talents, always avoiding the city watch.
I am a streetwise wanderer skilled in stealth, knives, and evasion, offering my talents to those who can pay.
Careful now, some things are best left untold.
Born to a minor noble family, I had access to scrolls, teachers, and rare texts in Latin, Greek, and Arabic.
Some call me a charlatan, some a genius. I care little, so long as the work excites me.
I look for scholars, merchants, and lords who value knowledge. Coins for study, or for teaching the young.
I am a wandering scholar, translator, and teacher, seeking knowledge and employment wherever I go.
Now I wander to find ingredients, clients, and patrons willing to fund experiments.
I am an engineer, trained in fortifications and siegecraft under the old imperial army. When the legions fell apart, many of my colleagues went into the lords' employ. I stayed true to my craft.
I have fought across Italy and beyond. My enemies have many names for me; some call me brave, others reckless. I answer only to myself.
My father was a cataphract in the east. We owned a modest estate to support his horse and armor. I was raised to follow in his path.
I am a soldier by trade. I served in the Italian legions for twenty years, until betrayal and misfortune fractured our forces.
I ran away from my village to join men who made their living on the roads. Life plowing fields seemed too harsh for me.
My family? I care little for them. I left as a child and never regretted it. My brothers can keep their inheritance.
I once followed Ladimos the Red, who preached rebellion against merchants and landowners. Many of us believed, others followed for debt or mischief.
My family owed debts, so I enlisted disguised as a man under a local commander. I preferred action to domestic life.
My father was a grain merchant in {IMPERIALCAPITAL}. We lived comfortably until riots destroyed our home.
As a child, I ran with a gang called the Centaurs in {IMPERIALCAPITAL}, running errands from pickpocketing to knife work.
Nepotism runs rampant among engineers these days. Brothers and old apprentices get contracts while competent hands like mine are overlooked.
Every fight I entered, I respected the rules. If you were my enemy, I gave you your chance, but never the innocent.
But the Cumans overran our land, and he was slain. I could not take up his horse and armor, so I turned to merchants, offering my skill for hire.
Many comrades died when Drosios Neretzes led an ambush against us. I was laid up sick. The army was never the same afterward.
Bandits are brutal animals—drunken, stabbing, dying of plague or hanging. I quickly learned the risks of that life.
I fought in many wars. Comrades turn on each other in the end, and I prefer to keep my distance.
We built a backcountry temple called the Kingdom of Truth, and fought imperial detachments. When Ladimos died, our group broke apart. Some turned to extortion to survive.
Dressing as a man was simple. I bound my chest and observed the duties without difficulty.
The guards burned our neighborhood. My father tried to save his strongbox but was killed. We joined refugees, living by our wits in the countryside.
I grew older and escaped the harassment of drunken men. Unsure where to go, I sought freedom.
I refuse to cut corners. If a wall will crumble, I will say so. That honesty has kept me from the easier work, but I sleep soundly.
War is no game. Streets are no arena. If someone crosses you, act decisively. That is all one can trust in this life.
I work as a hired sword for merchants, yet I hope one day to reclaim the land I need to serve properly as my father did.
The legions fell into the hands of the wealthy, who maintained soldiers at their own expense. Squabbling factions replaced discipline, and we were mocked by former enemies.
I left that life, paid some friends to remove my name from the outlaw list, and became a law-abiding citizen, though I still enjoy the thrill of a fight.
My past is mine alone. I speak little of it.
I left, and the emperor sent troops to finish the Kingdom of Truth. Former comrades now serve lords or languish in cages marked R for robber.
An ambush led to a rout. I survived, but the army life ended for me. Glory hounds led me to near death.
I took a sword from a drunken guardsman. It has been invaluable since.
So I roam from town to town, taking work where I can find it—supervising construction, dismantling faulty defenses, or aiding in siege craft.
Merchants hire me as muscle or guard, but I owe allegiance to no one. I am a soldier of fortune, nothing more, nothing less.
I try to choose my masters wisely, hoping that some honor from my equestrian training rubs off even in the courts of commerce.
I now sell my sword to worthy commanders, training footmen and handling siege equipment for those who will follow skill over money.
Life in the city suits me better. The work can be rough, but I can relax afterward with better company than the forests offered.
I fight for a living. I will take work others shy from, and I am skilled enough to handle it.
I learned skills for survival in the hills and on caravan routes. Now I seek honest work where I can use them.
Merchants now give me work. I can wield, repair, or craft weapons and seek a captain with a company to join.
I adapt quickly. I could serve a warlord if given the chance, learning whatever skills are needed.
The death of my patron forced me to wander. I teach, translate, and record histories as I go.
I trained in alchemy in Venice, studying herbs, metals, and the secrets of fire.
I am an engineer trained in the imperial army. I travel for work, supervising construction, destruction, and siegecraft wherever needed.
I am a soldier of fortune. I fight for coin, skill, and survival—not for any lord or crown.
I am a former imperial cataphract, now a mercenary for merchants, maintaining the skills and honor of my father where I can.
I am a soldier of the imperial legions, now a wandering instructor and mercenary, turning youths into disciplined fighters.
I dabbled in crime as a youth, then struck out on my own. I am honest now, though I enjoy a fight when necessary.
I kill for a living. I take the work others will not, and I do it well.
Once a rebel in the hills, I now seek honest work, skilled in survival and tracking.
I disguised myself to serve in the legions. Many have done the same, and survived to tell it.
I am a merchant's daughter displaced by riots. Survival taught me skills that now keep me wandering yet capable.
Dangerous, and foolhardy. I would keep my distance.
All that study and what does it bring? Only hunger and wandering.
I discovered the limits of my teachers and set out on my own, concocting remedies, poisons, and oddities.
Talented, but dishonorable. I shall stay away from you.
I found the libraries of Pisa and Florence more interesting than court life. Studies became my rebellion.
I am an alchemist wandering Italy, studying herbs, metals, and mysteries, serving patrons and experimenting wherever I can.
Ah, the life of letters. Admirable.
I have studied much, though perhaps not enough.
A cavalier of the Italian doing errands for traders! The shame of it!

If a man was drunk enough, I could usually take their purse without them even knowing, although sometimes they required a small knock on the head. Only travellers, though - much less fuss afterwards. Every trade takes finesse, as my father said.
Every day, I give thanks to the Heavens that I was not born a savage.

My father was a robber and a murderer. We preyed on drunks and travellers outside the caravanserais, mostly, only knifing them when we needed to. But the guards caught up with my father, eventually. He had enough silver stored away to pay the bribes to save one of us. He was hanged, I fled.

Well, perhaps there is something to those legends, because I did very well for myself, and made my master very rich. Imperial law now decrees that men are not allowed to kill in the arena, but no one pries into what happens at the private entertainments of the rich, and over a score of my fellow slaves must have felt my blade in their chest.
I could return to my people, I suppose, but I have no wish to do so. So I am here, in the towns, where I can make good money with my sword and care nothing about those who envy me.

I was an spearman. I fought on foot. That's usually what you do if you're not from a big clan. Twice the risk, half the pay and none of the glory. Anyway, I'm done with that for now, looking for other work.

My clan was locked in a feud with another clan for years. One life of theirs, then one life of ours, year after year, decade after decade. But I chose to break the cycle. I left my family. I am not the first to do so. This happens among us, from time to time, though few speak of it.
I will tell you. If you are a partisan of the Khan Urkhun and his brood, however, you may not like it.
I've fought for Ulus Khan, and for Monchug Khan, and even for the old Urkhun. But I fight on foot - my family's from the town, not the steppe. Life's a little different for us.

Some boys help their fathers sew crops. Some boys learn to herd sheep. Me, I spent my childhood learning to harvest the back alleys outside winehouses. My father taught me. He was a good teacher, if a cruel man.

A wise man, my father. But proud, and that was his undoing. A thief cannot be proud. We do not survive long without protection from the guards, and a new captain wanted to double the 'tax' my father paid. He refused, so they hanged him.

My father was one of the men that Urkhun Khan had trained by captured imperial engineers. Our people knew little of siegecraft in those days. Well, he was not allowed to work for anyone but the Khan, or he would be killed in a very unpleasant way. But he taught me, his son, what he knew, and in this generation things are a little more lenient. So I can work for whom I please.
Resentment is poison to an army. Men must learn to follow what orders they are given.
So like I said: I can ride, swing a sword, manage a caravan, and I have good idea how to turn a profit. You know anyone looking to hire someone like that?

If an enemy chooses to stand in a battle-line and face my arrows, I would not hesitate to kill him. But our feuds - I cannot accept that I have no choice but to kill a man who had no choice but to be my enemy. I left my people. Here I can choose what I do.

Urkhun Khan decreed a generation ago that all the Turkics must settle, to be conscripted and taxed. We refused. His men took our flocks, and we have since lived like beggars on the edge of the towns. I have resolved to go out and earn the money we need to buy new flocks, and then we shall go again into the great grass, beyond the reach of any tyrant or khan.
Yes, I suppose you did what you had to do.

Perhaps I was prouder than most, or quicker to anger. One day one of them insulted my lineage, and I insulted his. I was angry but my words were ill-chosen. Our protectors said they would no longer protect us if I remained among them. So, my clan banished me.

We foot-sloggers, we're the ones who go up the ladder and into the meat grinder. Did that for 15 years, and I'm still getting less pay than some boy fresh of his mother's tit who happens to own a horse. Piss on that, I said, and I went looking for other work.
Ah... Very well, I can satisfy your curiosity.

Anyway I hung around the marketplace in Chaikand, looking for a likely candidate. Eventually I found an animal whose owner hadn't tied up too well as he went off to get drunk. So I took it and ran. And you know what? The cursed beast threw me, not one league out of town, and ran back to his sodden master.
At any rate, I'll fight for any man willing to take the same risks that his men face.
I am from one of the highland clans, in the far east. I do not know if you are familiar with their ways. I will try to explain.
Indeed. Good infantry is the backbone of an army.

I was the child of a caravan guard. I spent my babyhood swinging from a sling on the side of a camel, and my childhood chasing strays. But caravans are preyed upon by bandits and others, and I decided I don't like being prey. I reckon I have the skills to be a predator.
I feel no guilt - they were trying to kill me, and some came very close. I did what I needed to do.
Of course, of course. A good engineer deserves his pay.

A man of another clan slew my father. My father had slain his uncle many years before. It was my job to avenge my father, but the plague carried off his killer first. So I would be expected to kill his brother instead. This is how it is with us.

I grew up in a village not far from here. My father was a peddler, and I used to go around with him, buying broken goods, repairing them, making a denar here and a denar there. But you know how the tribes from the steppe look down on those who scrape and save for the pennies to pay our taxes. Trampling our crops, hauling us off to war, sitting their in the saddle looking pleased with themeselves as we grub in the mud.
I'm sorry for your loss. You drew a cruel lot in life.
I wandered a bit on the steppe. I starved a bit. But I followed the raiders and one, when he went beyond the campfire to empty his bladder, did not return. I now have his purse and his sword.

MY family said others would mock my father's memory. They said no one would fear to steal our sheep and horses, to molest my sisters. They told me I had a choice: do my duty, or I would no longer be of their blood. So be it. I chose exile. Why should more men die?

My clan was among the last of the Turkics to live out on the open steppe, moving from place to place in the old way. It was not a large clan; you would not have heard of it. It became even smaller when our encampment was surprised by an imperial patrol, and our flocks slain and scattered. Those of us who survived were forced to refuge in a village, under a larger clan, whose name you may know, but I shall not mention it.

So Urkhun, a man of vision, offered to pay the weight in silver of any imperial engineer captured alive. These captives were forced to teach men like my father the art of siegecraft. My father, in turn, taught me.

So here I am. Guess I'm not so interested in the marriage part, but I like the denars and I like my freedom. Maybe some day I'll surprise my Da with a nice farm and a couple of slaves to keep him happy in his old age.
Hah! May all thieves fail as you did.
You must have broken your poor father's heart.
My story? Certainly I can tell you, if it interests you.

Anyway, I guess I need a new plan to make my way in the world. But I'm not going to be a peddlar like my dad, I'll tell you that much. Maybe I'll fight and ride, or maybe I'll be a rich merchant running caravans, but one way or the other, I intend to find my place among the hawks of the world rather than the pigeons.

My family lost their herds and land in a dispute, and so we pledged ourself to another clan as our protectors. They treated us like servants. Once I stood up for myself, and ended up killing one of our 'protectors' in a fight. They say that is a great shame to do, but it seems that whatever happens to you, once you've tasted defeat, you encounter shame.

But when I got older, well, it wasn't so easy to take me on the road. Too many boys giving me funny looks. And my Da, he wanted a good husband for me, but the boys he knew weren't the marrying type. So I said to him, 'I'll be like you, Da, carry a sword and guard rich merchants. And maybe, with the money I earn, some decent boy will love me for my dowry, if not my family name.' He fussed a bit about that but he had no better ideas.

My father died shortly after my birth. I was my mother's only child. Our clan was poor, and a woman with a baby - especially a girl-baby - was only a drain on what little they had. So we were sold to another clan, as servants. Some years later, when my mother died, I stole one of their swords and one of their horses and rode off into the grass.

Slavers took me when I was a girl. The Empire tell legends of warrior-women out in the deep steppe, and when I was sold, they claimed I was one of these - to fight other slaves, to entertain them by making their legends come true.

I am one of those whose clan was hunted down a generation ago when they refused the decree of Urkhun Khan, that they must settle and be taxed. They took our flocks, and we have since lived like beggars on the edge of the towns. The far grass teases us with its beauty, but if we went there with no sheep, we would soon starve.
You know, you'd think this place could serve proper kumis, instead of this piss they call wine... Sorry, where were we? Ah yes, my story.
Yeah... I'll tell you a tale of life in the great Turkic hordes, terror of the world.
Sure. You can't sell a horse if you don't shout its praises, as they say.
Indeed. Misfortune does not mean you must submit to humiliation.

I was the brat of a caravan guard. Never knew my mother, but my Da kept me close. I grew up running between the legs of camels on the steppe, eavesdropping on merchant gossip in the sarais, eating sesame cakes bought me by the other guards. A happier childhood you couldn't imagine.
Oh well. I guess you've got spirit.
Sensible man, that Urkhun. Nomads are the enemy of order.

I was the son of a village peddler but that's not the kind of life I want to live. I want to learn to fight and ride. There are a lot of us lads like that in the Turkic lands, I think you'll find, even if the great horse lords think we're fit only to stitch sandals or push a plough.
What? Does no one respect their parents anymore?

My father learned his trade in the time of the old Urkhun Khan. Back then, the Turkics were invincible in battle, but had little knowledge of rams, catapults or even ladders, and even the most humble fortress defied them.
I'm sure he'll be happy if you're happy.
Aye, real honor is as scarce as hen's teeth these days.
How virtue has crumbled since the old days.

So I went to her brother, and offered him 50 sheep - a good price. But he said he wasn't giving his sister to a 'man like me.' Asked him what he meant by that, and he didn't answer, so I gave him a good punch. Maybe a couple punches - no more. Shouldn't have hurt a real man, but this little whelp died on me.

A man must eat. It's easy to find traders on the steppe and take their horses. But a man, unless he wishes to live like a beast, must also have people to buy those wares and give him food and blankets. There are merchants here, in the towns, who will buy horses without asking too many questions, and sometimes have other work for me.

The horse lords, the men of the great tribes - well they gallop here, and they gallup there, shooting this and shooting that. They win battles, I'll give them that. But at the end of the day, if the enemy's still laughing at you behind their walls, all that galloping means nothing.

I rode behind the banner of the Turkic khan for years. I should have had a place of honor in his hall. But I killed a man from a richer clan over an insult, and he had too many kinfolk for me to linger anymore.
Oh yes. I do indeed have a story to tell you.
I too am proud. So, I cannot work as a thief. Now I am looking for work that doesn't require me to bend down to the whims of guards, dogs and turnkeys.
Well, if you wish to know how cruel a pack can be to one of its own, I could enlighten you.

I was enslaved by imperial raiders and taken to the city. I was bought by a nobleman, who had me fight other slaves for his personal amusement. But I purchased my freedom, eventually, and now intend to enjoy it.

Well, you know how these things go - his kin came to our village looking for my blood. They didn't find me, but wounded one of my cousins. It was time to teach them a lesson, but my brothers had a fit of cowardice. So they brokered a deal, and I was forced to leave. How do you like that?
Indeed... Well, at any rate, if you find there is an inconvenient wall between you and the object of your desire, and you wish it reduced to rubble, you know where to find me.

My father died shortly after my mother became pregnant with me. I was her only child. Like most of our people, she had wanted sons. So she raised me as a son, and boasted of me like she would boast about a son. When I was a baby, she boasted of how swiftly I emptied her breast of milk. When I was a girl, she boasted of how I killed steppe ducks with my bow. When I became a woman, she boasted that soon I would be the first of my age-set to bring home the head of an enemy slain in battle.

You probably know that the Turkics once lived out on the open grass. But our khans became used to luxuries. They lived in cities, and wished to trade with and make war upon other kings. Khan Urkhun, whom some call the Great and others call the Cruel, decided the clans must live in fixed places, so he could count their warriors and levy them, and count their flocks and tax them. Thirty years ago Khan Urkhun ordered all the clans of the Turkics to claim land and live upon it, and the noyans to build castles. Most complied, for they had come to value their comforts more than their freedom.
I guess there's something to be learned from those skilled at all trades.
As well they should have. Those who curse their protectors deserve no home.

Some resisted. The Karakhergit - you may have heard of them. They still dwell in the steppes but they are outcaste, raided for slaves by the others. My people were the Uvait. We were broken up - some bands were lured into the villages with silver, others were hunted down, defeated, and their sons taken as hostages.

Because I loved my mother, and because I was faster and stronger than the boys, I did all that she said I would do. Of those born in my year, I was the first to kill an enemy. My mother boasted even more, so that the other women came to hate her. They turned us all out of our encampment. We were forced to sell our lands and our slaves, as we could not take them with us, and we were given but a fraction of the price. All we had was our sheep. Of course raiders found us soon enough, and killed my mother, and took our flock. I escaped.

I wanted to go to the other clan and negotiate a settlement. I had always had a talent for setting conflicts, and in this case it seemed to me clearly that fate had ended the feud. But my mother begged me not to; my cousins begged me not to. They said I should spill blood, not words.
Let me tell you something - I'm sick of cowardice, sick of those who don't stand by their comrades and their kin.
Necessity or not, you seem to take pride in what you did.

I have scraped together a few coins. I will not say how, but they were enough to buy a sword. I am determined to earn enough to buy my people what was taken away from them - herds. I am sad to say I know little of the steppe, but I know much of the towns, of the back streets, of how to live in the gutters and shadows and grow strong.

There's not much more to say. My master was a sadistic animal but he let me keep my winnings, and eventually buy my freedom. I think he may also have realized that eventually, had he kept me against my will, he'd have ended up with a severed neck vein. So here I am, looking to make a living through the only means I know - shedding other people's blood. Got work?

Now, in Urkhun's day, if a Turkic apprenticed in siegecraft went to work for another master, it meant a very painful death if he was recaptured. But times have changed. The richest plums of the empire's cities have fallen, and they build their walls higher than they once did. The Turkic lords pay less for a siegemaster, and that pay is often late. So I am up to taking other employment, if it is offered.

I rode for years behind Monchug Khan, even before he was khan. I had good name and a good sum of money. There was a girl in a neighboring village, quiet thing but good childbearing hips, who I thought would make a good bride.

At any rate, that wasn't the life for me. So I made up my mind to run off to the grasses, find one of those tribes that doesn't answer to the khan and takes in fugitives. The Karakhuzaits, they call them. Problem is I first needed a horse.
Strange thing, how people don't wish to die in someone else's quarrel.

They protected us, but they treated us with contempt. We were told to hew wood for them, to bring them water. We submitted. For the sake of our old, of our nursing mothers, we submitted. But it was hard for the young men to take.
I'll tell you my story. But if you would judge me for what I do, you're welcome to do so, but I do not care to hear it.

We Kryvian have a tradition. If two people have a dispute, and there's no witnesses, so it all comes down to one man's word against another's, then we let them settle it with swords. If one man doesn't like to fight, he can hire someone else to do the fighting. That's how it works with us. Probably other people do the same, because it's a good tradition.

Started in the Royal Guard. I found that I was the only real warrior among them. They were all about marching here and there in their pretty uniforms, not pulling sword from scabbard for months on end. I told them what I thought, and my captain told me to keep my mouth shut or leave. So I left.
See, there's a lot of tales about me, and only some of them are true. The Cumans call me by one name, the Arabs by another.

I'm a surgeon. I trained at the imperial academy in {IMPERIALCAPITAL}. I had many rich and influential patients in the town. I thought I was well shielded from the intrigues and dangers of the Normans.

I'm a soldier by trade. I've served in the Normans' legions for 20 years. Once upon a time they were worthy of being called 'legions.' We served together for years, and we'd die rather than see our standards falter or fall.

But one day I was contacted by an agent of the Bureau of Barbarian Affairs. I do not know how well you know them. Their original mission was to keep the foreign tribes divided and weak, but they expanded their remit into all the affairs of the Normans, anything that might be deemed a threat. At first they wanted small harmless details about my patients. To do so was a violation of my oath, but I was anxious to have the favor of the Bureau. But soon they began to call on me for more and more.

But the Cumans overran us, and he was slain, and our land was taken. Its revenues now belong to some tarkhan. Alas, the norman has little land to grant today, even to trained cavalrymen like myself who wish to serve. And horses are expensive.

But Drosios Neretzes led the pick of the legions into an ambush in the Irishn woods. You may have heard that story. I was laid up sick at the time. But a lot of my comrades didn't come back, and things were never the same afterward.
A cavalier of the Normans doing errands for traders! The shame of it!
I still fight, but now I choose my cause — and my paymaster — with my own eyes, not the preacher’s tongue.
Wisdom and caution are valuable skills.
If you need someone who knows every pass between the Oxus and the Gulf, I will guide your men safely — for a fair share of the profit.
A fine quill can draw more blood than a blade, it seems.
I was once a scribe in the diwan of Rayy, copying decrees and tax edicts under the vizier’s seal. It was dull work, but safe — until the Sultan’s cousin accused my master of treason.

Years later, the Sultan’s levy took my best camels and left me with debt. So I took to guarding caravans instead of owning them. There is more honor, I think, in defending others’ goods than losing your own.
Since then, I’ve hunted men and beasts alike. Both bleed the same color when struck cleanly.
But when I charted the stars too accurately, my patron feared I had learned to predict his death. He burned my scrolls and cast me out for sorcery.
Now I write contracts for mercenaries, love letters for merchants, and lies for anyone who pays. But perhaps it’s time to serve a master whose words I need not twist.
I was a scribe of Rayy’s court until the vizier fell from favor. Now I sell my pen and sword to those who pay in coin instead of promises.
The frontier teaches a man what the cities forget.
If your cause is just, I will serve you. If not, I will still serve — but I will pray for your soul.
I am an astronomer of Isfahan, once favored by princes. Now I seek a patron brave enough to trust both sword and science.
Do you believe a sword can find enlightenment?
I could use an eye as sharp as yours.
Few men would test you twice, I think.
Now I travel with soldiers, for they are the only men who still look to the heavens for guidance. If you’d like, I can tell you which hour favors victory — or vengeance.
If you pay fairly and shoot straight, I’ll ride with you. Betray me, and I’ll put an arrow in your banner from a mile away.
Now I carry both sword and rosary. I no longer kill for anger, but I still kill when the world demands it.
A man who knows the heavens is a dangerous ally indeed.
A strange creed, but perhaps a wise one.
Many men have fought for faith, few for truth.
Keep your eyes on the stars, scholar. I’ll watch the ground.
I am a huntress from the northern hills. My aim never falters, and neither does my will.
You wish to know why I carry a man’s bow? Because no man in the hills could best me with it.
Ah, a fellow traveler beneath the stars! Do you know that Mars has risen red three nights in a row? It bodes poorly for kings, but well for mercenaries.
I led caravans from Nishapur to Baghdad. Now I hire my sword and wit to those who respect the desert and its dangers.
The roads of Persia make warriors of us all.
If you seek fortune guided by reason and the stars, I will serve you — and perhaps write our story among the constellations.
We wandered from shrine to shrine, begging bread and teaching patience. I learned to fight without hatred — to see death as another guest on the road.

When the executions began, every man who’d dipped a pen in the vizier’s ink was marked. I fled with nothing but my inkwell and a stolen horse. They say ink is cleaner than blood — I have learned otherwise.
You look like someone who can read a ledger and swing a sword. I used to do only the first.
I’ve seen both zealots and unbelievers die the same way. If you fight for something more than plunder, I’ll ride beside you.
I rode with the ghazis of Anatolia, where the Crusaders press upon our borders and the Greeks build walls higher than the sky. We fought beneath the banner of faith, or so they told us.
I prefer prayers that strike harder.
You smell of dust and travel. Good — you might understand the road’s hunger.
I was once a soldier, now a dervish. I have learned that to master the blade, one must first master the heart.
A bold woman with a steady hand is always welcome.

Once I was a soldier of Merv, proud and quick to anger. Then I met a dervish who said, “The sharpest blade is the one turned inward.” I struck him for his insolence. When he smiled through the blood, I followed him for seven years.
My father traded silks between Nishapur and Baghdad. I learned early that a caravan’s heart is not its beasts, but its guards. Gold draws blades like a lamp draws moths.
I am a ghazi from the Seljuk frontier. I’ve fought in Anatolia, Aleppo, and the Taurus passes — for faith once, and now for gold.
But after every victory, the spoils went to the emirs, and the poor buried their sons in the dust. I began to wonder if God favors courage or coin.
A soldier’s god is whoever pays his wages.
When bandits struck near Kermanshah, I rallied the guards myself and broke them with a feigned retreat. The merchants began to call me “The Falcon of the Road.” A foolish name, but I wore it proudly.

My tribe lived along the northern slopes near Tabriz. My brothers hunted gazelle, but I hunted bandits. When the caravan raids grew bold, the emir offered silver for their heads — and I brought him three.
He praised my aim but refused to pay, saying a woman’s kill did not count. So I shot his falcon from the sky and left before he could summon guards.
If you need a man who can read decrees and command men alike, I am your servant. I only ask to die in a better story than the one I wrote myself.
I studied in the madrasah of Isfahan under the pupils of Omar Khayyam himself. Geometry, poetry, astronomy — the trinity of divine order, or so he called it.
I'm an engineer. Many of us learned our trade through castle works and the military musters of the dukes. Fortifications and bridges were built in haste in these unsettled times.
But when the ducal purse ran thin, patronage slackened and local magnates took charge of repairs; often they paid in promises and favors rather than coin.
I refused to let poor workmanship stand unchallenged; that cost me commissions, so I wander and offer honest plans for stone and timber wherever a lord will pay me fairly.
For coin I mend towers or undermine walls; if you need a breach or a buttress, I know the measures to do it right.
An engineer trained on ducal and castellans' works. I can build, restore, and when necessary, reduce a wall to rubble with siegecraft.
Integrity is a brave thing in these parts.
Or the fastest way to be poor and friendless.
I trained as a surgeon in the capital's infirmary and once tended the nobility. I thought learning would shield me from the world’s worse ways.
Then a secret office of the court sought my hands for more than healing — for extracting information. My refusal brought threats to my practice and to my family.
Shame and ruin followed. I fled the city and now wander, binding wounds in the field and drinking to blot out the memories.
I heal for coin now. I prefer field wounds and honest pay; I will apply my skill where honour is kept.
A trained surgeon ruined by court intrigues, now wandering and mending men where pays are honest.
You too are victim of the state's reach.
You broke your oath and now topple further.
My father was a knight of small estate; when he fell in battle, a neighbouring steward wove claims to our land and tried to bind me into marriage with his cousin.
I would not marry that man — he was coarse and drunken — so I saddled my father's horse and rode off with his sword and a hope of better fortune.
I know courtly ways and the basics of riding; if I find a lord who will take me as a retainer I will learn further and perhaps one day reclaim my birthright.
If a fighting company will have me, I will serve and learn the craft. I will not be trodden under a steward's heel forever.
A noble's daughter who fled a forced marriage; she rides and fights while she hunts the means to reclaim her estate.
You show spirit — that counts for much.
Takes more than spirit to make a captain.
I've ridden with men from the borderlands and the river lands, fought Pomerans and pagans, and have been known in many a market and tower.
I've bested men who thought themselves sterner, and I've been wounded and healed. Ask the smithy — he'll tell you about my scars.
War is not play; it strips vanity away. If you have a quarrel, end it quick, or pay me well to do so.
I take work with merchants and captains; I'm no man's pet but I keep my own counsel and my own coin.
You want to hear of me? I suppose I can spare a few lines.
My father served as a mounted man-at-arms for a duke in the east; we held a small estate so long as horses and arms were paid for.
When raids by pagans took his life and our land, the castellan gave what he would and said little else. Horses are costly and a mounted man without a steed is but a foot soldier.
I refuse the footman's life if I can help it, so I ride with merchants and captains to earn coin and save to buy my own horse and tack.
I pick my employers and my fights. When I can, I help shepherd lads into competent cavalrymen.
A former mounted man raised to the saddle by his father. Now a hired blade while I save for a horse of my own.
It is not without some reluctance that I tell this story, for it hardly does honour to my name.
You wear your father's name well.
A proud aim; let us see if you keep it.
I served in a duke's retinue for twenty years. There was honour, once, in steady watch and in the keeping of lines.
But a string of bad commanders and empty purses left men disillusioned. Reforms that promised much gave us less than the tax-collector's ledger.
I teach recruits now or sell my sword to captains who will pay and keep their word. I can turn raw lads into something like soldiers.
I will train a host for coin, and I know siegecraft enough to instruct men in battering and defense.
A veteran instructor and siege-hand; I know how to make soldiery of folk and how to take a town.
There's a need for instructors more than heroic tales.
Every man grows old and sings of better days.
Me and some lads from the glen ran off to make our fortunes on the roads rather than break our backs in the fields. We thought to take what we could from those who travel with coin.
But we were rougher than clever, and many of us died or were hanged when the patrols came. I learned quick that banditry is a poor teacher of longevity.
So I paid what I could and had my name cleared, and now I work in towns where the law is a little kinder and the wages less likely to end me on a gibbet.
Life in the city is cruder but steadier. I can work as escort or watchman for merchants — coin is coin, and it keeps the gallows distant.
Once an outlaw, now seeking honest work. I can fight and survive; I prefer merchants and well-paid captains.
Oh, I suppose I can tell you.
A knave who couldn't abide knavery - strange indeed.
What do you want to know about? My family? Piss on them. I left as a lad and never regretted it. They can keep what they had; I want to make my own way.
I've been in scuffles and small wars for a harvest of years. Men often show their teeth in battle; I'm no fool to their loyalty.
That's all I say of the past.
I fight well and do the work men avoid. If coin and hard labor are required, I'm available.
A man who kills for a living. He prefers to let the sword speak rather than tales of honor.
You may have heard of a mad preacher promising a righteous duke and the end of rent and burdens; many followed and some took to arms.
For a time we struck at tax collectors and rich men, but when leaders turned to looting and extortion the dream soured and the duke sent a host against us.
I fled the ruin, and learned the secret ways of the hills — how to track, scout, and run a caravan clear of danger.
Now I sell my skills to captains who pay and keep to the code. I know how to move goods and men unseen.
An ex-rebel turned practical guide and scout. I keep my head low and my coin steady.
A sad ruin of good intent.
Rebellion and brigandage are sisters in these parts.
My family had debts, so I took a captain's press. I was not born for a loom; the spear was nearer my nature.
Dressed as a man, I learned the march, the watch, the long cold of river crossings. It was not hard to hide the truth when a helm hides truth.
An ambush ended our muster and I walked away rather than follow useless winds of glory. Now I take mercantile work and quiet guard work where oaths mean more than show.
I can wield spear and sword and mend arms; if a captain seeks discreet, steady hands, I'd answer.
Once a foot-soldier disguised as a man; now a reliable guard and steady sword for hire.
There's always work for the brave.
My father ran a granary in the capital. During riots the store was looted and the house burned; the mob took coin and life without care.
We tried to find shelter with kin but there was no food and no mercy; so we were forced onto the road, living by theft and what little we could beg.
I killed a drunken guard who threatened my child and took his sword. It has fed us and kept us sheltered since.
I'm adaptable and can take retainer work with a warband; I owe little and ask coin for my skill.
A merchant's child turned refugee who learned to fight. I will serve and learn quickly.
I'll tell you my story. Keep it if you will.
A girl of letters turned to sword — strange fate.
I was orphaned and took to the alleys, learning to pick pockets and run errands for a gang. I did what was needed for bread.
As I grew older they wanted me for worse work. The gang expected obedience; when they turned on me I took what I could and fled during the chaos of a siege.
I carry a knife and a secret. I can be useful for those who wish a quiet answer to their enemies.
If you need someone to remove an obstacle quietly, name your price and I will see to it.
An orphan learned in the arts of stealth and steel. I sell precision and discretion to those who can pay.
You have survived where many would have perished.
You are the dregs of the street, my lady.
A seasoned fighter who has seen border fights and river skirmishes. If your host needs men who won't flee at the first river's crossing, I am for hire.

I'm a surgeon. I trained at the imperial academy in {IMPERIALCAPITAL}. I had many rich and influential patients in the town. I thought I was well shielded from the intrigues and dangers of the Portuguese.

I'm a soldier by trade. I've served in the portugueses' legions for 20 years. Once upon a time they were worthy of being called 'legions.' We served together for years, and we'd die rather than see our standards falter or fall.

But one day I was contacted by an agent of the Bureau of Barbarian Affairs. I do not know how well you know them. Their original mission was to keep the foreign tribes divided and weak, but they expanded their remit into all the affairs of the Portuguese, anything that might be deemed a threat.
