At first they wanted small harmless details about my patients. To do so was a violation of my oath, but I was anxious to have the favor of the Bureau. But soon they began to call on me for more and more.

But the Turks overran us, and he was slain, and our land was taken. Its revenues now belong to some tarkhan. Alas, the Portuguese have little land to grant today, even to trained cavalrymen like myself who wish to serve. And horses are expensive.
A cavalier of the Portuguese doing errands for traders! The shame of it!
The rivers teach a man more than a tutor ever will.

I was born beneath the birch roofs of Novgorod and my father sold furs and honey to merchants who sailed for the Baltic and the western lands. I learned the ways of the river, how to steer a ladya and read the weather by the reeds.

Novgorod's veche can be a blessing and a burden: one year a decision favours a house, the next year a different vote leaves you with half your debts. When a dispute over toll rights turned my father's cargo into a legal ruin, we lost what we had.

So I took to hired work, piloting river convoys and running merchant escort. Where the Dnieper meets the sea, you learn new tongues and how the Greeks price a bale of cloth. I keep my oar ready; a good captain will pay for steady hands more than gossip.
If you know a merchant convoy that needs a pilot on river and sea, send him my way. I can guard goods and keep the oars moving through night fog.
Novgorod born, raised to trade and the river. When civic decisions ruined my father's business I became a boatman-for-hire and occasional escort for caravans heading to the sea.
Novgorod men are worth their salt on the water.
So you turned commerce into sword work — a common but sorry trade.
The border keeps a man's valour tested daily.

I come from the western marches in the principality of Galicia (Halych), where Polish and Hungarian claims press upon our lands. We keep heavier mail and heavier horses — the fields there take a different breed of warrior.

Our prince raised a levy; my manor's men were conscripted and my household ruined to equip a border garrison. When a neighbouring magnate seized what was left, I answered him with steel and the courts refused me remedy.
I sold my last horse, took a new captain's oath, and rode eastwards. If you want an experienced horseman used to mixed border warfare and riding in rough country, I'm for hire.
I will serve a captain who seeks riders who can fight in broken ground, hold a ford, and harry enemy convoys. I ask fair wage and good feed for my mount.
Galicia-born border rider and former lesser boyar. Loss of land and court remedy sent me into service as a mounted fighter-for-hire.
A border horseman brings good discipline and knowledge of heavy cavalry work.
So a boyar becomes a mercenary — not uncommon where borders bled men and coin.
Medicine and prayer have kept more houses from ruin than any sword.
I was taught herbal lore and liturgy in a convent near Pereiaslavl. We tended the poor and the wounded; monks and nuns kept libraries with Greek and Slavonic remedies written in margins.

When raids tore through near villages, the convent sheltered women and bandaged the men who returned. The prince demanded nurses for his camp and took two of our sisters. When discipline there proved a cruelty to the poor, I left rather than serve a banner that treated people as fodder.

I mind wounds and set broken bones; I've seen Byzantine surgical notes and know poultices that stop fever. I'll travel with captains who let me tend the wounded, not barter them away as bargaining chips.
If you lead men into harm and value them after the fight, hire me to tend the wounded and keep your men from dying of infected cuts.
Trained at a Pereiaslavl convent, schooled in herbals and liturgy; I left service to princely camps and now offer field medicine to those who will not trade the wounded like cattle.
A healer who knows both the monasteries and the field is rare and necessary.
A convent-born woman on the road — some call that folly, others call it courage.
Ask about wars and you'll hear old men sing my name in taverns.
I served in the druzhina of the Prince of Chernigov for many seasons. Our clan raised me to the spear; we rode under banners, and the name of our prince carried weight for many leagues.

When princely quarrels came—land claims, old feuds—the druzhina was called to take sides. I saw brothers-in-arms broken by tricks and councils. The prince changed, the pay grew slim, and the boyars fought like wolves over spoils.

I kept faith with my comrades, but when the prince took a course I could not fathom, I left rather than stain my name. Now I sell my sword to captains who still remember how to lead men without betrayal.
If you command a small band that wants steady spearwork and someone who knows siege and field tactics, I'm not greedy.
Veteran of Chernigov's druzhina, turned to free service after court intrigues and unpaid wages left my household bare.
A druzhina-man's worth is the oath he keeps.
Princely quarrels are no place for honour, only for coin.
The steppe is no tale; it's where boys learn a hard measure of the world.

I grew up near Pereyaslavl, where the plains turn to grass and the raids come like storm-winds. We learned to ride and ride fast; a man who could not catch a stray foal could not keep his head long in these parts.

Our village paid tribute and held watch at the river ford. When a raid took my brother and burned our granaries, the local prince could spare no men. I swore to buy horses for the village and took a captain's pay to learn scouting among the frontier companies.
Now I follow a captain as a guide and skirmisher. I know how to pick a patrol's ground, where to find water, and when to fall back. If a lord needs eyes on an open plain, I can be them.
I'm for hire to border captains and anyone moving across plains who requires a man who knows steppe roads and ambush grounds.
Pereyaslavl frontier-born scout — we ride, watch, and trade blows for coin. I keep my eyes open for a captain who pays promptly.
Good scouts keep more men alive than any bravado.
So you turned family revenge into a soldier's trade.
Words keep power; a man who reads them keeps his head longer.

I served in the princely chancery at Kiev—copying charters, sealing grain allotments, setting down the revenues. St. Sophia's bells were not merely for show; I know more prayers than barters, and more lines than a ploughman.

Court is a place of gifts and knives. A false phrase in a charter, and a lord's steward is ruined; a secret kept too long and a rival prince grows suspicious. When a noble's letter cost me friends, I chose exile rather than be the tool of faction.
I have travelled to Byzantium in a prince's retinue, seen Hagia Sophia's mosaics, and learnt to judge a contract by its hand. I will write for coin, read treaties, and keep your payroll honest.
If a lord wants an honest account, or a captain needs a clerk for pay and supplies, I'll take the work — if the price fits the risks.
Former chancery scribe from Kiev, schooled in both church and court. I trade words for coin, and I prefer work that keeps my hands clean of blood.
A scribe who has seen Constantinople brings rare wisdom.
Courts eat men like you who keep too many secrets.
Where Polotsk coin clinks, men learn two markets at once.

My family traded along the rivers to the Dvina and into Baltic markets. We bartered furs, wax and honey for salt and iron. Polotsk men take pride in a double tongue — Slav and Norse in a single mouth.

But trade is not all ledgers and honest scales. Pirates and rival houses took to threatening convoys; a neighbour's loan became a claim on our storehouses. When the boyar who guaranteed our credit failed, our ships were seized.

I took to hiring as an armed factor, escorting goods and settling accounts at market. I know ports from Ladoga to the mouth of the Dnieper. A captain who travels the sea with my counsel will lose fewer cargos.
I can manage convoys, strike bargains in the north, and supervise loading and inspection. If you have goods to move, I'll keep them from vandals and drowners alike.
Polotsk-born trader; when family trade failed I became an armed caravan factor and convoy escort — equal parts bookkeeper and watchman.
A merchant who can fight is worth his weight in salt.
Trade and fighting make poor partners, but both pay.
The forests don't forgive a bad step.

I came from the pinelands by Smolensk; our houses hide under needles and the furthest roads smell of wolf. My father taught me to set snares, to follow the trail of a boar, to read the flight of a grouse.
When raiders grew bolder and taxes heavier, our village could not survive from trapping alone. I took a blade and sold my tracking to a local commander who needed men who knew where the wolves hide.
As a woodsman I can scout, forage, and keep a small band's bellies full in hostile country. If you reward skill, I will show you how a forest can become a fortress.
If you need a guide to move through woods and marsh, or someone to find game and trap lines for a winter camp, I'm the man for the price.
Smolensk woodsman turned scout. I trade game and fur knowledge for coin, and prefer small bands who value foraging and stealth.
A woodsman knows how to keep men alive where others die.
Scouts are easy to come by; men who live by their wits are rare.
We in Rostov remember our fathers' oars.
My kin came down from the north — Varangians who settled near Rostov and married local women. We kept the oar and the axe, but learned Slav speech and faith.

I served in a prince's retinue as a household man, and later on ships that ran down the coast. When the prince rewarded foreign-born retainers with lands and I was overlooked, I had to choose between begging and leaving my oars for sale.
So I took to the roads as a free sword. I like to be among men who know both the sea and shield — a company that sails in winter and cages men in battle is my sort.
If you have an outfit that fights by sea and field, I can row, fight on deck, and stand in the line when the banners fall.
Rostov-born with Varangian ancestry — shipborn and shield-hardened. I offer seamanship and swordwork to captains who demand both.
Varangian blood gives steady hands in a storm and steady feet in a shieldwall.
So you traded landless discontent for a life of hire. Many have done worse.
A smith's hands are never idle; nor are they forgiven easily.
I worked the bellows in Suzdal and learnt to temper mail and shape spear points. Princes need good iron, and my work once kept a town from fear of the northern raids.

When the prince demanded weapons and seized a third of my stock for his levy, I protested. The boyar took that as an insult. My forge was given to another smith and I was offered a lowly post — a wage that would not cover coal.

I took my hammer and left, seeking a captain who would pay for custom work and not take my trade for granted. I will mend broken blades and teach recruits how to hold a sword so it doesn't shatter their hand.
If your company needs armour repaired or weapons made, I can be hired for fieldwork or as an armorer. I prefer honest coin to princely robbery.
Suzdal smith, skilled in mail and spear. Dispossessed by princely requisition, I now offer armour-smithing to those who pay fair.
A master smith is invaluable to any fighting company.
A smith who leaves his forge for coin has reasons that go beyond brass wages.
The sea speaks a different language than the court.
I was born where the sea meets the land in Tmutarakan. Greek merchants, Khazars, and coastal princes all pass through our harbours. From them I learned to repair hulls and to bargain in Greek coins.

A gale and a bad cargo claim once ruined my brother's tavern, and the prince took our ship as security. No verdict came quick enough. I could either watch the sea rot my tools, or I could take my craft to those who needed it for coin.
So I became a shipwright and occasional helmsman for hire — building boats for raiding captains, fitting hulls for trade, and teaching men seamanship when we sail into Greek and Armenian ports.
If you plan sea raids or trade down the Dnieper to the Bosporus, I can build and fix your boats, and show your men how to take a longship in a squall.
Tmutarakan-born mariner and shipwright; Greek-facing and seaworthy. I sell boatsmithing and helmsmanship to captains of trade or war.
A Black Sea man has his uses in any campaign.
Who trusts a man who mixed with Greeks? Many do, many more don't.
Novgorod gives a man a voice and then sometimes a boot to the road.
I commanded a small militia raised by the veche to protect trade and push back raiders. Novgorod's assembly can be wise, but it is fickle; a council decision can elevate or cast out a man.

When I refused a mandate that I felt threatened my people's grain stores—preferring a cautious watch to a reckless sortie—the veche men turned on me and blamed me for missing an easy prize. Voices are loud in an assembly.
They exiled me. I keep my sword and my men in smaller companies now. I offer discipline, training, and a knowledge of militia craft for captains tired of raw recruits.
If you command levies or townsmen and want some steady training, hire me. I'll teach a man to hold the line without needing a nobleman to bite his shield.
Former veche militia commander from Novgorod, cast out by political voice. I train soldiers and command small, disciplined companies for pay.
A captain who can train raw men into a wall of spears is a treasure.
The veche eats its own sometimes; better a man on the road than dead in a pit.

I am Scottish. But for 20 years, I fought for the Empire. Indeed, most Scottish my age learned their trade in the legions. We saw no dishonor in it. They fed us well, they paid us well, they respected our courage.

My family was not one of the greatest clans of the Scottish, but neither are we among the poorest. When I came of age, my family sent me to join the Wolfskins. You may have heard of this tradition - for three years we live in the woods and do not eat cooked meat, wear spun cloth, or sleep under a roof, and according to the law we are beasts, not bound by the laws of men.

My uncle - he had a great herd of cows, and in the Scottish upcountry that is only kind of wealth we value. But they were taken by his chief herdsman, a man we trusted. So we took up spears to get them back, but my uncle was now poor, but the thief had many kinsmen. Having nothing else to lose, my uncle ordered that even the women of our family take up spears and ride out to fight, and so we did.

I do things in the old way, and so whenever an enemy falls to my spear, I take their head! Let's see - I have Brechtan the Old, Lamaich the Lame -- don't let the names fool you, these were great warriors - Archan the Bull, so many others! A true Scottish never boasts, because his deeds are hung over the hearth for all to see. At least that's the way it used to be.

But there's no legions any more. And since Caladog became king, well, he's gotten the young to think that to fight for the Empire is treason. Treason to what? 'scottish'? There is no scottish. Never has been. Just a bunch of quarreling warlords, who'll steal your cows as soon as you turn your back on them.

Well now, I am a warrior of the Scottish. There is no greater boast than that, I will tell you! But perhaps if you hire me, I can tell you more later about the great names I have slain and the heads I have taken.

I am Scottish by birth but I served with the Empire. Many of us did. A brave lord, a captain who cares for his men... What does it matter in which language your oath of fealty is given, as long as you honor it?
I'm a surgeon. I trained at the imperial academy in {IMPERIALCAPITAL}. I had many rich and influential patients in the town. I thought I was well shielded from the intrigues and dangers of the Serbs.

I'm a soldier by trade. I've served in the Serbs' legions for 20 years. Once upon a time they were worthy of being called 'legions.' We served together for years, and we'd die rather than see our standards falter or fall.

But one day I was contacted by an agent of the Bureau of Barbarian Affairs. I do not know how well you know them. Their original mission was to keep the foreign tribes divided and weak, but they expanded their remit into all the affairs of the Serbs, anything that might be deemed a threat. At first they wanted small harmless details about my patients. To do so was a violation of my oath, but I was anxious to have the favor of the Bureau. But soon they began to call on me for more and more.

But the Turks overran us, and he was slain, and our land was taken. Its revenues now belong to some tarkhan. Alas, the Serbs have little land to grant today, even to trained cavalrymen like myself who wish to serve. And horses are expensive.
A cavalier of the Serbs doing errands for traders! The shame of it!
A sword arm is the easiest way to earn a living, if one survives.
And yet you still walk among men, not waves.
A precise hand is worth more than a sword arm sometimes.
I am a Norman sailor. The sea is my teacher; my skill is my coin.
From the fields of Normandy to the hills of Calabria, I learned that steel can speak louder than words.
Healing hands are often the last hope in a dying land.
I fought under many banners, earned coin from lords and captains, and survived betrayals and battle alike.
Now I wander between lands, offering my blade to those who can pay, keeping loyalty minimal but honor intact.
I studied in Palermo, tending to the sick and wounded. I learned herbs, bandages, and the ways of balancing life and death.
Wars and famines taught me that skill alone cannot save everyone. Yet skill is precious to those who can survive.
I look for those who reward skill and courage, not arrogance or cruelty.
Now I wander, offering my aid for those in need, hoping to leave behind less death than I find.
Yet still wandering, as the coin runs dry.
I seek those who value life, but do not shrink from the work it takes to preserve it.
A soldier of fortune, then. Admirable.
A healer’s work is never done.
I am a Norman sellsword. My blade and skill are my coin, and I trust few men with either.
Gold is a fair master, though it has no conscience.
I am a Sicilian outlaw, clever and deadly. I offer my services for coin or cause, and trust only my own judgment.
History remembers the brave, but not always the clever.
I am a Norman mercenary. I offer my sword and my counsel to those who can pay for both.
A life on the knife’s edge indeed.
Born in Palermo, I learned to read and write in monasteries. I traveled with armies, courts, and merchants, recording deeds and events.
I am a Sicilian medic. Life is precious, and skill my tool to preserve it.
I learned that truth is often bent by power, yet recording it preserves it for those who care to read.
I move unseen where others cannot.
I am a Norman knight, trained from boyhood. My skills are my coin, and my sword is my word.
Now I wander, collecting stories, writing letters for those who cannot, and chronicling deeds for posterity.
Raised near Rouen, I learned to move silently, track men and animals, and find paths through forests unknown to many.
And yet your eyes have seen much death, I imagine.
I seek tales of valor and folly alike, and those who value the pen as well as the sword.
I scouted for lords and mercenaries alike, mapping terrain, finding enemy camps, and returning with knowledge that saved lives.
I am a Norman archer, trained in the forests of my homeland. I offer my bow to those who pay and value skill.
Now I wander alone or with small bands, selling information and guidance to those who need it most.
And yet your journey is no less dangerous than theirs.
I value keen eyes, quick feet, and those who respect skill over bluster.
Few can match your skill in the wild.
I am a Sicilian chronicler. My pen records deeds, my eyes witness history, and my path follows both.
A knight without a liege? Bold choice.
And yet you risk much alone.
A subtle hand and a clever mind. Impressive.
I am a Norman scout. My eyes and feet are my tools, my knowledge my currency.
A mind for machines and men alike.
Yet I sense a burden upon your conscience.
Gold moves faster than men, and sometimes teaches more.
You live dangerously. I hope the law does not find you.
Trust is a rare commodity in your trade, I see.
Born in Messina, I learned trade and coin. I traveled markets, ports, and caravans, learning whose word was worth trusting.
I am a Sicilian engineer, trained to build and destroy. My services are precise, and my reputation follows my conscience.
I am a Sicilian spy and messenger. Secrets are my coin, discretion my shield.
I made deals, paid bribes, avoided thieves, and sometimes made war through contracts rather than swords.
Many knights would call you aimless. Perhaps, but courage has its own reward.
Now I wander as a merchant of information, goods, and occasionally mercenary contacts.
I value careful calculation, profit, and those who can keep their word when others do not.
A keen mind for coin and men.
A good eye and steady hand matter more than the color of your banner.
And yet business can be deadly here.
The sea has hardened you well.
I am a Sicilian merchant. Knowledge and coin are my trade; discretion my ally.
I fight for gold, and perhaps for glory, though the first feeds the second more often.
Born in Palermo, I learned early that laws serve those who enforce them, not those they claim to protect. Bandits became my teachers, until I grew cleverer than most.
My home was Normandy, but I found my future on the battlefields of southern Italy. I learned that loyalty is earned in coin, not birthright.
I served many lords, and many fell, but I endured. Skill in arms and knowledge of terrain made me valuable, even when my comrades died.
Now I wander as a mercenary captain, hiring out my services where they are needed, and refusing work that dishonors my name.
I survived by my wits and blade, raiding merchant caravans and avoiding the watch. Some call me villain, some call me liberator, depending on whose eyes they see through.
I fought in Sicily, Calabria, and Apulia, where archers were prized and killed in great numbers. I survived where many did not, and learned how to value my life and aim.
I value strong men and smart strategies. Those who pay me wisely get the advantage; those who do not, get only my shadow.
Now I wander, offering my sword to any who need skill in arms, for coin or for cause, though I trust few men completely.
Life has a way of forcing men to take paths they did not plan.
I seek those who value skill and patience over pomp and bluster, and who reward those who can keep them alive in battle.
I seek lords or captains who honor skill and courage, who do not waste lives on petty quarrels.
Raised in Messina, I learned early that words can kill as well as swords. I moved among merchants, priests, and soldiers, taking note of secrets and opportunities.
I tinker with wood and metal, and sometimes men get caught in the gears.
I became a messenger, a spy, and occasionally a saboteur. I never chose sides permanently, but always learned whose favor was worth cultivating.
I have fought in many fields, though not all under banners I could respect.
I trained in Palermo as an engineer. Castles and bridges were my education, and siege engines my tutors.
I worked under lords and captains alike, fixing walls and machines that might crumble or crush. Some feared my honesty, some appreciated it.
Now I wander between courts and camps, offering intelligence and discretion, and keeping my own counsel above all else.
Now I wander, offering knowledge of machines of war, hoping my conscience does not crush me first.
I work for those who pay and those whose plans intrigue me. Loyalty is conditional; usefulness is eternal.
Now I wander, selling my bow to lords, captains, and merchants who need someone unseen and deadly at range.
Skill is my trade; discretion is my shield. I build what is asked, or unbuild what threatens the weak.
I fought in Italy with my kin, carving a name for ourselves, though the battles were costly, and many of my brothers fell to fever and steel alike.
Now I wander openly, offering my services to those who pay, for protection, intelligence, or muscle, and leaving vengeance behind where I can.
Born in Normandy, I was trained from youth to ride and wield sword and lance. Our lands were small but proud, and the church watched closely over our upbringing.
The sea has taught me more than any lord or tutor.
From the forests of Normandy, I learned the bow before the sword. Hunting foxes and deer gave me patience, and the skirmishes in our county honed my skill against men.
I trust few, pay attention to all, and take work that suits my talents. Honor is scarce, but coin speaks.
Born on the coast of Calabria, I learned the winds and tides, the handling of sails and oars, and how men reveal their hearts in storms.
I see what others miss, hear what others ignore.
I sailed to Sicily, Malta, and beyond, escorting merchants, raiding corsairs, and surviving mutinies that would have broken lesser men.
Now I wander from port to port, offering my seamanship and knowledge of currents, tides, and coastal defenses.
I trust the wind more than lords, and the sea more than men. Yet coin and survival keep me moving.
I have seen many battles, and lived to tell the tale.
Time and wounds catch us all. Now I prefer a quieter life, but I cannot sit idle.
So I wander, offering my sword to causes I deem worthy and training those willing to learn.
A knight without a banner. Noble still.
I offer skills of information gathering and reconnaissance. Payment must be prompt.
Now I wander to assist those in need, and occasionally fight for causes that align with justice.
Experience counts more than the shield you carry.
I can train men in sword and lance, and guide small companies through minor campaigns.
Faith teaches patience, but patience must be balanced with action. I have seen the heretic and the thief, and I have struck when called.
A retired knight, skilled in combat and leadership, now wandering and offering my services where needed.
Faith tempered with steel. I respect that.
I wander now, selling my sword or knowledge to anyone who can afford it. All the glory in the world doesn't matter when you need food and a roof.
I offer guidance, combat skill, and knowledge of scripture to those who seek it.
But I am cautious. One misstep and your life ends, or worse, your reputation.
I can teach both sheep and men to obey commands. Not a bad skill in the wars these days.
From Andalusia, I learned the arts of disguise and eavesdropping young. Now I serve any who can afford me.
I am a spy and scout. I move unseen, gather secrets, and sell them to those who can pay.
I take my vows seriously, but swords are sometimes necessary.
Sheep are honest animals. You must be honest to tend them. So when the war came to our lands, I took up arms in defense of the village.
I have heard many secrets, seen many things. The world is full of intrigue, and I profit where others fail.
A monk with martial skills. Interesting.
I served a few years, fought, killed, and survived. Came out the other end with a few scars and a lot of stories.
But peace is rare. War comes again. So I wander, selling my sword and sheep knowledge wherever I can.
I was trained in the monastery in scripture and sword. Our abbey sent monks to defend the surrounding lands when invaders came.
Once I rode with a lord's company, loyal to a fault. I fought in countless skirmishes and sieges.
You wish to know about me? It's a tale of trade and travel.
I hail from the Kingdom of Valencia, born to a family of merchants. From an early age, I learned the routes of the coast and inland, guiding caravans and trading goods.
When the political climate became unstable, rival merchants and brigands threatened our operations. I took up a blade alongside my ledgers, protecting our wares and scouting new trade routes.
Now I wander through towns and ports, offering my skills as a scout and merchant adviser. I know how to read terrain, avoid ambushes, and negotiate deals where others fail.
I respect knowledge, caution, and honor in commerce. Those who lie, cheat, or plunder find little patience from me.
A man of skill and prudence, indeed.
And yet your path is perilous for one so fair-minded.
I am a Christian Valencian merchant-scout. Skilled in trade, reconnaissance, and navigation, I wander seeking work and opportunity where both honor and profit meet.
A monk trained in both faith and arms, now wandering to assist and protect.

I'm a soldier by trade. I've served in the spanish's legions for 20 years. Once upon a time they were worthy of being called 'legions.' We served together for years, and we'd die rather than see our standards falter or fall.

You may have heard of Ladimos the Red. He preached that the Heavens were getting ready to unload their wrath on landowners and merchant, that we had to drive them out and live pure lives and we'd be rewarded with a Pure Emperor, come down from the skies. This was some 10 years ago. Well, a lot of us ran off to follow him, some of us believed him and some had debts and some just wanted to take a lick at those that oppressed us.

But the Cumans overran us, and he was slain, and our land was taken. Its revenues now belong to some tarkhan. Alas, the spanish has little land to grant today, even to trained cavalrymen like myself who wish to serve. And horses are expensive.
Yes, I gather information for a living.
You lived, then. Good for you.
A cavalier of the spanish doing errands for traders! The shame of it!
From shepherd to soldier, now wandering mercenary. I know terrain, livestock, and men.
Fought with crude weapons at first, then some knight took pity and gave me a proper sword. I learned fast, and survived, enough to make a name in the village.
I hope your sheep are still alive, then.
I was a female soldier disguised as a man. Now I wander, trained, skilled, and ready to work wherever my sword is needed.

I lived in a small coastal village across the gulf. The north is a hard place — jarls quarrel over grazing and ships, and a lord’s feud can burn a whole hamlet down. My mother tended the sick with herbs and song; I learned at her knee until the raid that took her and the man I was to wed.

I was the finest youth in my village for sword and axe; folk said I fought like a berserker. At coming-of-age I rode south to find war and coin, first serving with the Vaegir guard but chafing at their discipline.

My father was a noted raider whose leg was cut in a raid and who kept us fed with spoils. We invested his victories in land and thralls, but I swore to earn for my own house and to buy a ship of my own.
I served in the imperial guard in the days of Arenicos. We were proud of order and formation, but when the emperor fell the city turned and the guard became the target of the mob.
I was a tiller of earth until a quarrel over a boundary fence ended with a man’s skull split by my hoe. Blood enmeshes a man — what started as anger took me beyond repair.

In our law when a matter cannot be settled, we let champions answer in single combat — it is an old way. If a man will not fight, he hires a champion to fight for him; the thing is that courage has a price.
My parents died when I was young and my sister married to a man who coveted the farm. He hired a crafty law-man to press his claim, and the thing awarded them our land.
My father was a draftsman, a builder for local jarls — towers, keeps and palisades. He taught me to draw plans and to mark timber for the keel and wall.
I come from a good house and always wished to be a shield-maiden. I trained with the village boys and learned the spear, but my father insisted a daughter should spin and bring dowry, not blood.
I do a man's work better than most men. I am not given to excuses: I show up sober, do the task, and collect my pay. That is my promise.

They wanted cattle and timber; they took everything else too. We fled into the birchwoods and I swore never to be helpless while others decided my fate. I will mend the wounded on the field, and if need be, I will learn to wound as well as I heal.

I then joined a shield-clan — the Skolderbroda — but their insistence on tight ranks and shield-walls bored me. I favor the bloody melee: charge, cleave, and send a man home with no use for his bragging.
I will not sell the homestead to fit out a crew, so I hire myself as a warrior until I can buy a longship and hire men to row her. I plan raids to bring back silver and people to trade or sell.
We tried to hold the peace, but loot and anger spread like wildfire. Some of my comrades looted and killed in the fury; later I would see what men do when law decays and I could not unsee it.
His kin came for blood-payment. I could have paid for one life, but not three. In the fury I killed again and then fled, for our thing would have hanged me.

I made a trade of it — championing men for coin. I fought for heads, ransoms and honor-claims. It paid well till the councils said I sold my sword too cheaply and banned me from being a lawful champion.
I left for the woods, living by trapping and selling furs. The life is quiet and it suits me better than court talk and oaths.
When he died I stayed with my uncle but the folk muttered I brought evil — a blemish on my shoulder looked like a witch-mark. The village elders demanded I leave and do not return.
I was married off and my husband insulted me in the market. I struck him down in a lawful duel, was judged not guilty by the thing — but I was disinherited and shamed, so I left.
You will not find me passed out when needed. You will not have to bribe guards to get me out of a cell. I do what must be done, and I do it well.

Perhaps one day my kin will find peace. For now I travel from longhouse to longship offering salves, poultices and steady hands to men who bleed for silver, and I will not return to be at any man's mercy again.
The captains told me to keep my mouth shut or leave; I left. Now I look for a warband that pays for a man who makes trouble and survives it.
When I have a vessel, I will sail to rich coasts and come home with enough to secure marriages for my siblings and land for my sons. Till then my sword and shield will do.
I left with nothing but the clothes on my back and one old sword. Now I roam, looking for honest pay to earn back what I lost and a captain whose men keep discipline even in hard times.
I do not boast of it. A farmer has no love for a sword, but the Heavens decided a different path. Now men in the cities pay me for sharp work that the law will not let them do.
So now I wander and mercenary-work keeps my hand. Duels are clean and quick; I prefer them to long sieges and dull guard duty. If your leader needs a man who does not flinch, my price is fair.
Now I trap and guide hunters, but I also serve as scout for war-parties that need men who can vanish into the trees and report on an enemy’s tracks.

I wandered and learned to survive among thieves and sellswords, until I stole a sword from a careless bandit and found I could trade woodcraft as well as a blade. Now I hire out as builder and muscle both.
A warrior’s life is harder than the stories; yet it is honest. I now fight for pay, free of the obligations that once bound me.
If a chief needs someone who protects his wagons or cuts down his enemies cleanly, I am that woman — and I do not ask for pity.
If you know of a warband seeking someone to bind wounds and keep men whole after a raid, send them to me.
Still, if your company wants a fighter who charges where most hesitate, I'm available for the right share.
If you know a captain who values seamanship and daring, send word — I'll earn my share and more.
If there's a company that needs men who can hold rank and train others, I will join — and make coin while I do.
If fate had allowed it I would have stayed the farmer. But now I sell my sword in the towns — and those who pay well need my sort.
Still, for raising champions, I know the law and the blade. I will train men and stand where others would flee.
I know the woods and marshes. I can read a camp’s signs and find the best place to strike.
I work for whoever pays: build a palisade by day, take a contract as a guard by night. The world gave me no mercy; I give none back.
I cannot return home, but the sea and shield-house welcome those with skill. I fight now for coin — and the life I chose.
If your leader needs a solid, loyal sword, tell them of me. I will show more than I boast.
I was an herbalist in a northern village until raiders burned it. I now travel and treat warriors' wounds—there are many of us on the roads of Calradia.
I've fought with many hosts—Skolderbroda, Vaegir land-levies and sea-forces. Others may claim it, but I'm the real thing.
My father left us wealth from raids but I must make my own way. I plan to buy a ship and bring home enough for kin and clan; till then I hire my blade.
I was once in the imperial guard. After riots and the fall of the emperor I lost my pay and place. Now I offer my blade to a captain who values order.
I was a farmer forced to flee after killing in a feud. Blood-money could not be raised; thus I took to the road and the sword.
I was a paid champion, solving disputes by single combat for coin and reputation until councils outlawed me. Now I offer my arm to captains and chiefs who want firm men.
A trapper turned scout. I know the forest paths and the ways of beasts — and people alike.
I was an orphan wandering the roads until a stolen sword made me more than a beggar. I can build and fight, in equal measure.
I am a shield-maiden — not uncommon in the north, but rare enough to be noticed. I fight for coin, for freedom, and for the taste of the wind.
I'm a woman who left the spindle for the spear. Hire me and I will prove myself in action rather than speech.
Look, friend, I'm here to drink, not talk. But if you really want to know, I'll give it you in brief.
I'll tell you my tale. But I warn you: I care little for your approval.
Pour a drink, stranger. I'll tell you what you need to know.
You are a dutiful son and an ambitious man.
I have heard of the riots in {IMPERIALCAPITAL}. Ugly business.
It sounds like you had little choice.
Councils these days. Always changing tradition...
A good scout can command a fine price.
Perhaps such customs teach husbands to behave better.
A dependable fighter is precious these days.
It's a cruel world, and a warrior's path has its own pains.
Leaving a gap in a shield-wall will get your fellows killed; some call that treason.
Pious words from one who plans to pillage.
Many witness testimony blamed the guard for the emperor's fall.
A man who cannot master his rage is a danger indeed.
What woman would relish a husk-smelling spouse?
A good enough reputation will get you coin and few questions asked.

We Suzdalians have a tradition. If two people have a dispute, and there's no witnesses, so it all comes down to one man's word against another's, then we let them settle it with swords. If one man doesn't like to fight, he can hire someone else to do the fighting. That's how it works with us. Probably other people do the same, because it's a good tradition.

I apprenticed to a master mason who worked on keeps and abbey walls. For years we raised scaffolds and cut stone to the bishop's plans; the guild taught more than craft — it taught how to survive courtly caprice.

When the duke's revenues frayed, monasteries and castellans paid in arrears and favours, and many a well-laid arch had to wait on a lord's temper. Corruption and kinship meant contracts were often a matter of who you knew rather than what you could build.

I speak plain: I wouldn't see a wall lean because a man was someone's nephew. That cost me commissions and friends, so I travel looking for honest contracts — repair a tower, bolt a gate, or pull down a rotten keep if that's what's needed.
At any rate, I'm handy with measuring, pulleywork and catapults when the need calls. Lords hire men who can keep their walls standing — and sometimes they hire men to bring them down.
Engineer by trade, trained on keeps and abbeys. If stone or timber stands in your way, I can mend it — and if your war needs a breach, I know those ways too.
A rare virtue in these parts.
Looked at another way, you make enemies faster than debts.
I trained as a surgeon in the city's infirmary, learning to stitch and set bone for knights and peasants alike. It seemed a noble calling.
Then an agent of the steward's chamber demanded I 'assist' in extracting confessions. I refused at first, but the threats to my reputation and family left me no choice.
What I did that night haunts me; my practice fell apart and I fled. Now I wander and patch wounds for coin, trying to bury the memory under more opium than skill.
If you need a surgeon who knows how to mend men after raids or sieges, I'll do it for fair pay. I can be discreet.
Trained surgeon, ruined by a single night of shame and blackmail. I still stitch wounds — I just don't speak much of my past.
The state makes victims of many.
You betrayed your Oath. That speaks for itself.
My father was a minor lord and a man-at-arms. When he fell in battle, a neighbouring steward put me under his ward and pressed a marriage upon me to secure the holding.
I refused to be matched with that drunkard and took my father's destrier and the sword he left me. The steward cried theft, but I rode away rather than wear the ring.
I am untested as a captain, but I know how courts and stables run. I seek a leader under whom to learn, ride, and perhaps one day take back what is mine.
I can ride, know courtly etiquette and the duties of stewardship; with training I might become a captain myself.
I fled a forced marriage and now take up the sword. A noble's daughter who would rather learn the sword than the spindle.
You've got spirit — that is certain.
Good luck reclaiming estates by sword alone.
I've been called by many names across the marches — a Breton calls me something, a Flemishman another. The sea has given me as many enemies as the fields.
I've been in a great many fights and I don't count the men I laid in the earth. Ask your innkeeper — he'll tell you: I do well by my sword and rarely by idle boasting.
War is not a courtly tournament; it breaks a man if he treats it as sport. If you have a quarrel, settle it quick and clean, or bring me coin and I'll settle it for you.
I do odds and ends for merchants, lordlings, and anyone who'll pay. I'm not a mercenary tied to banners — I'm a man who sells his arms to the highest honest purse.
A soldier of fortune who has seen coasts and castles. If your campaign needs a steady blade, I'm the sort to stand in the gap.
You speak like a man who's seen more than his share.
You talk of poetry then act like a butcher. No thanks.
My father rode as a man-at-arms for the count; he kept a small holding so he might maintain his horse and kit. We were raised to ride and sit in stirrups before we could read a psalm.

When war came and my father's muster was called, land-grabbers and new lords changed the distribution of fiefs, and our little holding went to a richer retainer. Without a horse, a would-be lancer is just another man.
So I took to serving merchants as an escort, learning to pick my fights and my employers carefully. My hope is to earn coin enough to buy a destrier and do right by my name.
I pick the companies that pay well and keep their word. When I have coin and horse, I will ride again under a banner I can respect.
A former man-at-arms who keeps the equestrian code alive. I can ride, fight from horse or foot, and teach others how to stand their ground.
There's honour in trying to restore what was lost.
Walking behind a cart does not suit a man meant for a saddle.
I served two decades in the county levies, the kind of men who once held borders and paid their taxes in sword-strokes. We kept watch over bridges and passed lances to the young.
But squabbling cupboards in the lord's hall, the replacing of seasoned knights with rich favourites, and a poor steward's taxes broke that order. Men left; the levies fell into disarray.
I won't drink myself to death, so I sell my sword to those worth following. I'm a good drillmaster for foot, and know a thing or two about siege-gear.
I'll join a fair captain who knows how to pay and keep men. I train foot to hold the line and teach serfs how to bear shield and pike when needed.
I am a veteran of the county levies. If you want steady infantry or a man who can turn lads into a line, I am for hire.
We need men who can teach the youth, not just bellow in taverns.
Old soldier stories — I have heard them all.
Me and some lads from the wood thought we'd make our living on the highways rather than scratch the earth. Took to ambush and road-weary merchants, thinking freedom lay in easy coin.
But bandits are a poor lot — drunken, quarrelsome, and easy prey for patrols. Some hanged, some died of pox, many betrayed each other. It wasn't the life I imagined.
I paid to have my name cleared, and now I seek honest work. That said, my hands are no stranger to blade and to the quick business of road-life.
Life's better in the city with coin and work. If your captain needs a man who knows how to take a road and keep it safe — or clear it — I'm your man.
I once ran with highwaymen. Now I prefer coin with fewer gallows nearby. You find such men often enough on the roads.
You went straight, then. Good for you.
Converted bandit — that'll make a good sermon.
What do you want to know? Family? Piss on them. Left home as a child and never regretted it. Let my sword speak for me.
I've fought in many small wars for one lord or another. Comrades turn on you, lords quarrel cheap, and few men share honest bread.
That's all there is to say.
I can fight, repair armor, and do work others shrink from. If you have unpalatable tasks, I do them.
I kill for a living. You need no further explanation if you've been on the road.
You're a cheerful sort. Good day to you.
You may have heard of a preacher in the hills who promised a saintly duke and just rule. Many followed him — peasants, debtors, soldiers tired of the lord's pinch.
We built a refuge and for a time held off small detachments. But leadership and hunger turned our chiefs to levying rents and handing out vengeance. The righteous began to look like common thieves.

When the king sent a larger host and the refuge fell, some were killed, some taken to galleys, and some folded into lordly retinues. I left with what skills I had: ambush, tracking, and the ways of backcountry survival.
I can find a trail, spot ambushes, and lead a caravan away from danger. A regular captain with steady pay would suit me.
Once a rebel, now a pragmatic bladesman. I know less of sermons and more of how to make coin and keep myself alive.
A sad twist of piety into profit.
Heresy and robbery seldom part ways. Keep your distance.
My family had debts, so I signed up under a captain who took anyone with an arm and a willing jaw. I liked the work better than the spinning wheel.
Dressed as a man, of course. Not hard to fool those who look only at a helm and a jerkin. I learned the drill, the watch, the march.
Then one day our commander led us into an ambush. I was routed with the rest. I left the banners and took to wandering with merchants and garrisons, always careful to keep my past to myself.
Merchants hire me as guard; I can also mend gear and teach swordwork. If a captain needs steady hands and discretion, I may be of use.
I once served in a troop as one of the lads; now I wander in search of honest work. You've no doubt met folk like me before.
There is work for the brave and resourceful.
A sad tale of disguise and strife.
My father kept granaries for the town. When rioters burned warehouses and took food, our house was sacked and my father slain for clutching his chest of coin.
We fled the city as refugees and lived by what we could steal from fields and wagons. Hunger makes a thief of honest folk quickly.
I took a sword from a drunken guardsman and learned it suited me well. I don't tell that tale for pity — only to say I can adapt.
I am adaptable. If there is need of a retainer who learns quickly, I can fill the gap.
A merchant's child turned wanderer. I've seen hunger and courts, and I know the world is rarely kind.
The starving must do what they can.
From merchant to marauder — it is a harsh turn.
As a child I ran with a gang of cut-purses in a city squalid with ships and merchants. They called themselves a company but were little more than scavengers.
They used me as a pick-lock and an eye for trouble, then as a blade when I grew. I could perform their dirtiest work for the price of a crust of bread.
When the siege came and the gang was slaughtered or scattered, I took what coin I could and took the road. I prefer to be my own danger now.
I can pick pockets, slip into houses, and do what needs doing quietly. If you have enemies who should vanish quietly, speak plainly and pay well.
An orphan of the alleys who learned how to survive. I do what pays and what keeps the gallows at bay.
A hard life — you have grit, at least.

We volhynian have a tradition. If two people have a dispute, and there's no witnesses, so it all comes down to one man's word against another's, then we let them settle it with swords. If one man doesn't like to fight, he can hire someone else to do the fighting. That's how it works with us. Probably other people do the same, because it's a good tradition.

I am welsh. But for 20 years, I fought for the Empire. Indeed, most welsh my age learned their trade in the legions. We saw no dishonor in it. They fed us well, they paid us well, they respected our courage.

My family was not one of the greatest clans of the welsh, but neither are we among the poorest. When I came of age, my family sent me to join the Routiers. You may have heard of this tradition - for three years we live in the woods and do not eat cooked meat, wear spun cloth, or sleep under a roof, and according to the law we are beasts, not bound by the laws of men.

My uncle - he had a great herd of cows, and in the welsh upcountry that is only kind of wealth we value. But they were taken by his chief herdsman, a man we trusted. So we took up spears to get them back, but my uncle was now poor, but the thief had many kinsmen. Having nothing else to lose, my uncle ordered that even the women of our family take up spears and ride out to fight, and so we did.

I do things in the old way, and so whenever an enemy falls to my spear, I take their head! Let's see - I have Brechtan the Old, Lamaich the Lame -- don't let the names fool you, these were great warriors - Archan the Bull, so many others! A true welsh never boasts, because his deeds are hung over the hearth for all to see. At least that's the way it used to be.

But there's no legions any more. And since that new guy became king, well, he's gotten the young to think that to fight for the Empire is treason. Treason to what? 'welsh'? There is no welsh. Never has been. Just a bunch of quarreling warlords, who'll steal your cows as soon as you turn your back on them.
Some speak well of their time in the Routiers. It is intended to teach you the ways of the woods. But the 'pack' I joined were all rich feral children, playing at being animals.

I am the prince of horsethieves! I have stolen Arabs mares from amid the tents and ridden them across the desert under the moon, I have taken French stallions from their paddocks, the sturdy ponies of the Turks, and the steady geldings of the imperial lancers. But, I'll be the first to admit, it is risky work, so sometimes I do other jobs.

Well now, I am a warrior of the welsh. There is no greater boast than that, I will tell you! But perhaps if you hire me, I can tell you more later about the great names I have slain and the heads I have taken.

I am welsh by birth but I served with the Empire. Many of us did. A brave lord, a captain who cares for his men... What does it matter in which language your oath of fealty is given, as long as you honor it?
